Buy and Sell Stock.desc: Initialize min_price to +infinity: we have seen no day yet, so ANY real price will count as a new minimum.
Initialize best = 0. Not trading is always allowed, so 0 is the worst we can ever do.
Day 0: the loop picks up price = 7, the first price in the array.
Is 7 < inf? Yes — the very first price is always a new minimum.
Record min_price = 7. Day 0 is currently the cheapest day to buy.
Day 1: price = 1. We move to the next day in the scan.
Is 1 < 7? Yes — day 1 is a cheaper place to buy than day 0.
Update min_price = 1. From now on every sell is measured against buying at 1.
Day 2: price = 5. The scan continues with min_price = 1 in hand.
Is 5 < 1? No — 5 is not a new minimum, so we consider selling today instead.
Selling today: 5 - 1 = 4 profit. Is 4 > best (0)? Yes — a better trade.
Update best = 4: buy at 1 (day 1), sell at 5 (day 2).
Day 3: price = 3. Still holding min_price = 1 and best = 4.
Is 3 < 1? No — 3 is not a cheaper buy day.
Selling today: 3 - 1 = 2. Is 2 > 4? No — keep the old best of 4 and move on.
Day 4: price = 6, the highest price we will meet after the minimum.
Is 6 < 1? No — so we test it as a sell day.
Selling today: 6 - 1 = 5. Is 5 > 4? Yes — this beats our previous best trade.
Update best = 5: buy at 1 (day 1), sell at 6 (day 4). This will turn out to be the answer.
Day 5: price = 4, the final day of the scan.
4 is not < 1, so we test selling: 4 - 1 = 3, which does not beat 5. Nothing changes.
The loop is done. Return best = 5 — the maximum profit (buy day 1 at price 1, sell day 4 at price 6).

Rotate Matrix.desc: Read the size: n = 3 for our 3x3 matrix [[1,2,3],[4,5,6],[7,8,9]].
Transpose phase begins. Outer loop takes i = 0 (first row of the upper triangle).
Inner loop starts at j = i+1 = 1, so the diagonal cell (0,0) is skipped and each pair swaps only once.
Swap (0,1) with (1,0): values 2 and 4 trade places across the diagonal.
Inner loop advances to j = 2, still on row i = 0.
Swap (0,2) with (2,0): values 3 and 7 trade places. Row 0 is now [1,4,7] — the old column 0!
Outer loop advances to i = 1: handle the pairs above the diagonal in row 1.
Inner loop starts at j = i+1 = 2 — only one pair left in this row.
Swap (1,2) with (2,1): values 6 and 8 trade places. The transpose is now complete: rows are the old columns.
Outer loop takes i = 2, but range(3, 3) is empty — no cell above the diagonal remains, so the transpose loop ends.
Phase 2 begins: reverse every row. First up is row 0 = [1,4,7].
Row 0 flips left-right: [1,4,7] becomes [7,4,1] — exactly the old first column read bottom-to-top.
Next, row 1 = [2,5,8] steps up for reversal.
Row 1 flips: [2,5,8] becomes [8,5,2]. The center cell 5 stays put, as it must for odd n.
Finally row 2 = [3,6,9] is taken by the loop.
Row 2 flips: [3,6,9] becomes [9,6,3]. The function ends — matrix is now [[7,4,1],[8,5,2],[9,6,3]], the 90-degree clockwise rotation.

Merge Overlapping Intervals.desc: Sort by start: the input [[2,6],[1,3],[8,10],[15,18]] becomes [[1,3],[2,6],[8,10],[15,18]], so any overlapping pair now sits side by side.
Start with an empty answer list; we will grow it block by block.
First interval: start = 1, end = 3 is unpacked from the sorted list.
merged is still empty, so the overlap test short-circuits to False — nothing to absorb into.
Open the first block: append [1,3]. merged = [[1,3]].
Overlap test: is 2 <= 3 (the open block's end)? Yes — [2,6] overlaps [1,3] on the points 2 and 3.
Absorb: the open block's end becomes max(3, 6) = 6. merged = [[1,6]] — one block now covers both intervals.
Overlap test: is 8 <= 6? No — there is a real gap (points 7 and below 8 are uncovered), and since starts only grow, block [1,6] is sealed forever.
Open a new block: append [8,10]. merged = [[1,6],[8,10]].
Overlap test: is 15 <= 10? No — another gap, so [8,10] is sealed too.
The sweep is done — return [[1,6],[8,10],[15,18]]: three disjoint blocks covering exactly the input's points.

Merge Two Sorted Arrays Without Extra Sp.desc: i = m - 1 = 2 points at nums1's last REAL value, 3. (nums1 = [1,2,3,0,0,0], nums2 = [2,5,6].)
j = n - 1 = 2 points at nums2's last value, 6.
k = 5 is the last slot of nums1 — the write position where the largest value will land.
j = 2 >= 0: nums2 still has unplaced values, so enter the loop.
Compare tails: nums1[2] = 3 vs nums2[2] = 6. Is 3 > 6? No — nums2's 6 is the largest remaining value overall.
Write 6 into slot k = 5: nums1 becomes [1,2,3,0,0,6]. The biggest value is now locked in the last slot.
Consume nums2's 6: j drops to 1, now pointing at 5.
Slot 5 is filled, so the write position moves left: k = 4.
j = 1 >= 0: keep merging.
Compare tails: nums1[2] = 3 vs nums2[1] = 5. Is 3 > 5? No — 5 wins the slot.
Write 5 into slot k = 4: nums1 becomes [1,2,3,0,5,6].
Consume the 5: j drops to 0, pointing at nums2's 2.
Write position moves left: k = 3.
j = 0 >= 0: nums2 still holds one value (2), keep going.
Compare tails: nums1[2] = 3 vs nums2[0] = 2. Is 3 > 2? YES — for the first time nums1's element wins.
Write nums1's own 3 into slot k = 3: nums1 becomes [1,2,3,3,5,6]. Note the read position i = 2 is LEFT of the write position k = 3 — no unread value is harmed.
Consume nums1's 3: i drops to 1, pointing at the 2.
Write position moves left: k = 2.
j = 0 >= 0: one nums2 value (the 2) still needs a home.
Compare: nums1[1] = 2 vs nums2[0] = 2. Is 2 > 2? No — a tie goes to the else branch, placing nums2's copy.
Write nums2's 2 into slot k = 2: nums1 becomes [1,2,2,3,5,6] (it already held a 2 there, so no visible change — but logically the slot now belongs to nums2's 2).
Consume nums2's last value: j drops to -1 — nums2 is fully placed.
Write position moves to k = 1 (it will not be used again).
j = -1, so the loop exits. nums1's untouched front [1,2] was already sorted and in place — final answer: [1,2,2,3,5,6].

Find Duplicate Number.desc: Both runners start at the chain's head: slow = nums[0] = 1. Think of each index as a node whose arrow goes to nums[index].
fast also starts at nums[0] = 1. The chain from index 0 is: 0 -> 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 4 -> 2 -> 4 ... (a tail, then a loop between 2 and 4).
Phase 1 begins. Because slow and fast start EQUAL, the equality check must happen after they move — hence the do-while shape.
Hare hops twice: first nums[1] = 3, then nums[3] = 2, so fast = 2.
Met yet? slow = 3, fast = 2 — not equal, loop again.
Tortoise hops once more: slow = nums[3] = 2.
Hare hops twice: nums[2] = 4, then nums[4] = 2, so fast = 2. The hare has lapped the loop 2 -> 4 -> 2.
Met yet? slow = 2 and fast = 2 — YES, the runners meet inside the cycle (at node 2, though in general the meeting node need not be the entrance).
Phase 1 ends: a cycle definitely exists and fast sits at the meeting node.
Phase 2: teleport slow back to the head, slow = nums[0] = 1. fast stays at the meeting node 2. Now both will walk ONE hop at a time.
slow = 1, fast = 2 — different, so walk both runners.
slow = 3, fast = 4 — still different, walk again.
fast hops: nums[4] = 2. Both runners now stand on node 2.
slow == fast == 2, so the loop exits. They met exactly at the cycle's entrance — the node with two incoming arrows (from indices 3 and 4).
Return slow = 2: the duplicated number. Indices 3 and 4 both hold the value 2, which is what created the cycle entrance.

Repeat and Missing Number.desc: n = 5: the array [3,1,2,5,3] should have been a shuffle of 1..5.
Closed form: expected_sum = 5*6/2 = 15 — what the sum WOULD be with no repeat/missing.
Closed form: expected_sq = 5*6*11/6 = 55 — the ideal sum of squares 1+4+9+16+25.
Initialize the running sum of the REAL array to 0.
Initialize the running sum of squares to 0. One pass will fill both totals.
Last element: x = 3 again (index 4) — the repeat contributes to the totals a second time; that is exactly the 'signal' the math will decode.
actual_sum = 11 + 3 = 14 (vs 15 expected — the missing 4 and extra 3 net out to -1).
actual_sq = 39 + 9 = 48 (vs 55 expected). The accumulation pass is done.
Equation 1: diff = 14 - 15 = -1, and algebraically diff = R - M. (Indeed 3 - 4 = -1.)
Square-sum clue: sq_diff = 48 - 55 = -7 = R² - M² = (R - M)(R + M).
Divide out the known factor: total = -7 // -1 = 7 = R + M. Two linear equations, two unknowns — solvable!
Return [3, 4]: 3 is the number appearing twice, 4 is the number that vanished. One pass, O(1) space.

Inversion Count.desc: Kick off: call sort_count on the whole array [5,3,2,4]. It will sort a copy and count inversions along the way.
Inside sort_count([5,3,2,4]): length 4 > 1, so this is not a base case — we must split.
mid = 4 // 2 = 2: the halves will be [5,3] and [2,4].
Recurse into the LEFT half [5,3]. (We now follow that inner call.)
Inside sort_count([5,3]): mid = 1, splitting into [5] and [3].
Both sub-calls hit the base case: sort_count([5]) returns ([5], 0) and sort_count([3]) returns ([3], 0) — single elements hold no inversions.
Merge [5] and [3]: i = 0, j = 0, inv starts at 0 + 0 = 0. Both lists have unread values, enter the loop.
Compare fronts: left[0] = 5 <= right[0] = 3? No — the right value must go first, which means it is out of order relative to the left half.
Place 3 into merged before 5.
Count the batch: 3 jumped over len(left) - i = 1 - 0 = 1 remaining left element (the 5). inv = 1 — that is the inversion pair (5,3).
Consume the 3: j = 1, right half exhausted, the while loop ends.
Flush the leftover left values: merged becomes [3,5].
sort_count([5,3]) returns ([3,5], 1) to the outer call: the left half is sorted and contributed 1 inversion.
Back in the outer call: recurse into the RIGHT half [2,4]. It splits into [2] and [4]; the merge takes 2 then 4 with no counting (2 <= 4), returning ([2,4], 0).
Combine the halves' banked counts: inv = 1 + 0 = 1. Now count the CROSS inversions while merging [3,5] with [2,4].
Merge loop: i = 0 (on 3), j = 0 (on 2), merged = []. Both halves have values, so compare fronts.
left[0] = 3 <= right[0] = 2? No — 2 must be placed first, jumping over the whole remaining left half.
Place 2 into merged: merged = [2].
Batch count: 2 is smaller than BOTH remaining left values (3 and 5), so inv += 2 - 0 = 2, giving inv = 3. Those are the pairs (3,2) and (5,2) — certified without comparing 5 to 2 directly!
Consume the 2: j = 1, now pointing at 4.
Next comparison: left[0] = 3 <= right[1] = 4? Yes — 3 is in correct order, no inversion involved.
Place 3: merged = [2,3]. Taking from the left never counts anything.
Consume the 3: i = 1, now pointing at 5.
Compare: left[1] = 5 <= right[1] = 4? No — 4 must be placed before 5.
Place 4: merged = [2,3,4].
Batch count: 4 jumps over len(left) - i = 2 - 1 = 1 remaining left element (the 5). inv = 4 — the final pair (5,4).
Consume the 4: j = 2 — the right half is exhausted, so the merge loop exits.
Flush the leftover left values: the 5 joins the end, merged = [2,3,4,5].
The top-level sort_count returns ([2,3,4,5], 4): a fully sorted array and 4 total inversions (1 from inside [5,3] + 3 cross pairs).
Back at the outer function: total = 4 — the inversion count of [5,3,2,4]. Return it.

Search in a 2D Matrix.desc: Read dimensions: m = 3 rows, n = 4 columns. Target is 16. Flattened row-by-row, the matrix is one sorted list of 12 values.
Set the virtual search window over flat indices: lo = 0, hi = 3*4 - 1 = 11. Virtual index k maps to cell (k // 4, k % 4).
Window check: 0 <= 11, so the window is non-empty — search on.
Un-flatten index 5: row = 5 // 4 = 1, col = 5 % 4 = 1 — so val = matrix[1][1] = 11.
Is 11 < 16? Yes — 16 (if present) must sit AFTER flat index 5, since everything up to index 5 is <= 11.
Discard the left half: lo = 6. The window is now flat indices 6..11 (cells from matrix[1][2] onward).
Un-flatten index 8: row = 8 // 4 = 2, col = 8 % 4 = 0 — so val = matrix[2][0] = 23.
Is 23 == 16? No — not an exact match, so decide which half to discard.
Is 23 < 16? No — 23 is too big, so 16 must lie BEFORE flat index 8.
Discard the right half: hi = 7. The window shrinks to flat indices 6..7 — just cells matrix[1][2] and matrix[1][3].
Un-flatten index 6: row = 6 // 4 = 1, col = 6 % 4 = 2 — so val = matrix[1][2] = 16.
Is 16 == 16? YES — the target is found at cell (1, 2) after only three probes.
Return True. Binary search inspected just 3 of the 12 cells — that is the power of treating the matrix as one sorted list.

Pow(x, n).desc: Call my_pow(x=2.0, n=10). The exponent 10 in binary is 1010 (shown as the array, most-significant bit on the left). We will read it right to left, squaring as we go.
n=10 is already non-negative, so exp = 10. (A negative n would flip to |n| here and we would take a reciprocal at the very end.)
result starts at 1.0, the empty product x^0. Powers of x whose bit is 1 will be folded into it.
base starts as x = 2.0. It will square every round: 2 -> 4 -> 16 -> 256, i.e. x^1, x^2, x^4, x^8 — one power per bit position.
Round 1: exp=10 > 0, enter the loop. We are looking at the lowest bit of 1010 (index 3 in the display).
10 % 2 == 0: the lowest bit is 0, so x^1 = 2.0 is NOT part of the answer. Skip the fold.
Square the base: 2.0 * 2.0 = 4.0. base now represents x^2, the power owned by the next bit.
exp = 10 // 2 = 5 (binary 101). The processed 0-bit is discarded.
Round 2: exp=5 > 0. We are now on the bit at display index 2, which is 1.
5 % 2 == 1: this bit is set, so the current power x^2 = 4.0 belongs in the answer.
Fold it in: result = 1.0 * 4.0 = 4.0. So far the answer holds x^2.
Square again: 4.0 * 4.0 = 16.0. base now represents x^4.
exp = 5 // 2 = 2 (binary 10). Two bits remain.
Round 3: exp=2 > 0. Now on the bit at display index 1, which is 0.
2 % 2 == 0: bit is 0, so x^4 = 16.0 is skipped — 10 = 8 + 2 has no 4 in it.
Square: 16.0 * 16.0 = 256.0. base now represents x^8.
exp = 2 // 2 = 1 (binary 1). One bit left — the most significant one.
Round 4: exp=1 > 0. Final bit, display index 0, value 1.
1 % 2 == 1: the 8s bit is set, so x^8 = 256.0 is part of the answer.
Fold: result = 4.0 * 256.0 = 1024.0 — that is x^2 * x^8 = x^10. The answer is complete.
base squares one last time to 65536.0 (x^16). It is never used again — harmless leftover work.
exp = 1 // 2 = 0. Every bit of the exponent has been consumed.
exp=0, so 0 > 0 is false — the loop exits after just 4 rounds instead of 10 multiplications.
n=10 is not negative, so no reciprocal is owed — skip straight to the return.
Return result = 1024.0. Binary exponentiation computed 2^10 with 4 squarings and 2 folds.

Majority Element (> n/2 times).desc: Call majority_element([2,2,1,1,1,2,2]). n=7, so the majority needs at least 4 occurrences — the 2s have exactly 4.
No candidate yet: candidate = None. The first element will be adopted immediately because count is 0.
count = 0 — it measures the current candidate's surplus of for-votes over against-votes.
i=0: num = 2, the first voter steps up.
count is 0, so adopt 2 as the candidate — with no active candidate, the current value takes the seat.
num (2) equals candidate (2): a vote FOR. count rises to 1.
i=1: num = 2 again — another supporter of the current candidate.
2 == candidate, so count grows to 2. The candidate has a 2-vote lead.
i=2: num = 1 — a rival value appears for the first time.
1 != candidate (2): a vote AGAINST. One 2-vote and this 1-vote cancel; count drops to 1.
i=3: num = 1 — another rival vote arrives.
Cancellation again: count falls to 0. The candidate 2 is now fully neutralized — the next element can seize the seat.
i=4: num = 1 arrives while the seat is vacant (count = 0).
count == 0, so 1 takes over as the new candidate — the algorithm forgets 2 entirely.
1 == candidate, so count = 1. The usurper holds a 1-vote lead.
i=5: num = 2 — the real majority strikes back against candidate 1.
2 != 1: cancellation drops count to 0. Candidate 1 is neutralized after holding the seat for just one element.
i=6: the final element, num = 2, arrives with the seat vacant again.
count == 0, so 2 is re-adopted as candidate. Its surplus vote (4 twos vs 3 ones) guaranteed it could not stay buried.
2 == candidate: count = 1. The scan ends with 2 holding the seat.
Return candidate = 2. Every cancellation killed one 2-vote AND one rival vote, and 2 had more votes than all rivals combined — so it had to survive.

Majority Element II (> n/3 times).desc: Call majority_element_ii([1,1,1,3,3,2,2,2]). n=8, floor(8/3)=2, so winners need at least 3 occurrences: 1 has 3, 2 has 3, 3 has only 2.
Slot 1 starts vacant: cand1 = None with count1 = 0.
Slot 2 starts vacant too. Two slots suffice because at most two values can exceed n/3.
i=0: num = 1. It matches neither slot (both None-with-0), so the vacancy checks will fire.
count1 == 0, so slot 1 adopts 1: cand1 = 1, count1 = 1.
i=1: num = 1 again — it matches slot 1's candidate.
Vote for slot 1: count1 rises to 2.
i=2: num = 1 for a third time — slot 1 keeps strengthening.
count1 = 3. Slot 2 is still vacant; no cancellation has happened yet.
i=3: num = 3 — a brand-new value. It fails 'num == cand1' (3 != 1), fails 'num == cand2', fails 'count1 == 0' (count1 is 3)...
...but count2 == 0, so slot 2 adopts 3: cand2 = 3, count2 = 1.
i=4: num = 3 — it matches slot 2's candidate this time.
Vote for slot 2: count2 = 2. State: slot1 = (1, 3 votes), slot2 = (3, 2 votes).
i=5: num = 2 — a third distinct value while BOTH slots are occupied. The else branch fires: a (1, 3, 2) triple will be cancelled.
Cancel one vote from slot 1: count1 drops to 2. One occurrence of 1 is 'paired off' against this 2.
And one from slot 2: count2 drops to 1. A triple of three DIFFERENT values (1, 3, 2) has been deleted — no true winner can lose its > n/3 status this way.
i=6: num = 2 again — still matches neither slot, and both counters are positive, so another triple dies.
count1 falls to 1 — the 1s are being whittled down by the stream of 2s.
count2 falls to 0 — slot 2's candidate 3 is fully cancelled and the slot becomes vacant.
i=7: num = 2, the final element. It matches neither candidate, count1 is 1 (not 0), but count2 IS 0...
...so slot 2 adopts 2: cand2 = 2, count2 = 1. Pass 1 ends with candidates 1 and 2 — the value 3 was correctly squeezed out.
PASS 2 begins. Surviving candidates are only POSSIBLE winners (in [1,2,3] two would survive yet neither qualifies), so each must be verified by a real count.
threshold = 8 // 3 = 2. A verified winner must appear STRICTLY more than 2 times.
Verify cand1 = 1 first.
nums.count(1) = 3, and 3 > 2 — candidate 1 is a confirmed winner. result = [1].
Now verify cand2 = 2.
nums.count(2) = 3 > 2 — candidate 2 is also confirmed. result = [1, 2]. (Had 3 survived instead, its count of 2 would have failed here.)
Return [1, 2] — both values appear 3 times, strictly more than n/3 = 2. Done in O(n) time with O(1) extra space.

Grid Unique Paths.desc: Call unique_paths(m=4, n=4): a 4x4 grid, robot at the top-left (0,0), target at the bottom-right (3,3), moving only down or right.
total = 4 + 4 - 2 = 6: every path makes exactly 3 down-moves and 3 right-moves, six moves in all — only their order varies.
pick = min(3, 3) = 3: we will choose which 3 of the 6 move-slots are downs, i.e. compute C(6, 3). Picking the smaller side keeps the loop short.
result = 1, which is C(3, 0) — the empty choice. Each loop round will grow it into C(4,1), C(5,2), then C(6,3).
Loop round 1: i = 1. We upgrade result from C(3,0) to C(4,1).
result = 1 * (6 - 3 + 1) // 1 = 4. Indeed C(4, 1) = 4. Multiplying BEFORE the // keeps the division exact.
Loop round 2: i = 2. Next upgrade: C(4,1) -> C(5,2).
result = 4 * (6 - 3 + 2) // 2 = 4 * 5 // 2 = 10 = C(5, 2). The product 4*5 of two consecutive integers is guaranteed divisible by 2.
Loop round 3: i = 3, the final round since pick = 3. Upgrade C(5,2) -> C(6,3).
result = 10 * (6 - 3 + 3) // 3 = 10 * 6 // 3 = 20 = C(6, 3). The binomial coefficient is complete.
range(1, 4) is exhausted (i would be 4 > pick), so the loop ends after just 3 multiply-divide rounds.
Return 20: the 4x4 grid has exactly 20 distinct monotone paths — no table, no recursion, just C(6,3).

Reverse Pairs.desc: Call reverse_pairs([6, 1, 2]). Expected pairs: (0,1) since 6 > 2*1 = 2, and (0,2) since 6 > 2*2 = 4 — the answer should be 2.
Hand the whole array to the recursive helper sort_count, which returns (sorted list, pair count).
Outer call: arr = [6, 1, 2], so n = 3. This segment is big enough to need splitting.
n = 3 is greater than 1, so we do not hit the base case — fall through to the split.
mid = 3 // 2 = 1: the halves are arr[:1] = [6] and arr[1:] = [1, 2].
Recurse on the left half [6].
Base case: [6] has one element — already sorted, zero pairs inside. Returns ([6], 0).
Back in the outer call: left = [6], count_left = 0. Now recurse on the right half [1, 2].
Inner call on [1, 2]: n = 2, mid = 1 — halves [1] and [2], both of which will hit the base case and return 0 pairs.
Inner call: count = 0 + 0 — single elements can hide no pairs.
Inner cross-count: x = 1 versus right = [2]. Is 1 > 2*2 = 4? No — the while never runs, j stays 0, so no cross pairs here.
count += 0: still 0 cross pairs inside [1, 2], as expected for an ascending pair.
Inner merge: compare fronts 1 <= 2 — take 1 from the left; after that a = 1 ends the merge loop.
Right leftover [2] is appended: merged = [1, 2] — the inner segment is sorted.
Inner call returns ([1, 2], 0) to the outer call's 'right' slot.
Outer call resumes: left = [6], right = [1, 2], count = 0 + 0. All remaining pairs must CROSS the halves.
Cross-count begins: pointer j = 0 will sweep the sorted right half [1, 2] exactly once, never moving backward.
First (and only) left value: x = 6. Every original index in the left half precedes every index in the right half, so any hit is a valid (i, j) pair.
Check right[0] = 1: is 6 > 2*1 = 2? Yes — this right value forms a reverse pair with x = 6.
j advances to 1. Key monotonicity: any LATER (larger) left value would beat 2*1 too, so j never needs to look back at index 0.
Check right[1] = 2: is 6 > 2*2 = 4? Yes — a second reverse pair for x = 6.
j advances to 2, which equals len(right) — the sweep has consumed the whole right half.
count += j adds 2: the first j = 2 right values (1 and 2) each pair with x = 6. count is now 2.
Counting done — now merge so the parent level would see a sorted segment. Compare fronts: 6 <= 1 is false, so the right half's 1 exits first.
Take 1 from the right: merged = [1], b = 1.
Next comparison 6 <= 2 is false again, so take 2 as well: merged = [1, 2], b = 2 — the right half is exhausted and the merge loop ends.
Leftover left half [6] is appended in one go: merged = [1, 2, 6], fully sorted.
The outer sort_count returns ([1, 2, 6], 2): a sorted array plus the 2 reverse pairs it counted.
Back at the top level: the sorted list is discarded (we only sorted to enable counting) and total = 2.
Return 2 — matching the hand check: pairs (0,1) and (0,2) of the original [6, 1, 2].

Four Sum.desc: Call four_sum([1, 0, -1, 0, -2, 2], target=0). We must find every unique quadruplet of values summing to 0.
Sort a copy: nums = [-2, -1, 0, 0, 1, 2]. Sorting powers both the two-pointer search and neighbor-based duplicate skipping.
n = 6 — just enough room for quadruplets (we need at least 4 elements).
result starts empty; quadruplets will be appended already sorted internally.
i = 0: first number is nums[0] = -2. The loop stops at n-4 = 2 so three slots always remain after i.
j = 1: second number is nums[1] = -1. Fixed prefix so far: (-2, -1).
need = 0 - (-2) - (-1) = 3: the last two numbers must sum to exactly 3.
Two pointers bracket the remaining window: left = 2 (value 0), right = 5 (value 2).
pair = nums[2] + nums[5] = 0 + 2 = 2.
2 < 3: the pair undershoots. Only a bigger left value can help (right already holds the maximum), so left moves to 3.
pair = nums[3] + nums[5] = 0 + 2 = 2 again — the duplicate 0 gives the same undershoot.
Still 2 < 3, so left advances to 4 (value 1).
pair = nums[4] + nums[5] = 1 + 2 = 3 — exactly what we need!
Record the first quadruplet: [-2, -1, 1, 2]. result = [[-2, -1, 1, 2]].
Step past the used third number: left = 5.
Step past the used fourth number: right = 4. The pointers have crossed.
left=5 < right=4 is false — the window for (i=0, j=1) is exhausted with one quadruplet found.
j = 2: second number becomes nums[2] = 0. Fixed prefix: (-2, 0).
need = 0 - (-2) - 0 = 2: the last two must now sum to 2.
Fresh window: left = 3 (value 0), right = 5 (value 2).
pair = nums[3] + nums[5] = 0 + 2 = 2 — an immediate hit.
Record [-2, 0, 0, 2] — it legally uses BOTH zeros, which live at different indices (2 and 3).
left moves to 4; right will move to 4 as well — the window is about to close.
right = 4. Now left == right, so no third-number/fourth-number pair remains.

Find Starting Point of Loop.desc: fast moves two steps: index 2 -> 3 (value -4) -> and the tail's link sends it back to index 1 (value 2). The hare has just wrapped around the loop for the first time.
slow is at index 2 and fast is at index 1 — still not the same node, so no collision.
fast is the node 2 (index 1), fast.next is the node 0 — both exist, so we iterate once more. Inside a cycle this check can never fail, which is exactly why a cycle is detected.
Iteration 3: slow moves from index 2 to index 3 (value -4).
fast jumps two: index 1 -> 2 -> 3, landing on value -4 as well.
slow == fast is True — both pointers are the SAME node object at index 3. A collision proves a cycle exists. Note the collision point (index 3) is NOT the loop start (index 1).

Now the second phase. Floyd's maths: if the distance from head to the loop start is L and the collision sits D nodes into the loop, then L and D are complementary — walking L steps from the head and L steps from the collision lands both on the loop start.
slow = head resets the tortoise to index 0 (value 3). fast stays parked at the collision, index 3.
while slow != fast: index 0 vs index 3 — different, so enter phase two. From here BOTH pointers move at the SAME speed, one step each.
slow = slow.next moves from index 0 to index 1 (value 2).
fast = fast.next — only one step now — and the tail link carries it from index 3 back to index 1 (value 2).
Check again: slow and fast are both the node at index 1, so slow != fast is False and the loop ends after exactly 1 step, matching L = 1.
Where they meet is, by Floyd's theorem, precisely the first node of the cycle — the node that two different pointers (index 0's chain and index 3's back-edge) both feed into.
return slow — the node holding 2 at index 1. Total cost: O(n) time and O(1) extra space, with no hash set needed.

node moves from the root down into node_a. From now on we are describing the prefix "a".

root.cnt_prefix goes from 1 to 2: the trie now stores two words in total.

The word "ac" ends here, so node_ac.cnt_end becomes 1. Insertion is finished.

The loop takes ch = 'a' and checks root.children: 'a' IS present, so we do not return None and the walk continues.
node descends into node_a, the node for the prefix "a".

Sudoku Solver.desc: We start solveSudoku on a board that is already filled except for three dots: (0,0), (0,1) and (8,0). Line 43 kicks off the recursive solve().
solve() begins its scan for the first empty cell. The outer loop sets i=0, so we are looking at row 0: ['.', '.', '4', '6', '7', '8', '9', '1', '2'].
The inner loop sets j=0, so the scan is standing on cell (0,0).
board[0][0] is '.', so this cell is empty — this is the cell we must fill before anything else.
We start guessing. The first candidate character is c='1'; we will ask isValid whether '1' can legally sit at (0,0).
isValid(0, 0, '1') is called. Inside it, one loop with counter i=0..8 does three jobs at once: checks column 0, checks row 0, and checks the top-left 3x3 box.
At i=2 the column test board[2][0] reads '1' — column 0 already owns a 1 (third row starts with 1). So '1' clashes.
isValid returns False: c='1' is rejected for (0,0). Back in solve(), the if on line 28 is false, so nothing is placed.
Next candidate: c='2'. isValid(0, 0, '2') runs again from i=0.
Column 0 and row 0 have no 2, but at i=5 the box test looks at box_row=3*(0//3)+5//3=1 and box_col=3*(0//3)+5%3=2, i.e. board[1][2]='2'. The top-left 3x3 box already contains a 2.
isValid returns False again — '2' is rejected for (0,0).
Third candidate: c='3'. Column 0 holds {6,1,8,4,7,9,2}, row 0 holds {4,6,7,8,9,1,2}, box 0 holds {4,6,7,2,1,9,8} — none of them is a 3.
All nine iterations of the checking loop finished without a clash, so isValid(0, 0, '3') returns True. Careful: legal right now does not mean correct forever.
Line 32 recurses: solve() is called again (depth 2) to fill the rest of the board on top of the guess '3'.
The new solve() rescans from (0,0). That cell now holds '3', so it moves on to j=1 where board[0][1] is '.' — the next empty cell.
Candidate c='1' for (0,1): isValid scans column 1 and hits board[5][1]='1', so '1' is rejected.
Candidate c='2' for (0,1): column 1 also contains board[4][1]='2', so '2' is rejected too.
Candidate c='3': at i=0 the row test board[0][0] reads '3' — the 3 we just guessed one cell to the left. Line 11 returns False, so '3' is rejected.
The loop keeps going: '4' clashes with board[0][2]='4' in the row, '6','7','8','9' all appear in row 0 as well, and '5' clashes with board[3][1]='5' down column 1. Every one of the nine digits fails.
Dead end. Cell (0,1) has no legal digit, so this solve() returns False on line 38 — the board as it stands cannot be completed.
Back in the depth-1 frame, the call on line 32 evaluated to False, so we fall into the else branch.
BACKTRACK: board[0][0] = '.' undoes the guess. This single line is what makes backtracking work — we erase the bad choice and keep trying other candidates.
The candidate loop resumes at c='4'. isValid fails fast: at i=2 the row test board[0][2] reads '4'.
Recurse again into solve() at depth 2, this time on top of the guess '5'.
Scanning again, (0,0) is filled, and board[0][1] = '.' is the next empty cell.
'1' still clashes with board[5][1]='1' and '2' with board[4][1]='2'. Then c='3' is tested — and this time row 0 starts with '5', not '3'.
isValid(0, 1, '3') walks all nine i values with no clash in column 1, row 0 or box 0, so it returns True.
Recurse to depth 3. Only one dot is left on the whole board: (8,0).
The scan runs through rows 0..7 finding no dots, then reaches i=8, j=0 where board[8][0] == '.'.
c='1' clashes with board[2][0]='1' in column 0; c='2' clashes with board[8][3]='2' in row 8. Next up is c='3'.
For c='3': column 0 = {5,6,1,8,4,7,9,2}, row 8 = {4,5,2,8,6,1,7,9}, bottom-left box = {9,6,1,2,8,7,4,5}. No 3 in any of them, so isValid returns True.
board[8][0] = '3'. Every cell on the board is now filled.
Recurse one last time (depth 4) to verify there is nothing left to do.
The double loop finds no '.' at all, so it falls through to line 40 and returns True — the base case that means 'solved'.
That True flows back up: each waiting frame sees `if solve(): return True` and returns True immediately, so no placed digit is ever undone.
solve() finishes with True and solveSudoku returns None — the answer lives in `board`, which was mutated in place. Final row 0 = 534678912 and row 8 = 345286179.

Implement Stack Using Array.desc: Constructor: we allocate a fixed array of 1000 slots, all pre-filled with -1. The first six slots are shown; -1 just means 'nothing meaningful here yet'.
top_idx = -1 marks an empty stack: there is no valid index yet, so -1 is the 'one before the first slot' sentinel.
push(10): first we move the pointer up, top_idx goes from -1 to 0.
arr[0] = 10 writes the value at the new top. The stack now reads [10] from bottom to top.
push(20): top_idx moves 0 -> 1.
arr[1] = 20. Stack from bottom to top is now [10, 20]; both operations were O(1) with no shifting.
push(30): top_idx moves 1 -> 2.
arr[2] = 30. Stack is [10, 20, 30] with 30 on top.
top(): the guard asks whether top_idx == -1. It is 2, so the stack is not empty and we skip the -1 return.
top() returns arr[2] = 30. Nothing was removed — top only peeks.
pop(): again the empty guard. top_idx = 2 is not -1, so there is something to remove.
val = arr[2] = 30. We grab the top value BEFORE moving the pointer, otherwise we would lose it.
top_idx goes 2 -> 1. Notice arr[2] still physically holds 30, but it is now outside the stack — logically deleted.
pop() returns 30. Stack is [10, 20].
size() returns top_idx + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2, because indices 0 and 1 are in use.
push(99): top_idx moves 1 -> 2 again — straight back onto the slot the old 30 was living in.
arr[2] = 99 overwrites the stale 30. This is why leaving garbage behind on pop is harmless: the next push always overwrites it.
pop() again: val = arr[2] = 99.
top_idx drops back to 1.
pop() returns 99 — the most recently pushed value, exactly the LIFO rule.
pop() once more: val = arr[1] = 20.
top_idx drops to 0; the stack is now just [10].
pop() returns 20, leaving only the bottom element 10 in the stack.
Final pop(): val = arr[0] = 10.
top_idx goes 0 -> -1, which is the empty sentinel again.
isEmpty() returns top_idx == -1, which is now True.
pop() on the empty stack: the guard top_idx == -1 is True this time.
So pop() returns the sentinel -1 instead of crashing on a negative index. Final state: empty stack, size 0.

Implement Stack Using Queue.desc: Constructor: self.q is an empty deque. A deque gives O(1) append at the back and O(1) popleft at the front — the two queue operations we are allowed to use.
push(1): append 1 to the back. q = [1].
The rotation loop runs len(q) - 1 = 0 times, so with a single element there is nothing to rotate — 1 is already at the front.
push(2): append 2. q = [1, 2] — but a stack must hand back 2 first, and the queue front is 1. We have to fix that.
The loop will run len(q) - 1 = 1 time: rotate every element that was already there behind the new one.
Rotation 1: popleft() takes 1 off the front and append puts it at the back. q = [2, 1]. Now the newest element, 2, is at the front.
push(3): append 3. q = [2, 1, 3].
len(q) - 1 = 2, so two rotations are needed to bring 3 to the front.
Rotation 1: popleft() = 2, appended to the back. q = [1, 3, 2].
Rotation 2: popleft() = 1, appended to the back. q = [3, 2, 1] — the queue now lists elements newest-to-oldest, exactly stack order.
The loop counter is exhausted, so push(3) ends. Cost of this push was O(n); the payoff is that pop and top become O(1).
top(): the queue is not empty, so we skip the -1 guard.
top() returns q[0] = 3 without removing anything — the last value pushed, which is what a stack's top must be.
pop(): the emptiness guard `if not self.q` is False because the deque holds 3 items.
popleft() removes and returns 3. q = [2, 1] and 2 — the next-newest — is automatically the new front.
push(4): append 4. q = [2, 1, 4].
Rotation 1 of 2: popleft() = 2 goes to the back. q = [1, 4, 2].
Rotation 2 of 2: popleft() = 1 goes to the back. q = [4, 2, 1]; 4 is at the front as required.
pop() returns popleft() = 4. q = [2, 1].
pop() again returns 2. q = [1]. The pops are coming out 3, 4, 2 — reverse of the push order 1, 2, 3, 4 minus what we already removed.
top() peeks q[0] = 1, the only element left.
pop() returns 1 and empties the deque. q = [].
pop() on the empty deque: `if not self.q` is now True.
So pop() returns -1 instead of raising IndexError.
empty() returns len(self.q) == 0, which is True. Whole run: pushes cost O(n) each, every read cost O(1).

Implement Queue Using Stack.desc: Constructor: input_stack = [] will receive every push. Think of it as the 'in' tray.
output_stack = [] is where elements go to be served, held in reversed (queue) order. Right end of each list is its top.
push(1): append to input_stack. input = [1].
push(2): input = [1, 2]. Top of input is 2, which is the WRONG end for a queue — we will fix it lazily.
push(3): input = [1, 2, 3]. Each push is O(1); no reordering happens yet.
peek(): output_stack is empty, so `if not self.output_stack` is True and we must transfer.
The while loop drains input_stack one pop at a time.
Transfer 1: input_stack.pop() gives 3 (its top) and it is pushed onto output. input = [1, 2], output = [3].
Transfer 2: pop 2, push it. input = [1], output = [3, 2].
Transfer 3: pop 1, push it. input = [], output = [3, 2, 1]. Popping a stack into a stack reverses the order, so the OLDEST element 1 is now on top of output.
input_stack is empty, so the while loop ends.
peek() returns output_stack[-1] = 1 — the front of the queue, exactly the first value we pushed.
pop(): this time `if not self.output_stack` is False (it holds three items), so NO transfer happens.
pop() returns output_stack.pop() = 1 and output becomes [3, 2]. Queue order so far: 1 served first. Correct FIFO.
push(4): it goes to input_stack, NOT output. input = [4], output = [3, 2].
pop(): output_stack is non-empty, so we must not transfer — if we dumped 4 on top of output now, 4 would jump the queue ahead of 2 and 3.
pop() returns 2. output = [3]. Order served: 1, 2.
pop() again: output = [3] is still non-empty, so no transfer.
pop() returns 3. output = []. Order served: 1, 2, 3.
pop() again: NOW output_stack is empty, so the transfer branch finally runs — this is the lazy refill.
The while loop sees input_stack = [4], so there is one element to move.
Move it: output_stack.append(input_stack.pop()) makes input = [] and output = [4].
The guard on line 19 checks output_stack again; it holds 4, so we do not return -1.
pop() returns 4. output = []. Every element was moved exactly twice overall, which is why pop is O(1) amortized.
empty() returns `not input_stack and not output_stack` = True, because both stacks are finally empty.

Min Stack.desc: Constructor: self.stack = []. Each entry will be a pair (value, minimum-of-everything-at-or-below-this-entry), so the minimum travels with the value.
push(5): current_min starts as the value itself, 5.
`if self.stack:` is False — the stack is empty, so there is no older minimum to compare against and 5 stays the minimum.
Append the tuple (5, 5). stack = [(5, 5)].
push(3): current_min tentatively 3.
The stack is non-empty, so we do compare with the minimum stored in the current top entry.
current_min = min(3, self.stack[-1][1]) = min(3, 5) = 3. Reading the old minimum is a single O(1) index — that is the whole trick.
push(7): current_min tentatively 7.
current_min = min(7, 3) = 3. 7 is bigger than the running minimum, so the minimum is carried forward unchanged.
Append (7, 3). stack = [(5, 5), (3, 3), (7, 3)] — value column 5,3,7 and min column 5,3,3.
getMin() returns self.stack[-1][1] = 3. No scanning of the stack at all: O(1).
top() returns self.stack[-1][0] = 7, the value half of the same top tuple.
pop() removes the whole tuple (7, 3). stack = [(5, 5), (3, 3)].
getMin() now reads the new top (3, 3) and returns 3 — still correct, and we never recomputed anything.
push(2): current_min tentatively 2.
current_min = min(2, 3) = 2 — a brand new minimum enters the stack.
getMin() returns 2, read straight off the top tuple in constant time.
pop() removes (2, 2). stack = [(5, 5), (3, 3)]. The minimum 2 leaves with it.
getMin() returns 3 again. The old minimum is restored for free because it was stored alongside 3 when 3 was pushed.
pop() removes (3, 3). stack = [(5, 5)].
getMin() returns 5 — correct, since 5 is the only value left.
top() returns 5 as well. Every operation in this whole run was O(1) time, at the cost of one extra integer per element.

Reverse Words in a String.desc: We enter reverseWords with s = "  the sky  is blue  " (20 characters, including two leading, two trailing and one doubled inner space).
s.split() with no argument starts scanning. Indices 0 and 1 are spaces, and split() with no argument silently skips runs of whitespace, so nothing is emitted yet.
Indices 2, 3, 4 are t, h, e. The run ends at the space in index 5, so the first word "the" is emitted.
Next non-space run is indices 6, 7, 8 = s, k, y, ended by the space at index 9. words = ["the", "sky"].

Indices 9 and 10 are two spaces in a row. Because split() has no argument it treats the whole run as one separator, so NO empty word is produced — this is the trap that manual splitting on " " falls into.
Indices 11, 12 = i, s give the word "is". words = ["the", "sky", "is"].
Indices 14..17 = b, l, u, e give "blue". words = ["the", "sky", "is", "blue"].
The two trailing spaces at indices 18 and 19 are skipped and the scan ends. Final words = ["the", "sky", "is", "blue"] — leading, trailing and duplicated spaces are all gone.
Line 5 builds words[::-1], a slice with step -1 that walks the list from the back. It starts at index 3 and takes "blue".
Next it steps to index 2 and takes "is". reversed_words = ["blue", "is"].
Finally index 0, "the". reversed_words = ["blue", "is", "sky", "the"] — a NEW list; the original words list is untouched.
Now " ".join walks reversed_words. It takes "blue" first with no separator in front of it. result so far: "blue".
Next it adds one space then "is": result = "blue is". join inserts the separator BETWEEN items, never at the ends, so no stray spaces appear.
Finally " " + "the": result = "blue is sky the". Line 7 returns that string — words reversed, spacing normalised, in O(n) time.

Roman to Integer.desc: We trace s = "MCMXCIV". First the dictionary of symbol values is built: I=1, V=5, X=10, L=50, C=100, D=500, M=1000. Dict lookups are O(1).
total = 0 is the running answer.
n = len(s) = 7, needed so the i+1 peek never runs off the end.
Iteration i=0: the loop points at s[0] = 'M'.
curr_val = roman['M'] = 1000.
Peek ahead: i+1=1 < 7 and s[1]='C' is worth 100. Is 1000 < 100? No — so this is a normal additive symbol.
total += 1000 -> total = 1000.
Iteration i=1: s[1] = 'C'.
curr_val = roman['C'] = 100.
Peek: s[2] = 'M' = 1000, and 100 < 1000 is True. A smaller symbol sitting directly before a bigger one means subtraction — 'CM' is 900.
total -= 100 -> total = 900. We deliberately go 'too low' now; the M on the next iteration adds the full 1000 back, netting 900.
Iteration i=2: s[2] = 'M'.
curr_val = roman['M'] = 1000.
Peek: s[3] = 'X' = 10, and 1000 < 10 is False, so we add.
total += 1000 -> total = 1900. Sanity check: 'MCM' really is 1900.
Iteration i=3: s[3] = 'X', curr_val = 10.
Peek: s[4] = 'C' = 100 and 10 < 100 is True, so 'XC' is a subtractive pair worth 90.
total -= 10 -> total = 1890.
Iteration i=4: s[4] = 'C', curr_val = 100.
Peek: s[5] = 'I' = 1 and 100 < 1 is False, so add.

Guard: is i == n? 3 != 8, so the string was not all whitespace and we keep going instead of returning 0.
sign = 1 by default (assume positive until we see otherwise).

sign = -1 records the minus so we can apply it once at the very end.
i moves past the sign to 4. Note only ONE sign is allowed — the digit loop below will reject a second '-'.
res = 0 will accumulate the magnitude of the number, with the sign applied only at the very end.

Overflow guard BEFORE multiplying: is res > (INT_MAX - digit) // 10, i.e. 0 > (2147483647 - 4) // 10 = 214748364? No, so res*10 + 4 is safe.

Guard again: 4 > (2147483647 - 2) // 10 = 214748364? No. If res had been, say, 300000000, this check would fire and we would clamp instead of building a number Python would happily let grow past 32 bits.

node 2.right is None (node 2 only had a left child), so the condition is False — node 2 is fully explored.

Pop node 1 (stack = []) and set last_visited = node 1.
while stack or curr: stack is [] and curr is None, so both are falsy and the loop ends.

Find inorder successor. Start temp = root.right (4).
Copy successor value (4) to current node. Node value becomes 4.
Delete successor value (4) from right subtree.

Kth Smallest Element in BST.desc: Initialize an empty stack. It will hold ancestors whose left side we are still exploring. Our tree is [3,1,4,null,2] and k=2.
Start the walk at the root: node points to 3.
count = 0 — we have not visited (popped) any value yet.
Outer loop check: the stack is empty but node is 3 (not None), so we enter the loop.
Inner loop check: node 3 exists, so we start sliding left toward the smallest value.
Push 3 onto the stack — we must visit its whole left subtree before visiting 3 itself.
Step left: node = 3.left = 1. Smaller values always live to the left.
Inner check again: node 1 exists, so we keep sliding left.
Push 1 onto the stack, on top of 3.
Step left: node = 1.left = None — node 1 has no left child, we've hit the smallest value's spot.
Inner check: node is None, so the slide-left loop ends. The top of the stack (1) is the smallest unvisited value.
Pop the stack: node = 1. This is the 1st value in ascending order.
count becomes 1 — we have now visited 1 value (the minimum, 1).
Is count (1) equal to k (2)? No — the 1st smallest is not what we want, keep going.
Move into 1's right subtree: node = 1.right = 2. Values there are bigger than 1 but smaller than 3.
Outer loop check: node is 2, so we continue — there is still tree to explore.
Inner check: node 2 exists, so we try to slide left from it.
Push 2 onto the stack, above 3.
Step left: node = 2.left = None — 2 is a leaf, nothing smaller below it.
node is None so the inner loop ends; pop the stack: node = 2, the next value in ascending order.
count becomes 2 — this pop is the 2nd smallest value of the whole tree.
Is count (2) equal to k (2)? YES — the value we just popped is the answer.
Return node.val = 2. Notice we never touched node 4 — early exit saved that work.

Lowest Common Ancestor in BST.desc: Start the descent at the root: node = 6. We are looking for the LCA of p=3 and q=5 in [6,2,8,0,4,7,9,null,null,3,5].
Loop check: node 6 exists, so we inspect where p and q lie relative to it.
Are both targets smaller than 6? p=3 < 6 is true AND q=5 < 6 is true — both live in 6's left subtree.
Step left: node = 6.left = 2. The LCA cannot be 6, because 2's subtree already contains both targets.
Loop check: node 2 exists — compare the targets against 2 next.
Are both smaller than 2? p=3 < 2 is false, so this condition fails immediately.
Are both larger than 2? p=3 > 2 is true AND q=5 > 2 is true — both targets sit in 2's right subtree.
Step right: node = 2.right = 4. We keep descending as long as both targets stay on one side.
Loop check: node 4 exists — test the targets against 4.
Both smaller than 4? p=3 < 4 is true but q=5 < 4 is false — they are NOT both on the left.
Both larger than 4? p=3 > 4 is false — they are not both on the right either.
Neither condition held, so we fall into the else branch: 3 and 5 straddle node 4 (3 < 4 < 5) — the paths to p and q split here.
Return node 4. It is the deepest node whose subtree contains both 3 (its left child) and 5 (its right child) — the LCA.

Construct BST from Preorder Traversal.desc: Create the shared cursor idx = [0]. It points at the next unused preorder value (8) and only ever moves forward.
Kick off build(inf): the root of the whole tree has no upper limit on its value.
Guard check: idx=0 is in range and preorder[0]=8 <= inf, so 8 belongs in this (root) subtree.
val = 8 — the first preorder value is always the root of the entire BST.
Consume 8: the cursor advances to idx=1. No other call will ever see 8 again.
Create the node for 8. The tree so far is just this root.
Build 8's LEFT subtree: call build(bound=8) — only values smaller than 8 may live there.
Guard: preorder[1]=5 <= bound 8, so 5 belongs under 8 on the left.
val = 5 — it becomes the root of 8's left subtree.
Consume 5: cursor advances to idx=2.
Create the node for 5 (it will be attached as 8.left when this call returns).
Build 5's LEFT subtree: call build(bound=5) — only values below 5 allowed.
Guard: preorder[2]=1 <= bound 5, so 1 belongs here.
val = 1 — the root of 5's left subtree.
Consume 1: cursor advances to idx=3. Next unused value is 7.
Create the node for 1.
Build 1's LEFT subtree: call build(bound=1) — values below 1 only.
Guard: preorder[3]=7 > bound 1 — 7 is too big to sit anywhere under 1's left side.
Return None WITHOUT consuming 7 — node 1 gets no left child, and 7 stays available for an ancestor.
Build 1's RIGHT subtree: call build(bound=5) — 1's right side inherits ITS caller's bound of 5.
The guard fails again (7 > 5), so return None — node 1 is a leaf. 7 must belong even higher up.
Return node 1 to its caller; back in 5's frame, line 13 completes: 5.left = 1.
Build 5's RIGHT subtree: call build(bound=8) — values between 5 and 8 land here.
Guard: preorder[3]=7 <= bound 8 — 7 finally found the subtree it belongs to.
val = 7 is consumed (idx advances to 4, lines 10-11) and its node is created — it will be 5's right child.
Build 7's LEFT subtree: call build(bound=7). The next value is 10.
10 > 7, so the guard fails: return None — 7 has no left child.
Build 7's RIGHT subtree: call build(bound=8). Still looking at 10.
10 > 8 too — return None. Node 7 is a leaf; 10 doesn't fit anywhere under 8's LEFT side.
Return node 7; back in 5's frame, line 14 completes: 5.right = 7.
Node 5's subtree is finished — return node 5; back in the ROOT frame, line 13 completes: 8.left = 5.
Build 8's RIGHT subtree: call build(bound=inf) — the right side inherits the root's unlimited bound.
Guard: preorder[4]=10 <= inf, so 10 belongs in the root's right subtree.
val = 10 — the root of 8's right subtree.
Consume 10: idx becomes 5 — every preorder value has now been used.
Create the node for 10; it will attach as 8.right.
Both of 10's child calls (build(10), then build(inf)) hit idx == 5 — the list is exhausted, so each returns None instantly: 10 is a leaf.
Return node 10; back in the root frame, line 14 completes: 8.right = 10.
The root frame returns node 8 — the whole tree is assembled: 8 with left 5 (children 1, 7) and right 10.
build(inf) hands back the root 8; bst_from_preorder returns it. Final level order: [8, 5, 10, 1, 7].

Inorder Successor in BST.desc: Initialize successor = None — we have not yet seen any value greater than x=8. Tree: [20,8,22,4,12,null,null,null,null,10,14].
Start the descent at the root: node = 20.
Loop check: node 20 exists, so we compare it against x=8.
Is 20 > 8? Yes — 20 comes after 8 in sorted order, so it is a valid successor candidate.
Record the candidate: successor = 20. It may be too big, but it is the best we have seen.
Step LEFT to find something smaller that is still > 8: node = 20.left = 8.
Loop check: node 8 exists — compare it with x.
Is 8 > 8? No — strict inequality fails, so 8 itself can never be its own successor.
Take the else branch and step RIGHT: node = 8.right = 12. Anything <= 8 (including 8's left subtree) is ruled out.
Loop check: node 12 exists — keep walking.
Is 12 > 8? Yes — 12 is a valid candidate and it is smaller (closer to 8) than our current candidate 20.
Update the candidate: successor = 12, replacing 20. Each update strictly tightens the answer.
Step LEFT again looking for something between 8 and 12: node = 12.left = 10.
Loop check: node 10 exists — one more comparison.
Is 10 > 8? Yes — 10 beats 12 as the closest value above 8 seen so far.
Update: successor = 10. Can anything between 8 and 10 exist below? Only in 10's left subtree.
Step LEFT: node = 10.left = None — 10 has no left child, so nothing between 8 and 10 exists.
Loop check: node is None — the descent has fallen off the tree, so the search is over.
Return successor — the node holding 10, the smallest value strictly greater than 8. Matches the inorder [4,8,10,12,14,20,22].

BST Iterator.desc: BSTIterator is constructed on the tree [7,3,15,null,null,9,20]; __init__ receives the root node 7. Sorted order will be 3, 7, 9, 15, 20.
Create an empty stack. Invariant: the stack always holds exactly the chain of nodes whose values are still owed, top = next smallest.
Call _push_left(7) to stage the path from the root down to the tree's minimum value.
node 7 is not None, so push it: stack=[7]. 7 must wait until its whole left subtree is served.
Step left: node = 7.left = 3, heading toward smaller values.
Push 3 as well: stack=[7, 3]. 3 is now the top — the smallest pending value.
node = 3.left = None, so the while loop ends: the left spine [7, 3] is fully staged and the constructor finishes.
First next(): pop the top -> node 3, the minimum of the whole tree. stack=[7].
Stage 3's successors: _push_left(3.right) is _push_left(None) — 3 has no right child, so nothing is pushed.
Return 3 — the first value of the sorted sequence.
Second next(): pop 7, the next smallest. The stack is briefly empty.
_push_left(7.right = 15) runs: push 15 -> stack=[15].
Step left from 15: node = 15.left = 9 — 9 comes before 15 in sorted order, so it must sit above 15 on the stack.
Push 9 -> stack=[15, 9]; 9.left is None so this spine ends here.
Return 7. Notice the stack again holds exactly the pending left spine [15, 9] — never the whole tree.
hasNext(): the stack holds 2 nodes, so len(self.stack) > 0 is True — more values remain.
Third next(): pop 9 off the top. stack=[15].
9 has no right child, so _push_left(None) stages nothing new.
Return 9 — sorted order emitted so far: 3, 7, 9.
Fourth next(): pop 15. stack=[] for a moment.
_push_left(15.right = 20): push 20 -> stack=[20]; 20 has no left child so the dive stops immediately.
Return 15. Only the value 20 is still owed to the caller.
Fifth next(): pop 20, the maximum. stack=[].
Return 20 — the full sorted sequence 3, 7, 9, 15, 20 has now been emitted.
hasNext(): the stack is empty -> False. Every node was pushed once and popped once — that is the amortized O(1) argument made visible.

Two Sum in BST.desc: findTarget starts with k=12 on the BST [5,3,6,2,4,null,7]. Create arr=[], soon to hold the inorder (sorted) values.
Kick off the recursive inorder walk from the root node 5.
inorder(5) first recurses left into 3, which recurses left into 2, which calls inorder on 2's empty left child.
That call sees node=None and returns immediately — time to visit 2 itself.
Append 2, the smallest value in the tree: arr=[2].
2 has no right child, so recursion unwinds to 3 and appends it: arr=[2, 3].
inorder(3) now descends into its right child 4 (values just above 3 live there).
4 is appended: arr=[2, 3, 4]. The root's whole left subtree is finished.
Back at the root: append 5 -> arr=[2, 3, 4, 5].
The right subtree visits 6 (no left child) and then its right child 7: arr=[2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7] — sorted, exactly as the BST promised.
Set two pointers on the sorted array: lo=0 (value 2) and hi=5 (value 7).
lo=0 < hi=5, so the pair-search loop runs — at least two distinct nodes remain in range.
9 is not 12, and 9 < 12: the sum is too small. hi already sits on the LARGEST value, so only a bigger left value can help.
Advance lo to 1 (value 3); the pair (2, anything) is permanently ruled out for reaching 12.
s = arr[1] + arr[5] = 3 + 7 = 10, still below 12.
Too small again -> lo=2 (value 4).
s = arr[2] + arr[5] = 4 + 7 = 11. One short of the target.
Still too small -> lo=3 (value 5).
s = arr[3] + arr[5] = 5 + 7 = 12 — exactly k!
The check s == k is finally true: 5 and 7 come from two different nodes of the tree.
Return True: the BST contains two distinct nodes (5 and 7) whose values sum to 12.

Recover BST.desc: recoverTree starts on [3,1,4,null,null,2]. A correct BST on these values would read 1,2,3,4 in inorder — we will watch for a drop. Create the empty stack.
The walker node starts at the root (value 3); it will dive down left spines.
prev = None: no node has been visited in inorder yet, so there is nothing to compare against.
first and second start as None — they will capture the two offending nodes when a drop appears.
Outer loop runs (node=3 is not None). The inner dive pushes 3: stack=[3].
Step left: node = 3.left = 1.
Push 1 as well: stack=[3, 1]; then node = 1.left = None will end the dive.
Pop the top: node=1 is the FIRST value in inorder order. stack=[3].
prev is None — 1 has no predecessor to compare with, so no drop check happens on the first visit.
prev now points at node 1: the baseline for the next comparison.
node = 1.right = None: 1 has no right subtree, so we will return to the stack.
The stack still holds [3]: pop it. Inorder so far: 1, 3.
prev.val=1 < node.val=3: the sequence rises, exactly what a healthy BST does. No offender yet.
prev moves forward to node 3.
node = 3.right = 4: inorder continues into the right subtree.
Push 4 (stack=[4]), step to 4.left = 2 and push it too: stack=[4, 2].
Pop node=2. Inorder so far: 1, 3, 2 — the sequence just went DOWN!
Drop detected: prev.val=3 > node.val=2. These two nodes are the corrupted pair (or its endpoints).
first was None, so first = prev — the node holding 3, a large value that appeared too early.
second = node — the node holding 2. If a later drop appeared, second would be overwritten there; with an adjacent swap it will not.
prev moves on to node 2 and the traversal continues normally.
node = 2.right = None; back to the stack, which still holds [4].
Pop node=4. Inorder so far: 1, 3, 2, 4.
prev.val=2 < 4: no second drop. The swapped values were inorder NEIGHBOURS — first=node(3), second=node(2) is exactly right.
node = 4.right = None and the stack is empty — the outer loop is about to end.
Swap the two VALUES: the node that held 3 now holds 2 and vice versa. The tree becomes [2,1,4,null,null,3] with inorder 1,2,3,4 — a valid BST, shape untouched.

Largest BST in Binary Tree.desc: largestBst runs on [5,2,4,1,3]. Define sentinels NEG=-inf and POS=+inf, used by empty-subtree reports and poisoned ranges.
Call solve(5) on the root. Whatever report it produces, its size slot [0] will be the final answer.
solve(5) needs its left report first, so it recurses into node 2 — post-order means children always report before parents.
solve(2) likewise recurses into ITS left child, node 1.
solve(1) calls solve(None) for 1's left child: the base case returns (0, inf, -inf) — a size-0 report whose range can never block a parent.
Back in solve(1): the left report unpacks to l_size=0, l_min=inf, l_max=-inf.
1's right child is also None -> right report (0, inf, -inf): r_size=0, r_min=inf, r_max=-inf.
BST test at 1: l_max=-inf < 1 < r_min=inf — trivially true for a leaf; the sentinels do their job.
Leaf 1 reports (0+0+1, min(inf,1), max(-inf,1)) = (1, 1, 1): a BST of size 1 spanning values [1, 1].
solve(2) receives its left report: l_size=1, l_min=1, l_max=1.
solve(2) recurses right into leaf 3, which reports (1, 3, 3) by the same leaf pattern: r_size=1, r_min=3, r_max=3.
BST test at 2: l_max=1 < 2 < r_min=3 — true. Everything left of 2 tops out at 1, everything right starts at 3.
Merge at 2: size=1+1+1=3, mn=min(1,2)=1, mx=max(3,2)=3. solve(2) reports (3, 1, 3) — the subtree {1,2,3} is one valid BST.
solve(5) receives its left report: l_size=3, l_min=1, l_max=3 — a 3-node BST lives on its left.
solve(5) recurses right into leaf 4 -> right report (1, 4, 4): r_size=1, r_min=4, r_max=4.
BST test at 5: l_max=3 < 5 holds, BUT 5 < r_min=4 FAILS — the right subtree contains 4, smaller than the root. The whole tree is not a BST.
Broken at the root: report (max(3, 1), -inf, inf) = (3, -inf, inf). The poisoned range would make any ancestor's test fail — here there is none.
solve(root) returned (3, -inf, inf); its [0] slot is 3. The largest BST subtree is {1, 2, 3} rooted at node 2 — answer 3.

DFS Traversal.desc: dfs = [] will collect vertices in the order we first touch them.
visited = [False]*5, shown as 0/1 below. Without it, edge 0-1 plus edge 1-0 would recurse forever.
Define the nested helper traverse(node). Being nested lets it read and mutate the outer `dfs` and `visited` directly.
traverse(0) is called — the very first frame is pushed onto the call stack.
Inside traverse(0): visited[0] = True, claimed before exploring anything.
dfs.append(0) → dfs = [0]. This is preorder: we record a vertex on entry, before its children.
Loop over adj[0] = [1, 2]; the first neighbour is 1.
visited[1] is False, so `not visited[1]` is True — 1 is unexplored and we dive in.
traverse(1) is called. Frame for vertex 0 is PAUSED mid-loop (it still owes us neighbour 2) and waits on the stack.
Inside traverse(1): visited[1] = True.
dfs.append(1) → dfs = [0, 1].
Loop over adj[1] = [0, 3]; first neighbour is 0.
visited[0] is True, so the if is False — we do NOT recurse back into 0. This one check kills the infinite ping-pong 0→1→0→1.
Next neighbour of 1 is 3.
visited[3] is False → recurse deeper instead of going back up. Depth-first always prefers 'go deeper' over 'go sideways'.
traverse(3) is called; the stack is now 0 → 1 → 3.
Inside traverse(3): visited[3] = True.
dfs.append(3) → dfs = [0, 1, 3]. Notice 3 is recorded BEFORE 2, even though 2 is a neighbour of the source — that is the DFS signature.
adj[3] = [1]; the only neighbour is 1.
visited[1] is True, so we skip. adj[3] is exhausted, so traverse(3) falls off the end and returns to traverse(1).
Back inside traverse(1): its for-loop over [0, 3] has no items left, so traverse(1) also returns — the stack unwinds to vertex 0.
Back inside traverse(0), the paused loop over adj[0] = [1, 2] resumes with its second neighbour, 2.
visited[2] is False → vertex 2 is a whole unexplored branch.
traverse(2) is called; stack is 0 → 2.
Inside traverse(2): visited[2] = True.
dfs.append(2) → dfs = [0, 1, 3, 2].
adj[2] = [0, 4]. Neighbour 0 is already visited, so it is skipped; neighbour 4 has visited[4] = False.
traverse(4) is called; stack is 0 → 2 → 4.
Inside traverse(4): visited[4] = True — all five vertices are now marked.
dfs.append(4) → dfs = [0, 1, 3, 2, 4].
adj[4] = [2] and visited[2] is True, so nothing to explore. traverse(4) returns, then traverse(2), then traverse(0) — the stack empties.
return dfs = [0, 1, 3, 2, 4]. Each vertex was entered exactly once and each edge inspected twice — O(V + E).

Number of Provinces.desc: We call findCircleNum on a 4x4 matrix. Cities 0-1 share a road and cities 2-3 share a road; there is no road between the two pairs, so the answer should be 2.
n = 4: the matrix has 4 rows, so there are 4 cities numbered 0, 1, 2 and 3.
parent = [0, 1, 2, 3]. Before reading a single road, every city is the leader of a province containing only itself.
size = [1, 1, 1, 1]: each of the four provinces currently holds exactly one city. We only trust size[i] when i is a leader.
components = 4. This counter is the answer-in-progress: it starts at n and drops by one every time two provinces merge.
Outer loop starts with i = 0. We will pair city 0 with every city that comes after it.
Inner loop starts at j = i + 1 = 1. We deliberately skip j <= i because the matrix is symmetric: cell (1,0) repeats what cell (0,1) already told us.
isConnected[0][1] = 1, so there is a direct road between city 0 and city 1. We must union them.
To merge, we first need the LEADER of each city, not the city itself. We call find(0) and then find(1).
Inside find(0): parent[0] is 0, which equals x, so the while condition is False and we never enter the loop. City 0 is already a leader.
find(0) returns 0 - the leader of city 0 is city 0 itself.
Now find(1): parent[1] is 1, again its own parent, so the loop body is skipped and find(1) will return 1. Back in the caller we get a = 0 and b = 1.
a = 0 and b = 1 are different leaders, so cities 0 and 1 really do live in separate provinces right now. Time to merge.
Union by size: size[0] = 1 is NOT less than size[1] = 1, so the condition is False and we skip the swap. Root a = 0 stays the bigger (here: tied) tree.
parent[1] = 0. City 1 now points at city 0, so parent becomes [0, 0, 2, 3] and both cities answer 'my leader is 0'.
size[0] += size[1] gives size[0] = 2: province 0 now holds two cities. size[1] is stale but harmless because 1 is no longer a leader.
components drops from 4 to 3. Provinces are now {0,1}, {2}, {3}.
Inner loop advances to j = 2 with i still 0.
isConnected[0][2] = 0 - no road from city 0 to city 2 - so the whole union block is skipped.
j = 3 next: isConnected[0][3] = 0 as well, so nothing happens and the inner loop for i = 0 is finished.
Outer loop moves to i = 1. Note we only look at columns 2 and 3 for this row - column 0 and 1 are behind the diagonal.
j = 2: isConnected[1][2] = 0, no road, skip.
j = 3: isConnected[1][3] = 0 too, so row 1 adds no new information. components is still 3.
Outer loop moves to i = 2.
Inner loop starts at j = 3, the only column to the right of the diagonal in row 2.
isConnected[2][3] = 1: cities 2 and 3 are directly connected, so we union them.
find(2) walks nowhere because parent[2] = 2, and find(3) likewise returns 3. So a = 2 and b = 3.
a = 2 differs from b = 3, so these are two distinct provinces and the merge proceeds.
size[2] = 1 is not less than size[3] = 1, so once again no swap is needed.
parent[3] = 2, so parent becomes [0, 0, 2, 2]: city 3 now hangs under leader 2.
size[2] becomes 2 - the province led by city 2 holds cities 2 and 3.
components drops from 3 to 2. The provinces are now {0,1} and {2,3}.
Outer loop reaches its last value, i = 3.
range(4, 4) is empty, so the inner loop body never runs for i = 3 and both loops finish.
We return components = 2. Two roots survive in parent = [0, 0, 2, 2] - cities 0 and 2 - which is exactly the number of provinces.

Number of Islands.desc: Guard check: grid = [[1,1,0],[0,1,0],[0,0,1]] is non-empty and its first row is non-empty, so we do NOT return 0 early.
Cache the dimensions: rows = 3 and cols = 3. These bound every neighbour check later.
Initialise count = 0 — no islands discovered yet; the scan is about to begin.
Outer scan starts with row r = 0; the inner loop will walk columns 0, 1, 2 of this row.
Cell (0,0) holds "1" — land that no BFS has sunk yet. We just discovered a brand-new island!
Count the new island: count goes from 0 to 1. Now we must sink ALL of it so it is never re-counted.
Sink the starting cell: grid[0][0] becomes "0". The grid itself is our visited marker — no extra set needed.
Seed the BFS queue with the island's first cell: queue = [(0,0)].
Pop the oldest cell: (row, col) = (0, 0). The queue is empty for now; we spread from here.
Check (0,0)'s neighbours: down (1,0) is "0" — fail; up (-1,0) is out of bounds — fail; right (0,1) is "1" — PASS!
Sink neighbour (0,1) immediately — sinking on arrival guarantees no cell ever enters the queue twice.
Append (0,1) to the queue so we can later spread from it. Left neighbour (0,-1) is out of bounds, so (0,0) is done.
Pop (0,1) — the BFS frontier advances one ring outward from the island's first cell.
Neighbours of (0,1): down (1,1) is "1" — PASS! (up is out of bounds; right (0,2) and left (0,0) are "0").
Sink (1,1): the third and last cell of this island turns to water on arrival.
Append (1,1); queue = [(1, 1)]. Every discovered land cell is queued exactly once.
Pop (1,1) and try to spread. Note the "1" at (2,2) touches (1,1) only DIAGONALLY — it is not a neighbour.
All four checks fail: down (2,1)="0", up (0,1) sunk, right (1,2)="0", left (1,0)="0". Nothing new to enqueue.
The queue is empty — BFS for island #1 is complete and all 3 of its cells are sunk. Back to the outer scan.
Second island discovered: count goes from 1 to 2.
Sink (2,2). The grid is now entirely water — nothing left for the scan to find.
Seed the new BFS: queue = [(2,2)] for island #2.
Pop (2,2): down and right are out of bounds, up (1,2) and left (2,1) are "0" — this island was a single cell.
Scan finished (r=2, c=2 was the last cell). Return count = 2 — the grid contained exactly two islands.

Flood Fill Algorithm.desc: Read the clicked pixel (sr,sc) = (1,1): old = 1. Only pixels wearing colour 1 will be repainted.
Guard: old (1) != color (2), so there IS work to do — we do not return early.
Cache dimensions: rows = 3, cols = 3. Every neighbour probe will be bounds-checked against these.
Seed the BFS queue with the start pixel: queue = [(1, 1)].
Paint the start pixel NOW: image[1][1] = 2. Painting before the loop means (1,1) can never re-enter the queue.
Pop the oldest pixel: (r, c) = (1, 1). We now try to spread paint to its four neighbours.
Neighbour down (2,1): it holds 0, not old (1) — this pixel is a wall, the paint stops here.
Neighbour up (0,1): in bounds and holds 1 == old — the paint can spread there!
Paint (0,1) on arrival: it becomes 2 the moment it is discovered, so it can never be enqueued twice.
Append (0,1) to the queue. Next neighbour right (1,2) holds 0 — wall; left (1,0) holds 1 — spreads!
Paint left neighbour (1,0) to 2 and it joins the frontier.
Append (1,0). Queue is now [(0, 1), (1, 0)] — the first BFS ring around the click is complete.
Pop (0,1). Its down neighbour (1,1) is already 2 (fails == old), and up (-1,1) is out of bounds.
Right neighbour (0,2) holds 1 == old — paint spreads to the top-right corner.
Paint (0,2) to 2 immediately upon discovery.
Left neighbour (0,0) also holds 1 — the last unpainted pixel of the top row is reachable.
Paint (0,0) to 2 and enqueue it. Queue: [(1, 0), (0, 2), (0, 0)].
Pop (1,0). Down neighbour (2,0) holds 1 == old — one more pixel to claim below.
Paint (2,0) to 2 and enqueue it. Up (0,0) and right (1,1) are already 2; left (1,-1) is out of bounds.
Pop (0,2): down (1,2) is 0 — wall; left (0,1) is already 2; other neighbours out of bounds. Nothing spreads.
Pop (0,0): both in-bounds neighbours (0,1) and (1,0) are already painted 2 — no new work.
Pop (2,0): up (1,0) is 2, right (2,1) is 0 — wall. Note (2,2) still holds 1: it only touches the region diagonally!
The queue is empty — every pixel connected to the click through colour-1 paths has been repainted.
Return the image: [[2,2,2],[2,2,0],[2,0,1]]. The 0-walls and the diagonal 1 at (2,2) survived untouched.

Detect Cycle in Undirected Graph (BFS).desc: Input: V=4, edges 0-1, 0-2, 1-2, 2-3 (a triangle plus a tail). Initialise visited = [F, F, F, F].
Outer loop tries start = 0 first — if the graph were disconnected, later starts would cover other components.
visited[0] is False, so vertex 0 belongs to an unexplored component — we do NOT skip it.
Seed the BFS queue with (0, -1): vertex 0 with sentinel parent -1, because a root has no parent.
Mark visited[0] = True at enqueue time — marking on pop would let 0 be enqueued again via its neighbours.
Pop the oldest entry: node = 0, parent = -1. We now scan 0's neighbour list [1, 2].
First neighbour of 0: nei = 1. Which of the three cases applies — unvisited, parent, or visited non-parent?
visited[1] is False — case 1: a normal first discovery of vertex 1 through the edge 0-1.
Mark visited[1] = True immediately, so no other branch can discover vertex 1 'for the first time' again.
Enqueue (1, 0): when vertex 1 is popped later it will remember it was reached FROM vertex 0.
Second neighbour of 0: nei = 2, also unvisited — another normal discovery via edge 0-2.
Mark visited[2] = True. Vertices 1 and 2 are now BOTH claimed as children of 0 — same BFS level.
Enqueue (2, 0). Queue is now [(1, 0), (2, 0)] and vertex 0's neighbour scan is finished.
Pop the next entry: node = 1, parent = 0. Scan 1's neighbour list [0, 2].
nei = 0 is visited, so check the elif: is 0 != parent? No — 0 IS the parent, this is just edge 0-1 seen backwards. Ignore it.
Next neighbour of 1: nei = 2 — the third side of the triangle, the edge 1-2.
visited[2] is True AND 2 != parent (0): vertex 2 was already reached via 0-2, and now again via 1-2 — two distinct paths!
Return True: the two meeting paths 0->2 and 0->1->2 close the triangle 0-1-2. The tail vertex 3 never needed visiting.

Detect Cycle in Undirected Graph (DFS).desc: Input: V=4, edges 0-1, 1-2, 1-3, 2-3 (a triangle 1-2-3 with pendant 0). Initialise visited = [F, F, F, F].
Outer loop picks s = 0 — the first vertex of the first (and here, only) component.
visited[0] is False, so this component is unexplored — we will launch a DFS rooted at 0.
Call dfs(0, -1). The sentinel parent -1 says: the root arrived from nowhere, no neighbour may be excused as 'parent'.
Inside dfs(0,-1): mark visited[0] = True — vertex 0 is discovered.
Scan 0's neighbours: adj[0] = [1]. First (and only) neighbour is nei = 1.
visited[1] is False — a tree edge. We will dive deeper into vertex 1.
Recurse: dfs(1, 0). The call stack grows — vertex 1 will know it was reached from parent 0.
Inside dfs(1,0): mark visited[1] = True.
Scan 1's neighbours: adj[1] = [0, 2, 3]. First up: nei = 0.
nei = 0 is visited, so check the elif: 0 != parent? No — 0 IS the parent, just our entry edge 0-1 seen backwards. Ignore.
Next neighbour: nei = 2, unvisited — another tree edge to follow downward.
Recurse: dfs(2, 1). Current DFS path is 0 - 1 - 2.
Inside dfs(2,1): mark visited[2] = True.
2's first neighbour is 1: visited, but 1 == parent — that is the edge 1-2 we just walked in on. Skip it.
2's next neighbour is 3: unvisited — extend the path to 0 - 1 - 2 - 3.
Recurse: dfs(3, 2). The call stack is now four levels deep.
Inside dfs(3,2): mark visited[3] = True. Every vertex is now discovered — but the cycle check is still to come.
Scan 3's neighbours: adj[3] = [2, 1]. First: nei = 2 — visited, and 2 == parent, so it is excused.
Next: nei = 1 — visited AND 1 != parent (2). Vertex 1 is an ancestor still on our path: edge 3-1 is a BACK EDGE!
Return True from dfs(3,2): the back edge closes the cycle 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1.
dfs(2,1) sees its recursive call came back True and immediately returns True too — the signal bubbles up.
dfs(1,0) propagates True the same way; then dfs(0,-1) does as well. The call stack unwinds completely.
Back in the outer loop: dfs(0, -1) returned True, so isCycle returns True — the graph contains a cycle.

Detect Cycle in Directed Graph.desc: Input: V=4, edges 0->1, 1->2, 2->3, 3->1. Start with indegree = [0, 0, 0, 0] — no incoming edges counted yet.
Scan every vertex's outgoing edges to count indegrees. First u = 0, whose list is [1].
Edge 0 -> 1: vertex 1 gains an incoming edge, indegree becomes [0, 1, 0, 0].
u = 3, edge 3 -> 1: vertex 1 now has TWO incoming edges (from 0 and from 3). indegree = [0, 2, 1, 1].
Collect every vertex with indegree 0: only vertex 0 qualifies. queue = [0]. These are the only safe starting peels.
processed = 0 — this counter will tell us at the end whether every vertex could be peeled off.
The queue is non-empty, so there is at least one peelable vertex — enter the peeling loop.
Pop u = 0: it has no incoming edges, so it cannot be part of any cycle — peel it off the graph.
Peeling 0 deletes its outgoing edge 0 -> 1: indegree[1] drops from 2 to 1. indegree = [0, 1, 1, 1].
Is indegree[1] now 0? No — vertex 1 is still fed by the edge 3 -> 1 from inside the cycle, so it is NOT peelable.
Back at the loop top: the queue is EMPTY, yet vertices 1, 2, 3 remain unpeeled — each one is kept alive by an edge from another member of the trio.
Final verdict: processed (1) != V (4). Three vertices could never reach indegree 0 — exactly the cycle 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 1. Return True.

Topological Sort (DFS).desc: Setup: V=4 with edges 1→0, 2→0, 3→1, 3→2 (adj = [[], [0], [0], [1, 2]]). We create visited = [False, False, False, False]: no vertex explored yet.
stack starts empty. A vertex will be appended only at the moment DFS FINISHES it, i.e. after all its descendants are already inside.
Main loop starts with u=0. We try every vertex as a DFS root so disconnected parts are never missed.
visited[0] is False, so we launch dfs(0) — vertex 0 becomes the root of the first exploration.
Inside dfs(0): mark visited[0] = True immediately, so no later call can enter 0 again.
adj[0] is empty — vertex 0 has no outgoing edges, so the neighbour loop body never runs.
dfs(0) is finishing: everything reachable from 0 (nothing) is done, so we append 0. stack = [0].
Back in the main loop, u advances to 1. visited[1] is still False.
visited[1] is False, so we launch dfs(1) as a fresh root.
Inside dfs(1): mark visited[1] = True. visited = [True, True, False, False].
dfs(1) scans its only neighbour v=0 (edge 1→0). visited[0] is already True, so we do NOT recurse — 0 is already safely below us in the stack.
dfs(1) finishes: its descendant 0 is already in the stack, so 1 goes on top. stack = [0, 1].
Main loop reaches u=2; visited[2] is False, so dfs(2) is launched.
Inside dfs(2): mark visited[2] = True. visited = [True, True, True, False].
dfs(2) checks its neighbour v=0 (edge 2→0): visited[0] is True, so no recursion happens.
dfs(2) finishes and appends 2. stack = [0, 1, 2] — note 2 sits ABOVE 0, its prerequisite target.
Main loop reaches u=3, the last unvisited vertex; dfs(3) is launched.
Inside dfs(3): mark visited[3] = True. Every vertex is now marked: [True, True, True, True].
dfs(3) checks its first neighbour v=1 (edge 3→1): visited[1] is True, so we skip recursion.
dfs(3) checks its second neighbour v=2 (edge 3→2): visited[2] is also True — skip again. Both of 3's targets are already deeper in the stack.
dfs(3) finishes and appends 3. stack = [0, 1, 2, 3]: every vertex is below the vertices that point at it.

Reverse the stack and return [3, 2, 1, 0]. Verify: 3 comes before 1 and 2 (edges 3→1, 3→2), and both 1 and 2 come before 0 (edges 1→0, 2→0). Every edge points left-to-right — a valid topological order.

Topological Sort (BFS/Kahn's Algorithm).desc: Setup: V=4 with edges 1→0, 2→0, 3→1, 3→2 (adj = [[], [0], [0], [1, 2]]). Start every in-degree at 0; we will count arrivals next.
Counting pass, u=1: its edge 1→0 lands on v=0, so indegree[0] becomes 1. (u=0 had no outgoing edges, so it contributed nothing.)
u=2: its edge 2→0 also lands on v=0, so indegree[0] becomes 2 — vertex 0 has two prerequisites.
u=3: edges 3→1 and 3→2 bump indegree[1] and indegree[2] to 1 each. Final counts: [2, 1, 1, 0] — only vertex 3 has no prerequisites.
Seed the queue with every vertex whose in-degree is 0. Only vertex 3 qualifies, so queue = deque([3]).
order starts empty — vertices will be appended here in a prerequisite-respecting sequence.
The queue holds [3], so it is non-empty and we enter the processing loop.
Pop the front: u=3. Its in-degree is 0, so nothing unplaced points at it — safe to emit.
Place vertex 3 first: order = [3]. Now we delete 3's outgoing edges 3→1 and 3→2.
Neighbour v=1 loses its prerequisite 3: indegree[1] drops from 1 to 0.
indegree[1] hit 0 — vertex 1 has no prerequisites left, so it joins the queue: [1].
Neighbour v=2 loses prerequisite 3 as well: indegree[2] drops from 1 to 0.
indegree[2] hit 0, so vertex 2 joins too. queue = [1, 2] — both unlocked by placing 3.
Next round: pop u=1 from the front. queue = [2].
Place vertex 1: order = [3, 1]. Now delete its single outgoing edge 1→0.
Neighbour v=0: indegree[0] drops from 2 to 1. Not zero yet — vertex 0 still waits for vertex 2, so it does NOT enter the queue.
Next round: pop u=2. The queue is now empty until something new unlocks.
Place vertex 2: order = [3, 1, 2]. Delete its edge 2→0.
Neighbour v=0: indegree[0] drops from 1 to 0 — its LAST prerequisite is gone.
Vertex 0 is finally free and joins the queue: [0].
Final round: pop u=0. queue = [].
Place vertex 0: order = [3, 1, 2, 0]. adj[0] is empty, so no in-degrees change.
The queue is empty, so the while loop ends. All 4 vertices were placed — no cycle existed.
Return [3, 1, 2, 0]. Check every edge: 3 before 1 ✓, 3 before 2 ✓, 1 before 0 ✓, 2 before 0 ✓. len(order) == V confirms the graph was a DAG.

Bipartite Graph Check.desc: Input: graph = [[1,3],[0,2],[1,3],[0,2]] — the square 0-1-2-3-0. n = 4 vertices.
color = [-1, -1, -1, -1]: nobody has a team yet. -1 doubles as our 'not visited' marker.
Outer loop begins with start=0 — any vertex may seed its component's coloring.
color[0] is -1 (uncolored), so we do NOT skip — vertex 0 starts a brand-new component.
Paint vertex 0 with team 0. The choice is arbitrary: flipping all colors in a component is symmetric.
The BFS queue starts with the seed vertex: queue = [0].
Pop u=0 and expand it. Its neighbours are 1 and 3 — both must take the OPPOSITE team of 0.
Neighbour v=1 is uncolored, so it gets 1 - color[0] = 1 - 0 = 1. color = [0, 1, -1, -1].
Enqueue vertex 1 so its own neighbours get checked later. queue = [1].
Neighbour v=3 is also uncolored: it gets 1 - 0 = 1 as well. color = [0, 1, -1, 1].
Enqueue vertex 3. queue = [1, 3]. Level 1 of the BFS (both of 0's neighbours) is fully colored team 1.
