Pop u=1 (team 1). Its neighbours are 0 and 2. queue = [3].
Neighbour v=0 is already colored 0 while u=1 has color 1 — DIFFERENT teams, so the edge 1-0 is fine and the elif is False; nothing happens.
Neighbour v=2 is uncolored: it gets 1 - color[1] = 1 - 1 = 0. color = [0, 1, 0, 1] — teams alternate around the square.
Enqueue vertex 2. queue = [3, 2]. Every vertex now holds a color; the remaining pops only VERIFY edges.
Pop u=3 (team 1). Its neighbours are 0 (team 0) and 2 (team 0). queue = [2].
Both checks pass: color[0]=0 != color[3]=1 and color[2]=0 != color[3]=1. Edges 3-0 and 3-2 cross teams — no conflict.
Pop the last vertex u=2 (team 0). Its neighbours 1 and 3 are both team 1. queue = [].
color[1]=1 != color[2]=0 and color[3]=1 != color[2]=0 — both of 2's edges are cross-team. The queue is empty: this component colored cleanly.
The outer loop tries start=1, 2, 3, but each already has a color (1, 0, 1), so 'continue' skips them — no second component exists.
Every edge joins opposite teams: RED = {0, 2}, BLUE = {1, 3}. The graph is bipartite — return True.

Shortest Path in DAG.desc: Input: V=4, edges [[0,1,2],[0,2,4],[1,2,1],[2,3,3]], src=0. Create 4 empty adjacency buckets (a fresh list per vertex).
First edge [0,1,2]: append (1, 2) to adj[0] — from vertex 0 you can reach 1 at cost 2.
The remaining edges [0,2,4], [1,2,1], [2,3,3] fill in the same way. Final adj = [[(1,2),(2,4)], [(2,1)], [(3,3)], []].
Phase 1 begins: visited = [False, False, False, False]; no vertex explored by the topological DFS yet.
order starts empty; DFS will append each vertex at the moment it FINISHES (all descendants done).
The main loop starts at u=0, which is unvisited, so dfs(0) launches.
Inside dfs(0): mark visited[0] = True, then look at 0's edges (1,2) and (2,4).
First edge of 0 goes to v=1, which is unvisited — recurse into dfs(1) before finishing 0.
Inside dfs(1): mark visited[1] = True. Its only edge is (2, 1).
Vertex 2 is unvisited, so dfs(1) recurses into dfs(2).
Inside dfs(2): mark visited[2] = True. Its only edge is (3, 3).
Vertex 3 is unvisited, so dfs(2) recurses into dfs(3).
Inside dfs(3): mark visited[3] = True. adj[3] is empty — vertex 3 is a sink.
dfs(3) finishes immediately (no descendants) and appends 3. order = [3].
Control returns to dfs(2): its descendant 3 is done, so 2 finishes. order = [3, 2].
dfs(1) finishes next (its subtree via 2 is complete). order = [3, 2, 1].
Back inside dfs(0), its second edge points to v=2 — but visited[2] is already True, so no recursion: 2 was fully handled through vertex 1.
dfs(0) finishes last. order = [3, 2, 1, 0] — reverse topological order. The main loop finds 1, 2, 3 already visited, so no more DFS calls happen.
Reverse it: order = [0, 1, 2, 3]. Every edge now points from an earlier position to a later one — safe to sweep left to right.
Phase 2 begins: dist = [inf, inf, inf, inf]; inf means 'no path found yet'.
The source costs nothing to reach: dist[0] = 0. dist = [0, inf, inf, inf].
Sweep at u=0 (dist 0): relax edge (1, 2). 0 + 2 = 2 < inf, so dist[1] = 2.
Still at u=0: relax edge (2, 4). 0 + 4 = 4 < inf, so dist[2] = 4 — the direct route, for now.
Sweep at u=1 (dist 2): relax edge (2, 1). 2 + 1 = 3 beats the current 4, so dist[2] improves to 3 — the two-hop route 0→1→2 wins.
Sweep at u=2 (dist 3, already FINAL because nothing after 2 can reach it): relax edge (3, 3). 3 + 3 = 6 < inf, so dist[3] = 6.
Sweep at u=3: dist[3] = 6 is not inf, but adj[3] is empty, so the inner loop does nothing and the sweep ends.
No entry is inf, so nothing becomes -1. Return [0, 2, 3, 6]: cheapest costs from source 0 to every vertex.

Dijkstra's Algorithm.desc: Input: V=3, edges 0-1 (w1), 0-2 (w6), 1-2 (w3), source = 2. Define INF as the 'unreached' marker.
dist = [inf, inf, inf]: before the algorithm runs, no vertex is known to be reachable.
The source is free to reach: dist[2] = 0. dist = [inf, inf, 0].
Seed the min-heap with (0, 2): 'vertex 2 is reachable at cost 0'. Tuples compare by first element, so the smallest DISTANCE always pops first.
The heap has one entry, so we enter the main loop.
Pop the cheapest entry: d=0, u=2. Vertex 2 is now SETTLED — no future route can beat cost 0.
Staleness check: d=0 is not greater than dist[2]=0, so this entry is fresh — proceed to relax 2's edges.
First neighbour of 2 is (v=0, w=6): candidate cost nd = 0 + 6 = 6 for the direct road 2→0.
6 < inf, so record dist[0] = 6. This is only TENTATIVE — a cheaper detour may still appear.
Push (6, 0) so vertex 0 becomes a settlement candidate. heap = [(6, 0)].
Second neighbour of 2 is (v=1, w=3): candidate cost nd = 0 + 3 = 3.
3 < inf, so dist[1] = 3. dist = [6, 3, 0].
Push (3, 1). The heap reorders itself so the smallest is in front: heap = [(3, 1), (6, 0)].
Pop the cheapest: (3, 1). Vertex 1 settles at cost 3 — the direct edge was the best way there. heap = [(6, 0)].
First neighbour of 1 is (v=0, w=1): candidate nd = 3 + 1 = 4 — the detour 2→1→0.
4 < 6: the detour beats the direct edge! dist[0] improves from 6 to 4. dist = [4, 3, 0].
Push (4, 0). Note the heap now holds TWO entries for vertex 0: fresh (4, 0) and stale (6, 0). heap = [(4, 0), (6, 0)].
Second neighbour of 1 is (v=2, w=3): nd = 3 + 3 = 6, but dist[2] = 0 — going back to the source is worse, so no update.
Pop the cheapest: (4, 0). Vertex 0 settles at cost 4 via the detour. heap = [(6, 0)].
Relax 0's edge to v=1 (w=1): nd = 4 + 1 = 5, not below dist[1] = 3 — skip.
Relax 0's edge to v=2 (w=6): nd = 4 + 6 = 10, not below dist[2] = 0 — skip. Nothing new is pushed.
Pop the leftover (6, 0) — the OLD entry for vertex 0 from before the detour was found. heap = [].
Staleness guard fires: d=6 > dist[0]=4, meaning vertex 0 was already settled cheaper. 'continue' discards the stale entry without touching anything.
The heap is empty — every reachable vertex has been settled, so the loop ends.
Return [4, 3, 0]: vertex 0 costs 4 (via the 2→1→0 detour), vertex 1 costs 3, and the source costs 0.

Bellman Ford Algorithm.desc: Call bellman_ford(V=4, edges=[[0,1,4],[0,2,5],[1,3,3],[2,1,-2]], src=0). We store 100000000 (10^8) as INF — the judge's sentinel for 'unreachable'.
Create dist with one slot per vertex, all set to ∞: before we look at any edge, no vertex is known to be reachable.
The source costs nothing to reach: dist[0] = 0. This is the seed from which all other distances will grow.
Start pass i=0 of at most V-1 = 3 passes. After pass k, every shortest path using at most k+1 edges is guaranteed final.
Reset the pass flag: updated=False. If a whole sweep of the edges changes nothing, we can stop early.
Edge (0,1,4): dist[0]=0 is known and 0+4=4 < ∞ = dist[1], so this edge relaxes.
Record the cheaper route: dist[1] = 0 + 4 = 4. Vertex 1 is now reachable via the direct edge 0->1.
Mark updated=True: this pass improved at least one distance, so another pass will be worth running.
Edge (0,2,5): dist[0]=0 and 0+5=5 < ∞ = dist[2] — relax it too.
dist[2] = 0 + 5 = 5. Two vertices reached so far, both directly from the source.
Edge (1,3,3): dist[1]=4 (just set!) and 4+3=7 < ∞ = dist[3], so vertex 3 gets its first price.
dist[3] = 4 + 3 = 7 via the path 0->1->3. Careful: this uses dist[1]=4, which is about to become stale...
Edge (2,1,-2): dist[2]=5 and 5+(-2)=3 < 4 = dist[1]. The NEGATIVE edge finds a cheaper route to 1: 0->2->1.
dist[1] drops from 4 to 3. But dist[3]=7 was computed FROM the stale value 4 — this is exactly why one pass is not enough.
Pass 0 ends with updated=True (three relaxations happened), so we do NOT break — the improvements must be propagated.
Pass i=1 begins with dist = [0, 3, 5, 7]. Now paths of up to 2 edges are final; this pass finalises 3-edge paths.
Edge (0,1,4): 0+4=4 is NOT < 3, skip. Edge (0,2,5): 0+5=5 is NOT < 5, skip. The first two edges have nothing left to offer.
Edge (1,3,3): dist[1] is now the fresh 3, and 3+3=6 < 7 = dist[3]. The improvement from pass 0 propagates one edge further.
dist[3] = 3 + 3 = 6 via 0->2->1->3, a 3-edge path. updated flips to True again.
Edge (2,1,-2): 5-2=3 is NOT < 3 = dist[1] — no more juice in the negative edge. Pass 1 made exactly one improvement.
Pass i=2 (the last allowed pass) begins. dist = [0, 3, 5, 6].
All four edges are tested: 0+4≥3, 0+5≥5, 3+3≥6, 5-2≥3 — nothing relaxes, so updated stays False for the whole pass.
updated is False, so the distances are provably stable — break out early instead of grinding through more useless passes.
Negative-cycle check: sweep every edge one final time, looking for anything that could STILL improve a distance.
No edge can relax (we just verified stability), so there is no negative cycle reachable from the source — we never return [-1].
Return [0, 3, 5, 6]: vertex 1 via 0->2->1 (cost 3) and vertex 3 via 0->2->1->3 (cost 6) — both use the negative edge.

Floyd Warshall Algorithm.desc: Call floyd_warshall(mat) on the 4x4 matrix shown; n = 4. Cells marked ∞ hold the sentinel 10^8 = 'no direct edge'.
Store the sentinel INF = 10^8. Every relaxation will first check both legs against INF so we never do arithmetic with 'infinity'.
Round k=0: from now on paths may stop over at vertex 0. Invariant: when this round ends, mat[i][j] is the best i->j path using only stopover 0.
i=0: routes 0 -> 0 -> j cost mat[0][0] + mat[0][j] = 0 + mat[0][j] — never an improvement, row 0 is unchanged this round.
i=1: mat[1][0] = ∞ — vertex 1 cannot even reach the stopover 0, so the whole row is skipped with one check. This guard saves the entire inner j loop.
i=2 CAN reach 0 (cost 2). For j=1: via_k = mat[2][0] + mat[0][1] = 2 + 4 = 6 — a brand-new route 2 -> 0 -> 1.
6 < ∞, so mat[2][1] = 6. Vertex 2 could not reach 1 directly; going through 0 connects them for the first time.
Still i=2: for j=3, via_k = 2 + 5 = 7 is NOT < 3 (the direct edge 2->3 is cheaper) — keep 3. For j=2 the leg mat[0][2] is ∞, skipped.
i=3: mat[3][0] = ∞, row skipped. Round k=0 is done — its only discovery was mat[2][1] = 6.
Round k=1: stopovers at {0, 1} are now allowed. Column 1 (ways INTO 1) and row 1 (ways OUT of 1) drive the updates.
i=0 reaches 1 for 4. For j=2: via_k = mat[0][1] + mat[1][2] = 4 + 1 = 5, and mat[0][2] is currently ∞.
mat[0][2] = 5: vertex 0 reaches 2 for the first time, via 0 -> 1 -> 2. Note this fresh value will power round k=2 updates.
The other j values for i=0 hit `continue`: mat[1][0] = ∞ and mat[1][3] = ∞, so stopover 1 offers no route to 0 or 3. i=2 (via 6+1=7 vs 0) and i=3 (∞) also change nothing.
Round k=2: stopovers {0, 1, 2}. Vertex 2 has edges out to 0 and 3, so vertices that can reach 2 are about to profit.
i=1 reaches 2 for 1. For j=0: via_k = mat[1][2] + mat[2][0] = 1 + 2 = 3, versus mat[1][0] = ∞.
mat[1][0] = 3: the path 1 -> 2 -> 0. Vertex 1 finally has a way back to 0.
Still i=1: for j=3, via_k = mat[1][2] + mat[2][3] = 1 + 3 = 4, versus mat[1][3] = ∞.
mat[1][3] = 4 via 1 -> 2 -> 3. Row 1 is now fully finite: [3, 0, 1, 4].
i=0 also reaches 2 (cost 5, found last round): j=3 gives 5 + 3 = 8, NOT < 5 — the existing 0->3 route stays. No other pair improves in round 2.
Round k=3: stopover vertex 3. But look at row 3 of the matrix — vertex 3 has NO outgoing edges at all.
For every i, each inner test finds mat[3][j] = ∞ (j != 3) and hits `continue`; the j=3 detour costs mat[i][3] + 0, never an improvement. Round 3 changes nothing.
All rounds done — return the matrix: every pair now holds its true shortest cost, and row 3 honestly keeps ∞ (vertex 3 can reach nobody).

Minimum Spanning Tree (Prim's Algorithm).desc: Call spanning_tree(V=4, edges=[[0,1,1],[0,2,2],[1,2,3],[1,3,4],[2,3,5]]). Create an empty adjacency slot for each of the 4 vertices.
No vertex is in the tree yet: visited = [F, F, F, F]. The array below shows 1 = in the tree, 0 = outside.
Seed the min-heap with (0, 0): 'vertex 0 may join the tree for free'. Heap entries are (offer_price, vertex).
total = 0 — the running sum of edge weights we actually pay for; it will become the MST weight.
count = 0 vertices absorbed so far; the loop stops the moment count reaches V = 4.
Pop the cheapest offer: (w=0, u=0). The heap is now empty — but not for long.
Vertex 0 is not visited, so it joins the tree as the seed: visited = [T, F, F, F].
Pay the attachment price: total += 0, still 0 — the seed vertex costs nothing.
count = 1: the tree now contains one vertex, {0}, and needs three more.
Publish vertex 0's edges as offers: push (1, 1) and (2, 2). Heap = [(1,1), (2,2)] — cheapest on top.
Pop (w=1, u=1): the cheapest way to grow the tree is the edge 0-1 of weight 1.
Vertex 1 joins the tree: visited = [T, T, F, F]. The tree is now the edge 0-1.
total = 0 + 1 = 1, and count becomes 2 on the next line. First real edge paid for.
Offers from vertex 1: neighbour 0 is visited (skipped by the if), push (3, 2) and (4, 3). Heap = [(2,2), (3,2), (4,3)].
Pop (w=2, u=2): vertex 2's cheapest offer is the direct edge 0-2 (2), beating 1-2 (3) which is still in the heap.
Vertex 2 joins: visited = [T, T, T, F], total = 1 + 2 = 3, count = 3.
Offers from vertex 2: neighbours 0 and 1 are visited, so only (5, 3) is pushed. Heap = [(3,2), (4,3), (5,3)].
Pop (w=3, u=2) — but wait, vertex 2 is ALREADY in the tree. This is the stale offer from edge 1-2.
visited[2] is True, so the stale entry is discarded with `continue` — this one line is what makes lazy deletion safe.
Pop (w=4, u=3): vertex 3's cheapest attachment is the edge 1-3 of weight 4 (cheaper than 2-3 of weight 5).
Vertex 3 joins: visited = [T, T, T, T], total = 3 + 4 = 7, count = 4 — every vertex is in the tree.
Back at the loop condition: count (4) is no longer < V (4), so the loop exits — the leftover offer (5, 3) is never even popped.
Return total = 7: the MST used edges 0-1 (1), 0-2 (2) and 1-3 (4), and correctly skipped 1-2 (3) and 2-3 (5).

Minimum Spanning Tree (Kruskal's Algorit.desc: Call spanning_tree(V=4, edges=[[0,1,1],[0,2,2],[1,2,3],[1,3,4],[2,3,5]]). DSU starts with everyone their own root: parent = [0, 1, 2, 3].
rank = [0, 0, 0, 0]: every DSU tree is a lone vertex of height 0. Rank only grows when two equal-height trees merge.
total = 0: the running sum of accepted edge weights — this number becomes the MST weight.
used = 0 edges accepted so far; we can stop the moment used hits V-1 = 3, because a spanning tree of 4 vertices has exactly 3 edges.
Sort edges by weight: [(0,1,1), (0,2,2), (1,2,3), (1,3,4), (2,3,5)] (already ascending here). First edge: u=0, v=1, w=1.
find(0) = 0 and find(1) = 1: both vertices are their own roots, so they sit in different components.
ru (0) != rv (1) — the edge connects two separate pieces, so it is safe: no cycle possible. We keep it.
Ranks are equal (0 == 0) so no swap happens; hang root 1 under root 0: parent[1] = 0. Components {0} and {1} are now one piece.
The merged trees had equal rank, so the result is taller: rank[0] becomes 1. rank = [1, 0, 0, 0].
Accept the edge 0-1: total = 0 + 1 = 1.
used = 1 of the 3 edges a spanning tree of 4 vertices needs.
Next cheapest edge: u=0, v=2, w=2.
find(0) = 0 (a root) and find(2) = 2 (its own root) — different components again.
rank[0] = 1 > rank[2] = 0, so no swap: the short tree {2} hangs under the taller root 0. parent = [0, 0, 0, 3].
Accept edge 0-2: total = 1 + 2 = 3. Ranks were unequal, so rank[0] stays 1 — the tree did not get taller.
used = 2; one more edge and the spanning tree is finished.
Next edge: u=1, v=2, w=3 — but careful, vertices 1 and 2 might already be connected...
find(1): parent[1] = 0 and parent[0] = 0, so root 0. find(2): parent[2] = 0, root 0 too. SAME root!
ru == rv == 0: vertices 1 and 2 are already connected (via 1-0-2), so edge 1-2 would close the cycle 0-1-2. Skip it — this is Kruskal's whole safety rule.
Next edge: u=1, v=3, w=4.
find(1) = 0 (climbs 1 -> 0), find(3) = 3 (still alone). Different components — vertex 3 finally gets connected.
rank[0] = 1 > rank[3] = 0: hang {3} under root 0. parent = [0, 0, 0, 0] — a single component containing everyone.
Accept edge 1-3: total = 3 + 4 = 7.
used = 3, which equals V - 1 — the spanning tree is structurally complete.
used == V-1 triggers the early exit: edge (2,3,5) is never examined. On big graphs this skip saves real time.
Return total = 7: the MST is {0-1 (1), 0-2 (2), 1-3 (4)}; the cycle edge 1-2 (3) and the heavy edge 2-3 (5) were rightly left out.

Maximum Sum of Non-Adjacent Elements.desc: Call maxSumNonAdjacent with nums = [2, 1, 4, 9]. We will keep just two rolling values instead of a whole dp table.
Base case: with only index 0 available the best sum is nums[0] = 2, so prev = 2.
prev2 = 0: the best sum of an empty prefix (two steps before index 1) is 0 — nothing picked yet.
Loop starts with i = 1, scanning value nums[1] = 1. prev = 2 covers prefix [2], prev2 = 0 covers the empty prefix.
TAKE choice: take = nums[1] + prev2 = 1 + 0 = 1. Taking index 1 bans index 0, so we may only add the empty-prefix best.
SKIP choice: skip = prev = 2. If we ignore nums[1], the best so far is still just {2}.
curr = max(take, skip) = max(1, 2) = 2. For prefix [2, 1] the best plan is to keep the 2 and skip the 1.
Slide the window, first half: prev2 takes prev's old value 2 — the prefix ending at index 0 is now 'two steps back'.
Slide, second half: prev = curr = 2. The rolling pair now describes prefixes ending at indices 0 and 1.
Next iteration: i = 2 scans value nums[2] = 4. Currently prev = 2 (prefix [2,1]) and prev2 = 2 (prefix [2]).
take = nums[2] + prev2 = 4 + 2 = 6: take the 4, and because index 1 is banned we pair it with the best of prefix [2].
skip = prev = 2: refusing the 4 leaves the previous best of 2 untouched.
curr = max(6, 2) = 6. Taking wins: the subset {2, 4} is the best for prefix [2, 1, 4].
Slide: prev2 becomes the old prev = 2 (best for the prefix ending at index 1).
Slide: prev becomes curr = 6. Rolling pair is now (prev2 = 2, prev = 6).
Final iteration: i = 3 scans nums[3] = 9, the last element. prev = 6 (prefix [2,1,4]), prev2 = 2 (prefix [2,1]).
take = 9 + prev2 = 9 + 2 = 11: take the 9, skip its neighbour 4, and add the best of prefix [2, 1] which is 2.
skip = prev = 6: without the 9 we would stay at the {2, 4} plan worth 6.
curr = max(11, 6) = 11. Taking the 9 clearly wins — subset {2, 9}.
Slide once more: prev2 = 6 — kept only for consistency, the loop is about to end.
prev = curr = 11: the best non-adjacent sum for the entire array is now stored in prev.
Loop finished — return prev = 11, achieved by picking values 2 (index 0) and 9 (index 3).

House Robber.desc: Call rob with nums = [1, 2, 3, 1]. The houses form a circle, so house 0 and house 3 are neighbours.
n = len(nums) = 4 houses on the circle.
Guard check: n == 1? No — 4 houses, so we proceed to the two-case circle-breaking plan.
Case A: drop the LAST house. Slice nums[:-1] = [1, 2, 3] and call rob_line on this straight street.
Inside rob_line for Case A: prev = 0 — best loot before seeing any house is nothing.
prev2 = 0 as well — the 'two houses back' best is also empty at the start.
First house of the line: money = 1 (index 0 of [1, 2, 3]).
take = money + prev2 = 1 + 0 = 1: rob this house on top of the (empty) best from two back.
curr = max(take, prev) = max(1, 0) = 1 — robbing the first house beats skipping it.
Slide the window: prev2 = 0 (old prev), prev = 1 (curr). Best after house 0 is 1.
Next house: money = 2 (index 1). Rolling pair is prev = 1, prev2 = 0.
take = 2 + prev2 = 2 + 0 = 2: robbing house 1 forces us to skip house 0.
curr = max(2, 1) = 2 — the {house 1} plan beats the {house 0} plan by 1.
Slide: prev2 = 1, prev = 2. Best using houses 0..1 of this line is 2.
Last house of Case A: money = 3 (index 2). prev = 2, prev2 = 1.
take = 3 + prev2 = 3 + 1 = 4: rob house 2 together with the best that skipped house 1 (which was {house 0} = 1).
curr = max(4, 2) = 4 — taking wins; the plan is houses 0 and 2 of this line.
Final slide of Case A: prev2 = 2, prev = 4.
rob_line returns prev = 4, so case_a = 4: the best loot when the LAST house of the circle is off-limits.
Case B: drop the FIRST house. Slice nums[1:] = [2, 3, 1] and run rob_line again with fresh prev/prev2.
Case B, first house: money = 2, prev = 0, prev2 = 0, so take = 2 + 0 = 2.
curr = max(2, 0) = 2 — rob the first house of this line.
Slide: prev2 = 0, prev = 2 after house 0 of Case B.
Case B, second house: money = 3, take = 3 + prev2 = 3 + 0 = 3.
curr = max(3, 2) = 3 — the lone house worth 3 beats the lone house worth 2.
Slide: prev2 = 2, prev = 3 after house 1 of Case B.
Case B, last house: money = 1, take = 1 + prev2 = 1 + 2 = 3 (houses worth 2 and 1 together).
curr = max(3, 3) = 3 — a tie: {2, 1} equals the lone {3}; either way the best is 3.
rob_line returns 3, so case_b = 3: the best loot when the FIRST house of the circle is off-limits.
Answer = max(case_a, case_b) = max(4, 3) = 4: rob houses 0 and 2 of the original circle for 1 + 3 = 4.

Frog Jump.desc: Call frogJump with heights = [10, 20, 30, 10]. We must move the frog from stone 0 to stone 3 as cheaply as possible.
n = 4 stones in total; the target is stone index 3.
prev = 0: reaching stone 0 costs nothing — the frog starts there.
prev2 = 0: placeholder for 'cost to reach stone i-2'; it becomes meaningful once i = 2.
Loop starts: i = 1, solving the cheapest way to stand on stone 1 (height 20).
Hop option: one = prev + |20 - 10| = 0 + 10 = 10 — come from stone 0 and climb 10 units.
Leap option starts as two = inf: there is no stone i-2 = -1, so leaping here is impossible.
Guard: is i > 1? 1 > 1 is False, so line 15 is skipped and two stays infinite.
curr = min(10, inf) = 10: the cheapest way to stand on stone 1 costs 10 energy.
Slide the window: prev2 = 0 (stone 0's cost), prev = 10 (stone 1's cost).
Next: i = 2, stone of height 30. Known: stone 1 costs 10 (prev), stone 0 costs 0 (prev2).
Reset the leap option to inf before testing whether a two-stone leap is legal here.
i = 2 > 1, so the leap is legal: two = prev2 + |30 - 10| = 0 + 20 = 20 — jump straight from stone 0.
curr = min(20, 20) = 20: both routes to stone 2 tie at 20 energy.
Slide: prev2 = 10 (stone 1), prev = 20 (stone 2).
Final iteration: i = 3, the target stone of height 10. prev = 20 (stone 2), prev2 = 10 (stone 1).
Hop from stone 2: one = 20 + |10 - 30| = 20 + 20 = 40 — expensive, we would climb to 30 then drop 20.
Leap from stone 1 (after resetting two to inf and passing the i > 1 guard): two = 10 + |10 - 20| = 10 + 10 = 20.
curr = min(40, 20) = 20: leaping over the tall stone 2 halves the cost — this is why greedy fails and DP wins.
Last slide: prev2 = 20, prev = 20. prev now holds the answer for the final stone.
Loop done — return prev = 20. Cheapest route: 0 -> 1 -> 3, paying 10 + 10.

Frog Jump with K Distance.desc: Call frogJumpK with heights = [10, 5, 20, 0, 15] and k = 2: from each stone the frog may jump 1 or 2 ahead.
n = 5 stones; our goal is the cheapest cost to stand on stone 4.
Allocate dp = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. dp[0] = 0 is already correct: the frog starts on stone 0 for free.
Outer loop: i = 1. We now price stone 1 (height 5) using already-final earlier stones.
best = inf — no arrival route for stone 1 has been priced yet.
Inner loop: j = 1, considering a jump from stone i - j = 0.
cost = dp[0] + |heights[1] - heights[0]| = 0 + |5 - 10| = 5.
best = min(inf, 5) = 5 — first candidate route recorded.
Inner loop continues: j = 2, which would mean launching from stone i - j = -1.
Bounds check: i - j = 1 - 2 = -1 is negative — stone -1 does not exist. Without this check Python would silently read dp[-1], the LAST cell!
break: larger j only goes further off the edge, so the inner loop ends for i = 1.
Lock in dp[1] = best = 5. dp is now [0, 5, 0, 0, 0] — stone 1 is final forever.
Outer loop: i = 2, pricing stone 2 (height 20). Candidates: stones 1 and 0.
j = 1: cost = dp[1] + |20 - 5| = 5 + 15 = 20 — via stone 1 the big climb is expensive.
best = min(inf, 20) = 20 so far for stone 2.
j = 2: cost = dp[0] + |20 - 10| = 0 + 10 = 10 — leaping straight from stone 0 skips the dip at stone 1.
best = min(20, 10) = 10 — the direct leap wins for stone 2.
Outer loop: i = 3, pricing stone 3 (height 0). Candidates: stones 2 and 1.
j = 1: cost = dp[2] + |0 - 20| = 10 + 20 = 30 — dropping from the tall stone 2 is costly.
best = min(inf, 30) = 30 after the first candidate.
j = 2: cost = dp[1] + |0 - 5| = 5 + 5 = 10 — arriving from the low stone 1 is far cheaper.
best = min(30, 10) = 10 — the two-stone leap wins again.
Final outer iteration: i = 4, the destination stone (height 15). Candidates: stones 3 and 2.
j = 1: cost = dp[3] + |15 - 0| = 10 + 15 = 25 — climbing up from the ground-level stone 3.
best = min(inf, 25) = 25 so far for the last stone.
j = 2: cost = dp[2] + |15 - 20| = 10 + 5 = 15 — hop over stone 3 directly from stone 2.
best = min(25, 15) = 15 — route 0 -> 2 -> 4 is the champion.
dp[4] = 15; the finished table is [0, 5, 10, 10, 15].
Return dp[n - 1] = dp[4] = 15: the frog's cheapest journey is 0 -> 2 -> 4 costing 10 + 5.

Climbing Stairs.desc: Call climbStairs with n = 5: count every distinct sequence of 1-steps and 2-steps that reaches step 5.
prev2 = 1: there is exactly one way to 'reach' step 0 — the empty climb (do nothing).
prev = 1: one way to reach step 1 (a single 1-step). The window now covers steps 0 and 1.
Loop starts at step = 2: the first stair whose count is not a base case.
curr = prev + prev2 = 1 + 1 = 2: climbs ending with a 1-step from step 1, plus climbs ending with a 2-step from step 0.
Slide the window: prev2 = 1 (old prev, ways to reach step 1).
prev = curr = 2. The window now stores ways(1) = 1 and ways(2) = 2.
Next loop turn: step = 3. Window holds prev = 2 (step 2) and prev2 = 1 (step 1).
curr = 2 + 1 = 3: the three climbs to step 3 are 1+1+1, 1+2 and 2+1.
Slide: prev2 = 2, remembering ways(2) as the new 'two steps below'.
prev = 3: the window has moved up to cover steps 2 and 3.
step = 4. Window: prev = 3 (ways to step 3), prev2 = 2 (ways to step 2).
curr = 3 + 2 = 5 ways to reach step 4 — Fibonacci is emerging: 1, 1, 2, 3, 5.
Slide: prev2 = 3, the count for step 3 moves into the 'two below' slot.
prev = 5. Window now covers steps 3 and 4.
Final loop turn: step = 5 = n. Window: prev = 5, prev2 = 3.
curr = 5 + 3 = 8: eight distinct move sequences climb a 5-step staircase.
Slide one last time: prev2 = 5 (ways to reach step 4).
prev = 8 — the loop range(2, 6) is exhausted, so we exit the loop.
Return prev = 8: the number of distinct ways to climb 5 stairs with 1- and 2-steps.

Coin Change.desc: Iterate i = 1. coin = 1 fits. dp[1] = min(4, dp[0] + 1) = 1. coin = 2 does not fit.
Iterate i = 2. coin = 1 fits: dp[2] = min(4, dp[1] + 1) = 2. coin = 2 fits: dp[2] = min(2, dp[0] + 1) = 1.
Iterate i = 3. coin = 1 fits: dp[3] = min(4, dp[2] + 1) = 2. coin = 2 fits: dp[3] = min(2, dp[1] + 1) = 2.

Coin Change II.desc: Create dp of length amount+1 = 6, all zeros. dp[i] will count the number of coin COMBINATIONS that sum to i.
Base case dp[0] = 1: there is exactly one way to make amount 0 — pick nothing at all. Every other entry stays 0 for now.
Outer loop takes coin = 1. Looping over coins on the OUTSIDE is what stops us from counting 1+2 and 2+1 as two different answers.
Inner loop: i = 1. We ask how many ways to make 1 while allowed to use coin 1 (amounts below 1 cannot use it, so the range starts at 1).
dp[1] += dp[1-1] -> dp[1] = 0 + dp[0](1) = 1. Every combination that made 0 becomes a combination for 1 by adding one coin of 1.
Inner loop: i = 2. We ask how many ways to make 2 while allowed to use coin 1 (amounts below 1 cannot use it, so the range starts at 1).
dp[2] += dp[2-1] -> dp[2] = 0 + dp[1](1) = 1. Every combination that made 1 becomes a combination for 2 by adding one coin of 1.
Inner loop: i = 3. We ask how many ways to make 3 while allowed to use coin 1 (amounts below 1 cannot use it, so the range starts at 1).
dp[3] += dp[3-1] -> dp[3] = 0 + dp[2](1) = 1. Every combination that made 2 becomes a combination for 3 by adding one coin of 1.
Inner loop: i = 4. We ask how many ways to make 4 while allowed to use coin 1 (amounts below 1 cannot use it, so the range starts at 1).
dp[4] += dp[4-1] -> dp[4] = 0 + dp[3](1) = 1. Every combination that made 3 becomes a combination for 4 by adding one coin of 1.
Inner loop: i = 5. We ask how many ways to make 5 while allowed to use coin 1 (amounts below 1 cannot use it, so the range starts at 1).
dp[5] += dp[5-1] -> dp[5] = 0 + dp[4](1) = 1. Every combination that made 4 becomes a combination for 5 by adding one coin of 1.
Outer loop takes coin = 2. Looping over coins on the OUTSIDE is what stops us from counting 1+2 and 2+1 as two different answers.
Inner loop: i = 2. We ask how many ways to make 2 while allowed to use coin 2 (amounts below 2 cannot use it, so the range starts at 2).
dp[2] += dp[2-2] -> dp[2] = 1 + dp[0](1) = 2. Every combination that made 0 becomes a combination for 2 by adding one coin of 2.
Inner loop: i = 3. We ask how many ways to make 3 while allowed to use coin 2 (amounts below 2 cannot use it, so the range starts at 2).
dp[3] += dp[3-2] -> dp[3] = 1 + dp[1](1) = 2. Every combination that made 1 becomes a combination for 3 by adding one coin of 2.
Inner loop: i = 4. We ask how many ways to make 4 while allowed to use coin 2 (amounts below 2 cannot use it, so the range starts at 2).
dp[4] += dp[4-2] -> dp[4] = 1 + dp[2](2) = 3. Every combination that made 2 becomes a combination for 4 by adding one coin of 2.
Inner loop: i = 5. We ask how many ways to make 5 while allowed to use coin 2 (amounts below 2 cannot use it, so the range starts at 2).
dp[5] += dp[5-2] -> dp[5] = 1 + dp[3](2) = 3. Every combination that made 3 becomes a combination for 5 by adding one coin of 2.
Outer loop takes coin = 5. Looping over coins on the OUTSIDE is what stops us from counting 1+2 and 2+1 as two different answers.
Inner loop: i = 5. We ask how many ways to make 5 while allowed to use coin 5 (amounts below 5 cannot use it, so the range starts at 5).
dp[5] += dp[5-5] -> dp[5] = 3 + dp[0](1) = 4. Every combination that made 0 becomes a combination for 5 by adding one coin of 5.
The inner loop for coin = 5 had only i = 5, and the outer loop has no coins left, so both loops finish.
Return dp[5] = 4. The four combinations are 5, 1+1+1+1+1, 1+2+2 and 1+1+1+2.

0/1 Knapsack.desc: n = len(wt) = 3, so there are three items: (weight 1, value 15), (weight 3, value 20) and (weight 4, value 30). Capacity W = 5.
dp has 6 slots, all 0. dp[w] = best value reachable with capacity w using the items considered SO FAR. With zero items every capacity is worth 0.
Outer loop: i = 0, offering item 0 (weight 1, value 15). dp currently reflects items 0..-1.
w = 5. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 1) so dp[4] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 0 from being used twice.
Skip item 0: value 0. Take item 0: 15 + dp[5-1] = 15 + 0 = 15. Compare 0 vs 15 — taking it wins, so dp[5] = 15.
w = 4. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 1) so dp[3] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 0 from being used twice.
Skip item 0: value 0. Take item 0: 15 + dp[4-1] = 15 + 0 = 15. Compare 0 vs 15 — taking it wins, so dp[4] = 15.
w = 3. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 1) so dp[2] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 0 from being used twice.
Skip item 0: value 0. Take item 0: 15 + dp[3-1] = 15 + 0 = 15. Compare 0 vs 15 — taking it wins, so dp[3] = 15.
w = 2. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 1) so dp[1] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 0 from being used twice.
Skip item 0: value 0. Take item 0: 15 + dp[2-1] = 15 + 0 = 15. Compare 0 vs 15 — taking it wins, so dp[2] = 15.
w = 1. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 1) so dp[0] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 0 from being used twice.
Skip item 0: value 0. Take item 0: 15 + dp[1-1] = 15 + 0 = 15. Compare 0 vs 15 — taking it wins, so dp[1] = 15.
Outer loop: i = 1, offering item 1 (weight 3, value 20). dp currently reflects items 0..0.
w = 5. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 3) so dp[2] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 1 from being used twice.
Skip item 1: value 15. Take item 1: 20 + dp[5-3] = 20 + 15 = 35. Compare 15 vs 35 — taking it wins, so dp[5] = 35.
w = 4. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 3) so dp[1] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 1 from being used twice.
Skip item 1: value 15. Take item 1: 20 + dp[4-3] = 20 + 15 = 35. Compare 15 vs 35 — taking it wins, so dp[4] = 35.
w = 3. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 3) so dp[0] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 1 from being used twice.
Skip item 1: value 15. Take item 1: 20 + dp[3-3] = 20 + 0 = 20. Compare 15 vs 20 — taking it wins, so dp[3] = 20.
Outer loop: i = 2, offering item 2 (weight 4, value 30). dp currently reflects items 0..1.
w = 5. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 4) so dp[1] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 2 from being used twice.
Skip item 2: value 35. Take item 2: 30 + dp[5-4] = 30 + 15 = 45. Compare 35 vs 45 — taking it wins, so dp[5] = 45.
w = 4. We sweep capacities DOWNWARD (5 down to 4) so dp[0] still belongs to the previous row — that is what keeps item 2 from being used twice.
Skip item 2: value 35. Take item 2: 30 + dp[4-4] = 30 + 0 = 30. Compare 35 vs 30 — skipping wins, so dp[4] stays 35.
Return dp[5] = 45. The winning pack is item 0 (weight 1, value 15) plus item 2 (weight 4, value 30): total weight 5, total value 45.

Unbounded Knapsack.desc: n = len(wt) = 2. Item 0 weighs 2 and is worth 5; item 1 weighs 3 and is worth 8. Each item may be picked UNLIMITED times. Capacity W = 5.
dp = [0, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0]. dp[w] will hold the best value for a knapsack of exact capacity w. dp[0] = 0 forever: an empty bag is worth nothing.
Outer loop: w = 1. We solve capacities in INCREASING order, so every smaller dp value we need is already final.
i = 0: item 0 weighs 2, and 2 <= 1 is False, so it cannot fit in capacity 1. Skip it and leave dp[1] = 0.
i = 1: item 1 weighs 3, and 3 <= 1 is False, so it cannot fit in capacity 1. Skip it and leave dp[1] = 0.
Outer loop: w = 2. We solve capacities in INCREASING order, so every smaller dp value we need is already final.
i = 0: item 0 weighs 2 and 2 <= 2, so it fits — we may put one copy of it in and fill the leftover capacity 0 optimally.
Candidate = dp[2-2] + 5 = dp[0](0) + 5 = 5, versus current dp[2] = 0. Compare — that is better, so dp[2] becomes 5.
i = 1: item 1 weighs 3, and 3 <= 2 is False, so it cannot fit in capacity 2. Skip it and leave dp[2] = 5.
Outer loop: w = 3. We solve capacities in INCREASING order, so every smaller dp value we need is already final.
i = 0: item 0 weighs 2 and 2 <= 3, so it fits — we may put one copy of it in and fill the leftover capacity 1 optimally.
Candidate = dp[3-2] + 5 = dp[1](0) + 5 = 5, versus current dp[3] = 0. Compare — that is better, so dp[3] becomes 5.
i = 1: item 1 weighs 3 and 3 <= 3, so it fits — we may put one copy of it in and fill the leftover capacity 0 optimally.
Candidate = dp[3-3] + 8 = dp[0](0) + 8 = 8, versus current dp[3] = 5. Compare — that is better, so dp[3] becomes 8.
Outer loop: w = 4. We solve capacities in INCREASING order, so every smaller dp value we need is already final.
i = 0: item 0 weighs 2 and 2 <= 4, so it fits — we may put one copy of it in and fill the leftover capacity 2 optimally.
Candidate = dp[4-2] + 5 = dp[2](5) + 5 = 10, versus current dp[4] = 0. Compare — that is better, so dp[4] becomes 10.
i = 1: item 1 weighs 3 and 3 <= 4, so it fits — we may put one copy of it in and fill the leftover capacity 1 optimally.
Candidate = dp[4-3] + 8 = dp[1](0) + 8 = 8, versus current dp[4] = 10. Compare — that is not better, so dp[4] stays 10.
Outer loop: w = 5. We solve capacities in INCREASING order, so every smaller dp value we need is already final.
i = 0: item 0 weighs 2 and 2 <= 5, so it fits — we may put one copy of it in and fill the leftover capacity 3 optimally.
Candidate = dp[5-2] + 5 = dp[3](8) + 5 = 13, versus current dp[5] = 0. Compare — that is better, so dp[5] becomes 13.
i = 1: item 1 weighs 3 and 3 <= 5, so it fits — we may put one copy of it in and fill the leftover capacity 2 optimally.
Candidate = dp[5-3] + 8 = dp[2](5) + 8 = 13, versus current dp[5] = 13. Compare — that is not better, so dp[5] stays 13.
w has reached 5, the last capacity, so the outer loop is finished and the table is fully built.
Return dp[5] = 13. The best pack is one item 0 (weight 2, value 5) plus one item 1 (weight 3, value 8) = weight 5, value 13.

Rod Cutting Problem.desc: A rod of length 3. price[0] = 1 for length 1, price[1] = 5 for length 2, price[2] = 8 for length 3. dp = [0, 0, 0, 0]; dp[i] = best money from a rod of length i, and dp[0] = 0.
Outer loop: i = 1. We now solve the sub-problem 'best value for a rod of length 1', using the already-final answers dp[0..0].
max_val = -1. This sentinel starts below any real price so the first candidate for length 1 always replaces it.
j = 1: try making the FIRST cut of length 1, sell that piece for price[0] = 1, and leave a rod of length 0 behind.
Candidate = price[0] + dp[0] = 1 + 0 = 1. Compare with max_val = -1: 1 beats -1, so max_val = 1.
All cuts for length 1 have been tried, so dp[1] = max_val = 1 is locked in and can be reused by longer rods.
Outer loop: i = 2. We now solve the sub-problem 'best value for a rod of length 2', using the already-final answers dp[0..1].
max_val = -1. This sentinel starts below any real price so the first candidate for length 2 always replaces it.
j = 1: try making the FIRST cut of length 1, sell that piece for price[0] = 1, and leave a rod of length 1 behind.
Candidate = price[0] + dp[1] = 1 + 1 = 2. Compare with max_val = -1: 2 beats -1, so max_val = 2.
j = 2: try making the FIRST cut of length 2, sell that piece for price[1] = 5, and leave a rod of length 0 behind.
Candidate = price[1] + dp[0] = 5 + 0 = 5. Compare with max_val = 2: 5 beats 2, so max_val = 5.
All cuts for length 2 have been tried, so dp[2] = max_val = 5 is locked in and can be reused by longer rods.
Outer loop: i = 3. We now solve the sub-problem 'best value for a rod of length 3', using the already-final answers dp[0..2].
max_val = -1. This sentinel starts below any real price so the first candidate for length 3 always replaces it.
j = 1: try making the FIRST cut of length 1, sell that piece for price[0] = 1, and leave a rod of length 2 behind.
Candidate = price[0] + dp[2] = 1 + 5 = 6. Compare with max_val = -1: 6 beats -1, so max_val = 6.
j = 2: try making the FIRST cut of length 2, sell that piece for price[1] = 5, and leave a rod of length 1 behind.
Candidate = price[1] + dp[1] = 5 + 1 = 6. Compare with max_val = 6: 6 does not beat 6, so max_val stays 6.
j = 3: try making the FIRST cut of length 3, sell that piece for price[2] = 8, and leave a rod of length 0 behind.
Candidate = price[2] + dp[0] = 8 + 0 = 8. Compare with max_val = 6: 8 beats 6, so max_val = 8.
All cuts for length 3 have been tried, so dp[3] = max_val = 8 is locked in and can be reused by longer rods.
Return dp[3] = 8. Selling the rod whole (one piece of length 3) earns 8, which beats 1+5 = 6 and 1+1+1 = 3.

Longest Common Subsequence.desc: Call longestCommonSubsequence(text1="abcd", text2="acd"). We want the length of the longest string that appears in both, in order (letters may be skipped).
m = len('abcd') = 4 and n = len('acd') = 3.

Build dp as a 5x4 grid of zeros. dp[i][j] will mean: the LCS length of the first i letters of 'abcd' and the first j letters of 'acd'. Row 0 and column 0 stay 0 forever because an empty string shares nothing.
Outer loop starts: i = 1, so we are placing text1[0] = 'a'.
Inner loop starts: j = 1, so we compare against text2[0] = 'a'. We are filling cell dp[1][1].
Compare text1[0] = 'a' with text2[0] = 'a' — they MATCH, so this shared letter can extend whatever was best before both of them.
dp[1][1] = dp[0][0] + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1. On a match we always come from the DIAGONAL, because both letters are consumed.
j = 2 now, comparing against text2[1] = 'c'. Filling dp[1][2].
'a' vs 'c' — no match, so the if is False and we fall to the else.
dp[1][2] = max(dp[0][2], dp[1][1]) = max(0, 1) = 1. On a mismatch we drop one letter — either the last of text1 (look up) or the last of text2 (look left) — and keep the better result.
j = 3, comparing 'a' with text2[2] = 'd'. Filling dp[1][3].
'a' != 'd', so dp[1][3] = max(dp[0][3], dp[1][2]) = max(0, 1) = 1. Row 1 is finished: 'a' alone matches 'acd' with length 1.
i = 2, so text1[1] = 'b' — a letter that does not appear in 'acd' at all.
j = 1: compare 'b' with 'a'. Filling dp[2][1].
'b' != 'a', so dp[2][1] = max(dp[1][1], dp[2][0]) = max(1, 0) = 1 — we inherit the 1 from the row above ('a' vs 'a').
j = 3: 'b' != 'd', so dp[2][3] = max(dp[1][3], dp[2][2]) = max(1, 1) = 1. Row 2 is a straight copy of row 1 — the useless letter 'b' added nothing.
i = 3, so text1[2] = 'c'.
j = 2 — this is the interesting cell dp[3][2], comparing 'c' with text2[1] = 'c'.
'c' == 'c' — a MATCH, the second one we have found.
dp[3][2] = dp[2][1] + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2. The diagonal cell dp[2][1] says 'ab' vs 'a' already share 1 letter; appending the matching 'c' to both makes 2 ('ac').
j = 3: 'c' != 'd', so dp[3][3] = max(dp[2][3], dp[3][2]) = max(1, 2) = 2 — the 2 propagates rightwards.
i = 4, the last row: text1[3] = 'd'.
j = 2: 'd' != 'c', so dp[4][2] = max(dp[3][2], dp[4][1]) = max(2, 1) = 2 — the 2 propagates downwards.
j = 3, the final cell dp[4][3], comparing 'd' with 'd'.
'd' == 'd' — the third and last match.
dp[4][3] = dp[3][2] + 1 = 2 + 1 = 3. Diagonal again: 'abc' vs 'ac' gave 2 ('ac'), and appending the matching 'd' makes 'acd' of length 3.
return dp[4][3] = 3. The bottom-right cell always holds the answer for the full strings: the LCS of 'abcd' and 'acd' is 'acd', length 3.

Longest Common Substring.desc: S1 = "abcd" so n = 4, and S2 = "abd" so m = 3. We are hunting the longest block of characters that appears contiguously in both.
Build a 5x4 table of zeros. dp[i][j] = length of the longest common SUFFIX of S1's first i characters and S2's first j characters. Row 0 and column 0 stay 0 (an empty prefix shares nothing).
max_len = 0. The table's cells are only local suffix lengths, so we must remember the biggest value we ever write.
Outer loop: i = 1, so we are matching S1[0] = 'a' against every character of S2.
j = 1: compare S1[0] = 'a' with S2[0] = 'a' and fill cell dp[1][1].
'a' == 'a' — the characters match, so the common run can be extended by one.
dp[1][1] = dp[0][0] + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1. We inherit the run that ended just before both characters (the diagonal cell) and add this matching pair.
max_len = max(0, dp[1][1] = 1): 1 beats 0, so max_len = 1.
j = 2: compare S1[0] = 'a' with S2[1] = 'b' and fill cell dp[1][2].
'a' != 'b', so dp[1][2] = 0. A substring must be contiguous: one mismatch breaks the run completely, unlike the subsequence version which would carry a value over.
j = 3: compare S1[0] = 'a' with S2[2] = 'd' and fill cell dp[1][3].
'a' != 'd', so dp[1][3] = 0. A substring must be contiguous: one mismatch breaks the run completely, unlike the subsequence version which would carry a value over.
Outer loop: i = 2, so we are matching S1[1] = 'b' against every character of S2.
j = 1: compare S1[1] = 'b' with S2[0] = 'a' and fill cell dp[2][1].
'b' != 'a', so dp[2][1] = 0. A substring must be contiguous: one mismatch breaks the run completely, unlike the subsequence version which would carry a value over.
j = 2: compare S1[1] = 'b' with S2[1] = 'b' and fill cell dp[2][2].
'b' == 'b' — the characters match, so the common run can be extended by one.
dp[2][2] = dp[1][1] + 1 = 1 + 1 = 2. We inherit the run that ended just before both characters (the diagonal cell) and add this matching pair.
max_len = max(1, dp[2][2] = 2): 2 beats 1, so max_len = 2.
j = 3: compare S1[1] = 'b' with S2[2] = 'd' and fill cell dp[2][3].
'b' != 'd', so dp[2][3] = 0. A substring must be contiguous: one mismatch breaks the run completely, unlike the subsequence version which would carry a value over.
Outer loop: i = 3, so we are matching S1[2] = 'c' against every character of S2.
'c' != 'a', so dp[3][1] = 0. A substring must be contiguous: one mismatch breaks the run completely, unlike the subsequence version which would carry a value over.
'c' != 'b', so dp[3][2] = 0. A substring must be contiguous: one mismatch breaks the run completely, unlike the subsequence version which would carry a value over.
'c' != 'd', so dp[3][3] = 0. A substring must be contiguous: one mismatch breaks the run completely, unlike the subsequence version which would carry a value over.
Outer loop: i = 4, so we are matching S1[3] = 'd' against every character of S2.
'd' != 'a', so dp[4][1] = 0. A substring must be contiguous: one mismatch breaks the run completely, unlike the subsequence version which would carry a value over.
'd' != 'b', so dp[4][2] = 0. A substring must be contiguous: one mismatch breaks the run completely, unlike the subsequence version which would carry a value over.
j = 3: compare S1[3] = 'd' with S2[2] = 'd' and fill cell dp[4][3].
'd' == 'd' — the characters match, so the common run can be extended by one.
dp[4][3] = dp[3][2] + 1 = 0 + 1 = 1. We inherit the run that ended just before both characters (the diagonal cell) and add this matching pair.
max_len = max(2, dp[4][3] = 1): 1 does not beat 2, so max_len stays 2.
Return max_len = 2. The best cell was dp[2][2] = 2, which corresponds to the shared substring "ab" ending at S1[1] and S2[1]. Note dp[4][3] = 1 for the shared "d" never overtook it.

Longest Palindromic Subsequence.desc: s = "bbab", so n = 4. We want the longest subsequence (characters in order, gaps allowed) that reads the same forwards and backwards.
dp is a 4x4 grid of zeros. dp[i][j] = LPS length inside the substring s[i..j]. Only the upper triangle (i <= j) is meaningful; the lower half stays 0 and that turns out to be useful.
First loop: walk i from 0 to 3 to seed the main diagonal, the smallest sub-problems.
Base case dp[0][0] = 1: the single character 'b' at index 0 is by itself a palindrome of length 1.
Base case dp[1][1] = 1: the single character 'b' at index 1 is by itself a palindrome of length 1.
Base case dp[2][2] = 1: the single character 'a' at index 2 is by itself a palindrome of length 1.
Base case dp[3][3] = 1: the single character 'b' at index 3 is by itself a palindrome of length 1.
length = 2: solve every substring of exactly 2 characters. Shorter substrings are already done, which is why we grow by length instead of by index.
Start index i = 0, so j = i + length - 1 = 0 + 2 - 1 = 1. The window is s[0..1] = "bb".
The boundary characters match: s[0] = 'b' and s[1] = 'b'. Both can safely wrap around whatever palindrome lives strictly inside.
dp[0][1] = dp[1][0] + 2 = 0 + 2 = 2. Here dp[1][0] is in the unused lower triangle and equals 0, which correctly represents the empty inside of a 2-character window.
Start index i = 1, so j = i + length - 1 = 1 + 2 - 1 = 2. The window is s[1..2] = "ba".
s[1] = 'b' and s[2] = 'a' differ, so they cannot both be palindrome endpoints. We must drop one of them.
Start index i = 2, so j = i + length - 1 = 2 + 2 - 1 = 3. The window is s[2..3] = "ab".
s[2] = 'a' and s[3] = 'b' differ, so they cannot both be palindrome endpoints. We must drop one of them.
length = 3: solve every substring of exactly 3 characters. Shorter substrings are already done, which is why we grow by length instead of by index.
Start index i = 0, so j = i + length - 1 = 0 + 3 - 1 = 2. The window is s[0..2] = "bba".
s[0] = 'b' and s[2] = 'a' differ, so they cannot both be palindrome endpoints. We must drop one of them.
Start index i = 1, so j = i + length - 1 = 1 + 3 - 1 = 3. The window is s[1..3] = "bab".
The boundary characters match: s[1] = 'b' and s[3] = 'b'. Both can safely wrap around whatever palindrome lives strictly inside.
dp[1][3] = dp[2][2] + 2 = 1 + 2 = 3. Here dp[2][2] = 1 is the LPS of the inner window "a".
length = 4: solve every substring of exactly 4 characters. Shorter substrings are already done, which is why we grow by length instead of by index.
Start index i = 0, so j = i + length - 1 = 0 + 4 - 1 = 3. The window is s[0..3] = "bbab".
The boundary characters match: s[0] = 'b' and s[3] = 'b'. Both can safely wrap around whatever palindrome lives strictly inside.
dp[0][3] = dp[1][2] + 2 = 1 + 2 = 3. Here dp[1][2] = 1 is the LPS of the inner window "ba".
Return dp[0][3] = 3 — the LPS of the whole string "bbab" is "bab" (or equally "bbb"), length 3.

Edit Distance.desc: word1 = "sea" so m = 3, word2 = "eat" so n = 3. We want the fewest insert / delete / replace operations that turn "sea" into "eat".
dp is a 4x4 grid of zeros. dp[i][j] = edit distance between the first i characters of "sea" and the first j characters of "eat".
dp[0][0] = 0: turning the first 0 characters of "sea" ("") into the empty string costs 0 deletion(s).
dp[1][0] = 1: turning the first 1 characters of "sea" ("s") into the empty string costs 1 deletion(s).
dp[2][0] = 2: turning the first 2 characters of "sea" ("se") into the empty string costs 2 deletion(s).
dp[3][0] = 3: turning the first 3 characters of "sea" ("sea") into the empty string costs 3 deletion(s).
dp[0][1] = 1: turning the empty string into "e" costs 1 insertion(s).
dp[0][2] = 2: turning the empty string into "ea" costs 2 insertion(s).
dp[0][3] = 3: turning the empty string into "eat" costs 3 insertion(s).
Outer loop: i = 1, working on word1[0] = 's' and filling row 1 of the table.
j = 1: compare word1[0] = 's' with word2[0] = 'e' to fill dp[1][1].
's' != 'e', so we pay 1 operation plus the cheapest neighbour: insert dp[1][0] = 1, delete dp[0][1] = 1, replace dp[0][0] = 0. The minimum is 0 (replace), so dp[1][1] = 1 + 0 = 1.
j = 2: compare word1[0] = 's' with word2[1] = 'a' to fill dp[1][2].
's' != 'a', so we pay 1 operation plus the cheapest neighbour: insert dp[1][1] = 1, delete dp[0][2] = 2, replace dp[0][1] = 1. The minimum is 1 (insert), so dp[1][2] = 1 + 1 = 2.
's' != 't', so we pay 1 operation plus the cheapest neighbour: insert dp[1][2] = 2, delete dp[0][3] = 3, replace dp[0][2] = 2. The minimum is 2 (insert), so dp[1][3] = 1 + 2 = 3.
Outer loop: i = 2, working on word1[1] = 'e' and filling row 2 of the table.
j = 1: compare word1[1] = 'e' with word2[0] = 'e' to fill dp[2][1].
'e' == 'e', so the last characters already agree — no operation is needed for this pair.
dp[2][1] = dp[1][0] = 1: the cost is exactly the cost of aligning the shorter prefixes "s" and "".
'e' != 'a', so we pay 1 operation plus the cheapest neighbour: insert dp[2][1] = 1, delete dp[1][2] = 2, replace dp[1][1] = 1. The minimum is 1 (insert), so dp[2][2] = 1 + 1 = 2.
'e' != 't', so we pay 1 operation plus the cheapest neighbour: insert dp[2][2] = 2, delete dp[1][3] = 3, replace dp[1][2] = 2. The minimum is 2 (insert), so dp[2][3] = 1 + 2 = 3.
Outer loop: i = 3, working on word1[2] = 'a' and filling row 3 of the table.
'a' != 'e', so we pay 1 operation plus the cheapest neighbour: insert dp[3][0] = 3, delete dp[2][1] = 1, replace dp[2][0] = 2. The minimum is 1 (delete), so dp[3][1] = 1 + 1 = 2.
j = 2: compare word1[2] = 'a' with word2[1] = 'a' to fill dp[3][2].
'a' == 'a', so the last characters already agree — no operation is needed for this pair.
dp[3][2] = dp[2][1] = 1: the cost is exactly the cost of aligning the shorter prefixes "se" and "e".
j = 3: compare word1[2] = 'a' with word2[2] = 't' to fill dp[3][3].
'a' != 't', so we pay 1 operation plus the cheapest neighbour: insert dp[3][2] = 1, delete dp[2][3] = 3, replace dp[2][2] = 2. The minimum is 1 (insert), so dp[3][3] = 1 + 1 = 2.
Return dp[3][3] = 2. Two operations suffice: delete the 's' from "sea" to get "ea", then insert 't' to get "eat".

Distinct Subsequences.desc: Initialize dp table of size len(t)+1 = 3 with [1, 0, 0] for s = 'ba' and t = 'a'.
Process first char 'b' from s. Inner loop j = 1 down to 1. 'b' != t[0] ('a'). No update.
Process second char 'a' from s. Inner loop j = 1. 'a' == t[0] ('a'). dp[1] += dp[0] => 1.

Wildcard Matching.desc: Loop starts. p[0] is '*', set star_idx = 0, match_idx = 0, p_idx = 1.
Next loop step. s[0] ('a') matches p[1] ('a'). Advance both.
Next loop step. p[2] is '*', set star_idx = 2, match_idx = 1, p_idx = 3.
Next loop step. s[1] ('d') != p[3] ('b'). Backtrack to star: p_idx = 3, match_idx = 2, s_idx = 2 ('c').
Next loop step. s[2] ('c') != p[3] ('b'). Backtrack to star: p_idx = 3, match_idx = 3, s_idx = 3 ('e').
Next loop step. s[3] ('e') != p[3] ('b'). Backtrack to star: p_idx = 3, match_idx = 4, s_idx = 4 ('b').
Next loop step. s[4] ('b') == p[3] ('b'). Advance both.
Loop terminates since s_idx == 5. Verify remaining pattern. None left. Return True.

Longest Increasing Subsequence.desc: Call lengthOfLIS(nums = [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18]). We want the LENGTH of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
tails = []. Key idea: tails[k] will hold the SMALLEST possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k+1. tails is always sorted, so binary search works on it.
Iteration 1: x = nums[0] = 10.
bisect_left([], 10) on an empty list returns 0 — there is nowhere for it to fit.
idx = 0 equals len(tails) = 0, so 10 is bigger than everything we have; it extends the longest chain.
tails.append(10) → tails = [10]. We now know an increasing subsequence of length 1 exists ending at 10.
Iteration 2: x = nums[1] = 9.
bisect_left([10], 9) = 0 — 9 belongs before 10, i.e. it would replace the length-1 chain's tail.
idx = 0 is NOT equal to len(tails) = 1, so we take the else branch instead of appending.
tails[0] = 9 → tails = [9]. The LIS length is still 1, but a chain ending in 9 is more useful than one ending in 10, because more future numbers can be appended after 9.
Iteration 3: x = nums[2] = 2.
bisect_left([9], 2) = 0.
idx = 0 != len(tails) = 1, so again we overwrite rather than grow.
tails[0] = 2 → tails = [2]. Still length 1, but the tail keeps getting smaller and therefore more promising.
Iteration 4: x = nums[3] = 5.
bisect_left([2], 5) = 1 — 5 is greater than 2, so it sorts past the end.
idx = 1 equals len(tails) = 1 → append: 5 can genuinely sit after 2.
tails.append(5) → tails = [2, 5]. The LIS length has grown to 2 (for example 2, 5).
Iteration 5: x = nums[4] = 3.
bisect_left([2, 5], 3) = 1 — 3 slots between 2 and 5.
idx = 1 != len(tails) = 2, so tails[1] = 3 → tails = [2, 3]. This is the crucial move: the answer length is unchanged at 2, but a length-2 chain ending at 3 beats one ending at 5.
Iteration 6: x = nums[5] = 7.
bisect_left([2, 3], 7) = 2 — larger than both.
idx = 2 == len(tails) = 2, so tails.append(7) → tails = [2, 3, 7]. Length is now 3 (2, 3, 7). Note this only worked because we had earlier shrunk the tail from 5 down to 3.
Iteration 7: x = nums[6] = 101.
idx = 3 == len(tails) = 3 → append. tails = [2, 3, 7, 101], LIS length 4 (2, 3, 7, 101).
Iteration 8 (last): x = nums[7] = 18.
bisect_left([2, 3, 7, 101], 18) = 3 — 18 fits between 7 and 101.
idx = 3 != len(tails) = 4, so no growth this time.
tails[3] = 18 → tails = [2, 3, 7, 18]. Length stays 4 but the best length-4 chain now ends at 18 instead of 101.
The for-loop is done, so return len(tails) = 4. Careful: [2, 3, 7, 18] is itself a valid LIS here, but in general tails is NOT the subsequence — only its LENGTH is guaranteed correct.

Largest Divisible Subset.desc: Sort nums. nums = [1, 2, 4, 8]. Initialize dp = [1, 1, 1, 1], parent = [-1, -1, -1, -1].
i = 1 (val 2): check j = 0 (val 1). 2 % 1 == 0, update dp[1] = 2, parent[1] = 0.
i = 2 (val 4): check j = 0, 1. 4 % 2 == 0, update dp[2] = dp[1] + 1 = 3, parent[2] = 1.
i = 3 (val 8): check j = 2. 8 % 4 == 0, update dp[3] = dp[2] + 1 = 4, parent[3] = 2.
Trace back from max_idx = 3: index 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> 0. Values: [8, 4, 2, 1]. Return reverse: [1, 2, 4, 8].

Longest String Chain.desc: Process 'a'. Predecessor by deleting character: ''. Not in dp. dp['a'] = 1. max_chain = 1.
Process 'ba'. Predecessors: 'a' (found, dp['a']+1=2), 'b' (not found). dp['ba'] = 2. max_chain = 2.
Process 'bca'. Predecessors: 'ca' (not found), 'ba' (found, dp['ba']+1=3), 'bc' (not found). dp['bca'] = 3. max_chain = 3.

Bitonic Subsequence.desc: Compute LIS ending at i. For i=1: 3 > 1 => lis[1] = 2. For i=2: 2 > 1 => lis[2] = 2.
Compute LDS starting at i. For i=1: 3 > 2 => lds[1] = 2. For i=0: 1 is not > any, lds[0] = 1.
Compute max bitonic length. i=0: 1+1-1=1. i=1: 2+2-1=3. i=2: 2+1-1=2. Max length is 3.

Matrix Chain Multiplication.desc: Compute n = 3 (matrices A1, A2, A3). Initialize dp of size 4x4 with 0s.

Set Matrix Zeroes.desc: Define function setZeroes. We are given an m x n matrix.
Initialize tracking flag col0 = 1. This variable tracks whether the first column should be zeroed later.
Scan row i=0. Since matrix[0][0] = 1, col0 remains 1. Scan inner cells in row 0; no zeroes found.
Scan row i=1. Check first column: matrix[1][0] = 1 (col0 stays 1). We find an inner zero at matrix[1][1] = 0!
Record the zero by setting markers in the first row & column: matrix[1][0] = 0 and matrix[0][1] = 0.
Scan row i=2. Check first column: matrix[2][0] = 1 (col0 stays 1). We find another inner zero at matrix[2][3] = 0!
Record markers for cell (2, 3): Set matrix[2][0] = 0 and matrix[0][3] = 0.
First pass complete. Now begin backward traversal from bottom-right cell (2, 3) to update cell values.
Updating row i=2. Since markers matrix[2][0] = 0 or matrix[0][j] = 0, inner cells at j=3, j=2, j=1 are zeroed.
Updating row i=1. Check cell j=3 (marker matrix[0][3]=0 zeroed it), cell j=2 (unchanged), cell j=1 (marker matrix[0][1]=0 zeroed it).
Updating row i=0. Check cell j=3 (marker matrix[0][3]=0 zeroed it), cell j=2 (unchanged), cell j=1 (marker matrix[0][1]=0 zeroed it).
Finally, check col0 flag to see if we should zero first column. Since col0 = 1, we do not update first column cells.
Dry run complete! All target cells are correctly zeroed in-place using O(1) extra space markers.

Reverse Linked List.desc: Define reverseList function, taking head of list.
Initialize prev = None. This pointer tracks the reversed part of the list.
Initialize curr = head (Node 1). This pointer traverses the original list.
Loop iteration 1. Save the next node: next_node = curr.next (Node 2). We must save this reference before breaking the link.
Reverse the link direction: curr.next = prev. Node 1 now points back to None (breaking link to Node 2).
Move prev pointer forward to curr: prev = curr (prev becomes Node 1).
Move curr pointer forward to next_node: curr = next_node (curr becomes Node 2). Loop iteration 1 complete.
Loop iteration 2. Save next node reference: next_node = curr.next (Node 3).
Reverse link: curr.next = prev. Node 2 now points to Node 1.
Move prev forward: prev = curr (prev becomes Node 2).
Move curr forward: curr = next_node (curr becomes Node 3). Iteration 2 complete.
Loop iteration 3. Save next node reference: next_node = curr.next (Node 4).
Reverse link: curr.next = prev. Node 3 now points to Node 2.
Move prev forward: prev = curr (prev becomes Node 3).
Move curr forward: curr = next_node (curr becomes Node 4). Iteration 3 complete.
Loop iteration 4. Save next node reference: next_node = curr.next (Node 5).
Reverse link: curr.next = prev. Node 4 now points to Node 3.
Move prev forward: prev = curr (prev becomes Node 4).
Move curr forward: curr = next_node (curr becomes Node 5). Iteration 4 complete.
Loop iteration 5. Save next node reference: next_node = curr.next (None).
Reverse link: curr.next = prev. Node 5 now points to Node 4.
Move prev forward: prev = curr (prev becomes Node 5).
Move curr forward: curr = next_node (None). Iteration 5 complete.
Loop ends since curr is None. Return prev (Node 5), which is now the new head of our fully reversed list in-place!

Pascal's Triangle.desc: Call generate(numRows=4). We create an empty list `triangle` that will collect the finished rows one by one.
Outer loop starts: r=0, the first (top) row of the triangle. range(4) will give us r = 0, 1, 2, 3.
Build row 0 pre-filled with 1s: [1] * (0+1) gives row = [1]. Every row's first and last cell is always 1.
Inner loop for c in range(1, 0) is empty — row 0 has no inner cells between its two edges, so nothing to compute.
Append the finished row [1] to the triangle. The triangle now holds its first row: [[1]].
Outer loop advances: r=1, the second row of the triangle, which will have 2 cells.
Build row 1 pre-filled with 1s: [1] * 2 gives row = [1, 1]. Both cells are edge cells, so they stay 1.
Inner loop for c in range(1, 1) is again empty — row 1 also has no inner cells to fill, only the two edge 1s.
Append [1, 1] to the triangle. Two rows are done: [[1], [1, 1]]. From the next row on, the inner loop finally does work.
Outer loop advances: r=2, the third row, which will have 3 cells — the first row with a true inner cell.
Build row 2 pre-filled with 1s: row = [1, 1, 1]. The middle cell (index 1) is a placeholder we still must overwrite.
Inner loop runs for the first time: c takes the single value 1 (range(1, 2)). We must fill row[1] from the row above.
row[1] = triangle[1][0] + triangle[1][1] = 1 + 1 = 2. Each inner cell is the sum of the two parents above it. row becomes [1, 2, 1].
Append the completed row [1, 2, 1]. The triangle is now [[1], [1, 1], [1, 2, 1]] — three rows done.
Outer loop advances to the final iteration: r=3, the fourth row, which will have 4 cells and 2 inner cells.
Build row 3 pre-filled with 1s: row = [1, 1, 1, 1]. Indices 1 and 2 are inner cells awaiting their sums.
Inner loop starts with c=1 (range(1, 3) gives c = 1, 2). First we compute the cell at index 1.
row[1] = triangle[2][0] + triangle[2][1] = 1 + 2 = 3. Its two parents in the row above are highlighted. row becomes [1, 3, 1, 1].
Inner loop advances: c=2, the second (and last) inner cell of row 3 still needs its value.
row[2] = triangle[2][1] + triangle[2][2] = 2 + 1 = 3. row becomes [1, 3, 3, 1] — the classic fourth row of Pascal's triangle.
Append [1, 3, 3, 1]. All 4 rows are built: [[1], [1, 1], [1, 2, 1], [1, 3, 3, 1]]. The outer loop is now exhausted.
Return the finished triangle [[1], [1, 1], [1, 2, 1], [1, 3, 3, 1]]. Total work: each cell computed exactly once from its two parents.

Next Permutation.desc: Call nextPermutation(nums=[1, 3, 5, 4, 2]). n = len(nums) = 5. We will edit nums in place.
Start i at n-2 = 3, the second-to-last index. We scan right-to-left looking for the first index where the value drops (nums[i] < nums[i+1]).
Check i=3: nums[3]=4 >= nums[4]=2, so the pair (4, 2) is non-increasing — no break point here, keep scanning left.
Condition was True, so we move the scanner one step left: i becomes 2.
Check i=2: nums[2]=5 >= nums[3]=4, still non-increasing (the suffix 5,4,2 is fully descending so far). Keep going left.
Condition was True again, so i moves left once more: i becomes 1.
Check i=1: nums[1]=3 >= nums[2]=5 is False — 3 < 5, the value finally drops! The loop exits with i=1 as the break point.
i=1 >= 0, so a break point exists (the array is not the last permutation). We now hunt for the element to swap with nums[1]=3.
Start j at n-1 = 4 (the last index). Scanning from the right, we want the FIRST element strictly greater than nums[i]=3.
Check j=4: nums[4]=2 <= nums[1]=3, so 2 is too small to be the successor of 3. Move j left.
Condition was True, so j steps left: j becomes 3, now pointing at value 4.
Check j=3: nums[3]=4 <= 3 is False — 4 is strictly greater than 3. Because the suffix is descending, this rightmost 4 is the SMALLEST value bigger than 3.
Swap nums[1] and nums[3]: 3 and 4 trade places. nums becomes [1, 4, 5, 3, 2]. The prefix is now the next-bigger choice; the suffix [5, 3, 2] is still descending.
Set up the suffix reversal: left = i+1 = 2, right = n-1 = 4. Reversing the descending suffix [5, 3, 2] makes it the smallest possible ascending tail.
Check left=2 < right=4 — True, there are still elements to mirror, so enter the reversal loop.
Swap nums[2] and nums[4]: 5 and 2 trade places. nums becomes [1, 4, 2, 3, 5]. The middle element 3 will not need a partner.
Move the left pointer inward: left becomes 3.
Move the right pointer inward: right becomes 3. The two pointers have now met in the middle.
Check left=3 < right=3 — False, the reversal is complete. The function ends: nums was rearranged in place to [1, 4, 2, 3, 5], the next permutation of [1, 3, 5, 4, 2].

Maximum Subarray Sum (Kadane's Algorithm.desc: Call maxSubArray(nums=[-2, 1, -3, 4, -1, 2, 1]). Seed max_sum with the first element: max_sum = -2. This handles all-negative arrays correctly.
Seed current_sum = -2 too: it tracks the best subarray sum that ENDS at the element we are currently looking at.
Loop starts at the second element: x = 1 (index 1). We ask: is it better to extend the old run or start fresh at 1?
current_sum = max(1, -2 + 1) = max(1, -1) = 1. The old run summing to -2 only drags us down, so we START FRESH at index 1.
max_sum = max(-2, 1) = 1. A new best overall sum: the subarray [1] beats [-2].
Next element: x = -3 (index 2). Extending will hurt, but a negative x alone would hurt more — let the max decide.
current_sum = max(-3, 1 + (-3)) = max(-3, -2) = -2. Extending the run [1, -3] is less bad than restarting at -3 alone.
max_sum = max(1, -2) = 1 — no improvement, the record stays at 1.
Next element: x = 4 (index 3). The running sum is -2, which is pure baggage now.
current_sum = max(4, -2 + 4) = max(4, 2) = 4. We DROP the negative prefix and start a brand-new run at index 3 — the key Kadane move.
max_sum = max(1, 4) = 4. New overall record: the subarray [4] is the best seen so far.
Next element: x = -1 (index 4). A small dip — worth absorbing if the run stays positive.
current_sum = max(-1, 4 + (-1)) = max(-1, 3) = 3. We extend: the run [4, -1] still sums to a healthy 3.
max_sum = max(4, 3) = 4 — the record is untouched, but the live run survives.
Next element: x = 2 (index 5). The live run [4, -1] carries sum 3 into this step.
current_sum = max(2, 3 + 2) = max(2, 5) = 5. Extending wins: the run is now [4, -1, 2] with sum 5.
max_sum = max(4, 5) = 5. New overall record thanks to riding through the -1 dip.
Final element: x = 1 (index 6). One last chance to grow the run.
current_sum = max(1, 5 + 1) = max(1, 6) = 6. The run extends to [4, -1, 2, 1] with sum 6.
max_sum = max(5, 6) = 6. The record updates one final time; the loop is now exhausted.
Return max_sum = 6, the sum of the best subarray [4, -1, 2, 1] (indices 3..6), found in one O(n) pass.

Sort Colors.desc: Call sortColors(nums=[2, 0, 2, 1, 1, 0]). Three Dutch-flag pointers: low=0 (next slot for a 0), mid=0 (scanner), high=5 (next slot for a 2).
Check mid=0 <= high=5 — True, the unexplored zone [mid..high] is non-empty, so we process nums[mid].
Inspect nums[mid]=nums[0]=2. It is not 0, so the first branch is skipped.
It is not 1 either, so we land in the else: nums[0]=2 belongs at the back of the array, in the 2s region.
Swap nums[mid]=2 with nums[high]=0: nums becomes [0, 0, 2, 1, 1, 2]. The 2 is parked at the back.
Shrink the 2s frontier: high becomes 4. IMPORTANT: mid does NOT advance — the value swapped in from the back (0) is unexamined and must be re-checked.
Check mid=0 <= high=4 — True, keep going; nums[0] now holds the freshly swapped-in value 0.
Inspect nums[mid]=nums[0]=0 — True this time: a 0 belongs at the front, in the low region.
Swap nums[low] and nums[mid] — both are index 0, so the array is unchanged. The swap is a harmless no-op when low == mid.
Grow the 0s region: low becomes 1. Everything left of low is now guaranteed to be 0.
Advance the scanner too: mid becomes 1. After a low-swap we always know the incoming value was already checked, so mid can move.
Loop continues (1 <= 4). Inspect nums[mid]=nums[1]=0 — another 0 for the front region.
Swap nums[1] with nums[1] — again low == mid, so nothing visibly changes in the array.
Grow the 0s region again: low becomes 2. Indices 0 and 1 are locked in as 0s.
Advance the scanner: mid becomes 2, moving into the unexplored middle zone.
Loop continues (2 <= 4). Inspect nums[mid]=nums[2]=2 — not a 0, and not a 1, so it must go to the back again.
Swap nums[2]=2 with nums[high]=nums[4]=1: nums becomes [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2]. Another 2 parked at the back.
Shrink the 2s frontier: high becomes 3. mid again stays put to re-examine the swapped-in value 1.
Loop continues (2 <= 3). nums[2]=1 is not 0, but the elif matches: nums[mid] == 1. A 1 is already in its natural middle zone.
For a 1 we simply advance the scanner: mid becomes 3. No swap needed — 1s settle between the 0s and 2s automatically.
Loop continues (3 <= 3). nums[3]=1 hits the elif again — another 1 that can stay exactly where it is.
Advance the scanner past it: mid becomes 4, which now exceeds high=3.
Check mid=4 <= high=3 — False: the unexplored zone is empty, so the loop ends. nums is sorted in place to [0, 0, 1, 1, 2, 2] in a single pass with O(1) extra space.

Two Sum.desc: Call twoSum(nums=[3, 5, 2, 7], target=9). Create an empty dict `lookup` that will remember each value we have already seen and its index.
Loop starts: i=0, num=3. enumerate hands us both the index and the value in one pass.
complement = target - num = 9 - 3 = 6. If a 6 existed earlier in the array, it would pair with this 3.
Is 6 in lookup? The dict is empty {}, so no — no earlier element pairs with 3.
Record what we saw: lookup[3] = 0. Now lookup = {3: 0}. Future elements can find 3 in O(1).
Loop advances: i=1, num=5. The dict currently remembers only {3: 0}.
complement = 9 - 5 = 4. We need an earlier 4 to complete the pair with this 5.
Is 4 in lookup {3: 0}? No — 5 has no partner yet, so we keep scanning.
Record lookup[5] = 1. Now lookup = {3: 0, 5: 1} — two candidates waiting for their complements.
Loop advances: i=2, num=2. Still no pair found; the hash map keeps the search O(1) per element.
complement = 9 - 2 = 7. Note: 7 IS in the array — but only at a LATER index, so the dict cannot know it yet.
Is 7 in lookup {3: 0, 5: 1}? No — we only ever look BACKWARD, which is exactly why each pair is found exactly once.
Record lookup[2] = 2. Now lookup = {3: 0, 5: 1, 2: 2}. The 2 now waits for a future 7.
Loop advances: i=3, num=7 — the last element, and the dict holds three earlier values.
complement = 9 - 7 = 2. We need an earlier 2 to pair with this 7.
Is 2 in lookup {3: 0, 5: 1, 2: 2}? YES — the 2 we stored at index 2 completes the pair: 2 + 7 = 9 = target.
Return [lookup[2], i] = [2, 3]: the earlier partner's index first, then the current index. nums[2] + nums[3] = 2 + 7 = 9. Done in one pass.

Longest Consecutive Sequence.desc: We copy nums = [2, 100, 3, 1] into a hash set num_set = {1, 2, 3, 100}. From now on every membership test like 'x in num_set' is O(1) on average instead of an O(n) scan. The array below shows the set's contents.
longest starts at 0 — it will hold the length of the best consecutive run we ever finish counting.
First pass of the for loop: num = 1 (this set happens to iterate in the order 1, 2, 3, 100). We will only spend counting effort on numbers that START a sequence.
Is 1 a sequence start? We look for num - 1 = 0 in the set. 0 is absent, so nothing comes before 1 — it truly starts a run, and we enter the if body to count it.
current_num = 1: this cursor will walk forward along the run 1, 2, 3, ... as far as the set allows.
current_streak = 1: the run already contains one number (the start itself, 1).
While-check: is current_num + 1 = 2 in the set? Yes — the run continues, so we enter the loop body to extend it.
Advance the cursor: current_num becomes 2. We are now standing on the second number of the run.
Count it: current_streak becomes 2. The run so far is 1 -> 2.
While-check again: current_num + 1 = 3 is in the set, so the run keeps going — enter the body once more.
current_num becomes 3 — the third consecutive number found in the set.
current_streak becomes 3. The run is now 1 -> 2 -> 3.
While-check: current_num + 1 = 4 is NOT in the set, so the run 1 -> 2 -> 3 ends here and the while loop exits.
Record the result: longest = max(0, 3) = 3. Our best run so far has length 3.
Next set element: num = 2. Notice we do NOT re-count the run from 2 — the start-check on the next line will reject it instantly.

num - 1 = 1 IS in the set, so 2 sits in the middle of a run that was already counted from its start (1). We skip the whole if body. This skip is exactly why the algorithm is O(n): each number is walked over at most once.
Next set element: num = 3 — the last member of the 1..3 run.
num - 1 = 2 is in the set, so 3 is not a start either — skipped with a single O(1) check, no counting work done.
Last set element: num = 100, far away from the 1..3 run.
num - 1 = 99 is not in the set, so 100 starts its own (possibly tiny) sequence — enter the if body.
current_num = 100: the counting cursor restarts at this new sequence start.
current_streak = 1: the run containing 100 has one member so far.
While-check: 101 is not in the set, so the while body never runs — 100 is a lonely run of length 1.
longest = max(3, 1) = 3 — the streak of 100 cannot beat the 1 -> 2 -> 3 run, so longest stays 3.
The set is exhausted, so the for loop ends. We return longest = 3, the length of the consecutive run 1 -> 2 -> 3.

Find Middle of Linked List.desc: slow starts at the head, the node with value 1. It will crawl one node per loop turn.
fast also starts at the head. It will jump two nodes per turn — so when fast has covered the whole list, slow has covered exactly half.
Loop check: fast is node(1) and fast.next is node(2) — both exist, so it is safe for fast to take a double step. Enter the loop.
slow takes one step: from node(1) to node(2), index 1.
fast takes two steps: 1 -> 2 -> 3, landing on node(3) at index 2. Fast is now one node ahead of slow.
Loop check: fast is node(3), fast.next is node(4) — both non-None, loop again.
slow steps to node(3) at index 2 — it has now covered 2 of the 6 nodes.
fast double-steps 3 -> 4 -> 5, landing on node(5) at index 4. The gap between the pointers grows by one each turn.
Loop check: fast is node(5) and fast.next is node(6) — still safe, one more turn.
slow steps to node(4) at index 3 — this is already the second-middle position of a 6-node list.
fast tries two steps: fast.next is node(6), and node(6).next is None — so fast becomes None, running off the end of the list.
Loop check: fast is None, so 'fast and fast.next' is False — the loop exits. Note the check on fast BEFORE fast.next is what prevents an AttributeError here.
Return slow = node(4) at index 3. Fast covered all 6 nodes in 3 turns, so slow covered 3 — for an even-length list this is the second of the two middle nodes, exactly what the problem asks for.

Merge Two Sorted Linked Lists.desc: Create dummy = ListNode(0) (index 0 in the visual; the cells after it are list1 = 1->3 and list2 = 2->4). The dummy gives us a fixed node to hang the merged list from, so we never special-case 'which node is the head?'.
curr = dummy. curr always marks the tail of the merged chain — the place where the next chosen node gets attached.
Loop check: list1 points at node(1) and list2 at node(2) — both lists still have nodes, so we enter the loop to pick the smaller front.
Compare the two fronts: list1.val = 1 <= list2.val = 2 is True, so node(1) is the smaller one and joins the merged list first.
Attach it: curr.next = list1, so dummy(0) now links to node(1). We re-use the existing node — no new memory.
Advance list1 past the node we just consumed: list1 = list1.next = node(3) at index 2.
Move the tail: curr = curr.next, so curr now sits on node(1) at index 1 — the current end of the merged chain.
Loop check: list1 = node(3), list2 = node(2) — both alive, loop again.
Compare fronts: list1.val = 3 <= list2.val = 2 is False — this time list2's node(2) is smaller, so control falls to the else branch.
Attach the smaller front: curr.next = list2, so node(1) now links across to node(2) at index 3. The merged chain reads 0 -> 1 -> 2.
Advance list2 past its consumed node: list2 = list2.next = node(4) at index 4.
curr moves onto the node just attached: node(2) at index 3 is the new tail of the merged chain.
Loop check: list1 = node(3), list2 = node(4) — both still non-None, enter a third time.
Compare fronts: list1.val = 3 <= list2.val = 4 is True — node(3) wins this round.
curr.next = list1: node(2) links back to node(3) at index 2. Merged chain: 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 3.
Advance list1: node(3) was its last node, so list1 = list1.next = None. list1 is now exhausted.
curr moves to node(3) at index 2 — the tail of the merged chain so far.
Loop check: list1 is None, so 'list1 and list2' is False — the merging loop stops. Only list2 has leftovers.
Append the leftover: list1 is None (falsy), so curr.next = list2 — node(3) links to node(4). Because list2's remainder is already sorted, one pointer assignment attaches ALL of it at once.
Return dummy.next = node(1): we skip the throwaway dummy and hand back the true head. Following the links gives the merged sorted list 1 -> 2 -> 3 -> 4.

Detect Cycle in Linked List.desc: slow (the tortoise) starts at the head, node(3). The list is 3 -> 2 -> 0 -> -4, and -4's next pointer loops back to node(2) — that back-edge is the cycle we must detect.
fast (the hare) also starts at the head. If there is a cycle, fast will eventually lap slow inside it — like a faster runner on a circular track.
Loop check: fast = node(3) and fast.next = node(2) both exist, so fast can safely take a double step. Enter the loop.
slow crawls one step to node(2) at index 1.
fast jumps two steps: 3 -> 2 -> 0, landing on node(0) at index 2.
Meeting check: slow is node(2) and fast is node(0) — different node objects, so no cycle proven yet. Back to the loop condition.
Loop check: fast = node(0) and fast.next = node(-4) both exist — loop again.
slow steps to node(0) at index 2.

fast jumps twice: first to node(-4), then THROUGH the cycle edge -4 -> 2, wrapping around to node(2) at index 1. In a list with no cycle fast would hit None instead — the wrap-around is the signature of a loop.
Meeting check: slow = node(0), fast = node(2) — still different nodes. But fast is now BEHIND slow inside the cycle, closing in by one node per turn.
Loop check: fast = node(2), fast.next = node(0) — both exist, one more turn.
slow steps to node(-4) at index 3, entering the deepest point of the cycle.
fast jumps 2 -> 0 -> -4 and lands on node(-4) at index 3 — the very node slow is standing on.

Meeting check: slow == fast compares object identity for ListNodes — both reference the same node(-4), so the tortoise and hare have collided. A collision is only possible if the pointers are trapped in a loop.
Return True — a cycle exists. Total work: O(n) time (fast gains one node per turn, so it laps slow within one cycle length) and O(1) extra space — just two pointers, no visited-set.

3 Sum.desc: nums.sort() turns [-1, 0, 1, 2, -1, -4] into [-4, -1, -1, 0, 1, 2]. Sorting is what makes the two-pointer sweep possible (moving left raises the sum, moving right lowers it) and puts duplicates side by side so we can skip them.
res = [] will collect every unique triplet whose values sum to exactly 0.
Outer loop: i anchors the first number of the triplet. range(len(nums) - 2) = range(4), so i runs 0..3 — the last two slots are reserved for left and right. First anchor: i = 0, nums[0] = -4.
Duplicate-anchor check: i > 0 is False for the very first anchor, so short-circuiting stops here and we do not skip.
Set up the two-pointer window for anchor -4: left = i + 1 = 1 (value -1) and right = len(nums) - 1 = 5 (value 2). We now search for a pair summing to +4.
Compute the sum: s = nums[0] + nums[1] + nums[5] = -4 + (-1) + 2 = -3.
Branch test: s = -3 < 0 is True — the sum is too small, and because the array is sorted the ONLY way to grow it is to slide left rightward onto a bigger value.
left moves from index 1 to index 2. The new left value is -1 again (the second copy of -1 in the array).
