New sum: s = -4 + (-1) + 2 = -3 — unchanged, since nums[2] is also -1.
Still negative (-3 < 0 held on line 13), so left advances again to index 3, value 0.
New sum: s = -4 + 0 + 2 = -2. Closer to zero, but still short.
s = -2 < 0, so left advances to index 4, value 1.
New sum: s = -4 + 1 + 2 = -1. Even the two largest partners cannot lift anchor -4 to zero.
s = -1 < 0 once more, so left moves to index 5 — colliding with right.
While-check: left < right is 5 < 5 = False — the window is empty, so no triplet exists with anchor -4. Back to the outer for loop.
Next anchor: i = 1, nums[1] = -1. We now need a pair to the right of index 1 that sums to +1.
Duplicate-anchor check: nums[1] = -1 vs nums[0] = -4 — different values, so this anchor is fresh and we proceed.
Reset the window for anchor -1: left = 2 (value -1) and right = 5 (value 2).
Sum: s = -1 + (-1) + 2 = 0 — exactly zero! We found a valid triplet.
Record it: res.append([-1, -1, 2]). res is now [[-1, -1, 2]].
Left-duplicate scan: nums[left] = nums[2] = -1 vs nums[left + 1] = nums[3] = 0 — different, so there is no run of equal left values to jump over.
Right-duplicate scan: nums[right] = nums[5] = 2 vs nums[right - 1] = nums[4] = 1 — different, nothing to skip on the right either.
After recording a triplet BOTH pointers must move (keeping either one would just rebuild the same triplet): left advances to index 3, value 0.
...and right retreats to index 4, value 1. The window is now [3, 4].
Sum: s = -1 + 0 + 1 = 0 — a second zero-sum triplet with the same anchor!
Record it: res.append([-1, 0, 1]). res is now [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]].
The duplicate scans on lines 20 and 22 found nothing to skip (0 != 1 on the left, 1 != 0 on the right), so we just advance: left becomes 4.
right becomes 3 — the pointers have crossed, so this anchor's search is exhausted.
While-check: left < right is 4 < 3 = False — exit the inner loop and return to the outer for.
Next anchor: i = 2, nums[2] = -1 — the SAME value as the previous anchor at index 1.
Duplicate-anchor check: i > 0 and nums[2] = -1 == nums[1] = -1 — True! Rerunning the search from this -1 would regenerate [-1, -1, 2] and [-1, 0, 1] as duplicates.
continue — skip this anchor entirely. This one-line guard is what keeps res free of duplicate triplets without any set/hashing machinery.
Final anchor: i = 3, nums[3] = 0. (range(4) means this is the last outer iteration.)
Duplicate-anchor check: nums[3] = 0 vs nums[2] = -1 — different values, so this anchor gets a full search.
Window for anchor 0: left = 4 (value 1) and right = 5 (value 2) — only one pair is even possible.
Sum: s = 0 + 1 + 2 = 3 — too big this time.
s = 3 > 0 (the elif on line 15 fired), so we shrink the sum the only way sorting allows: right retreats to index 4, colliding with left.
While-check: left < right is 4 < 4 = False — no pair works for anchor 0, and i = 3 was the last anchor, so the outer for loop ends too.
Return res = [[-1, -1, 2], [-1, 0, 1]] — every unique triplet summing to zero, found in O(n^2) time with no duplicate filtering pass needed.

Trapping Rain Water.desc: We start the two-pointer sweep on height = [3, 0, 2, 0, 4]. left begins at index 0 and right at the last index 4 — the pointers will walk toward each other.
left_max and right_max both start at 0. They will remember the tallest wall seen so far from each side; water above a bar is limited by the SHORTER of the two side walls.
ans starts at 0 — this accumulator will collect every unit of trapped water as we visit each bar exactly once.
Loop check: left=0 < right=4, so there is still a gap between the pointers — enter the loop.
Compare the two boundary bars: height[left]=3 < height[right]=4, so the LEFT side is the limiting wall. We can safely settle the water above index 0 using left_max only.
Is height[0]=3 >= left_max=0? Yes — bar 0 is taller than any left wall seen so far, so it becomes the new wall and holds no water itself.
Update the boundary: left_max = 3. From now on, shorter bars on the left side can hold water up to height 3.
Done with index 0 — advance the left pointer inward to index 1.
Loop check again: left=1 < right=4 — pointers have not met, keep sweeping.
height[left]=0 < height[right]=4 — the left side is still the limiting wall, so process index 1 from the left.
Is height[1]=0 >= left_max=3? No — bar 1 sits BELOW the left wall of height 3, so water is trapped above it; fall into the else branch.
Trapped water above index 1 = left_max - height[1] = 3 - 0 = 3 units. ans grows from 0 to 3.
Index 1 settled — move the left pointer inward to index 2.
Iteration 3: height[left]=2 < height[right]=4, so we again process the left bar at index 2.
Is height[2]=2 >= left_max=3? No — bar 2 is 1 unit below the wall of 3, so a little water sits on top of it.
Trapped water above index 2 = 3 - 2 = 1 unit. ans grows from 3 to 4.
Advance the left pointer to index 3 — only two bars remain between the pointers.
Iteration 4: height[left]=0 < height[right]=4 — process index 3 from the left side one more time.
height[3]=0 is below left_max=3 (the check on the line above failed), so trapped water = 3 - 0 = 3 units. ans grows from 4 to the final 7.
Advance left to index 4 — it now sits on the same bar as right.
Loop check: left=4 < right=4 is False — the pointers met, every bar has been settled. Exit the loop.
Return ans = 7. Check by hand: indices 1, 2, 3 hold 3 + 1 + 3 = 7 units between the walls of height 3 and 4.

N Meetings in One Room.desc: zip pairs each start with its end: start=[1,0,3,5], end=[2,6,4,7] become meetings = [(1,2), (0,6), (3,4), (5,7)] — now each meeting is one tuple we can sort as a unit.
Greedy key move: sort by FINISH time (x[1]). Ends 2,6,4,7 reorder the tuples to [(1,2), (3,4), (0,6), (5,7)] — finishing early leaves the most room for later meetings.
count = 0 — no meetings have been scheduled into the room yet.
last_end = -1, a sentinel earlier than every real time, so the very first meeting is always allowed to start.
First tuple from the sorted list: s=1, e=2 — the meeting that finishes earliest of all.
Is s=1 > last_end=-1? Yes — the room is free before time 1, so this meeting fits.
Book it: count goes from 0 to 1. Meeting (1,2) is our first pick.
The room is now busy until time 2: last_end = 2. Any future meeting must start strictly after 2.
Second tuple: s=3, e=4 — the next-earliest finisher among the remaining meetings.
Is s=3 > last_end=2? Yes — meeting (3,4) starts after the room frees up at time 2.
Book it: count goes from 1 to 2 — two non-overlapping meetings so far.
Update the marker: last_end = 4. The room is occupied through time 4 now.
Third tuple: s=0, e=6 — this long meeting started way back at time 0.
Is s=0 > last_end=4? No — meeting (0,6) overlaps the booked (3,4), so the greedy REJECTS it. count and last_end stay unchanged; this is the skip that makes the greedy optimal.
Fourth and final tuple: s=5, e=7 — the meeting that finishes last.
Is s=5 > last_end=4? Yes — it begins after the room frees at time 4, so it fits.
Book it: count goes from 2 to the final 3 — meetings (1,2), (3,4), (5,7) all fit back-to-back.
last_end = 7, though no meetings remain — the loop is finished after this tuple.
Return count = 3: the maximum number of meetings one room can host from this schedule.

Subset Sums.desc: Initialize sums = [], the list that will collect one total per subset of arr = [2, 3]. With 2 elements there are 2^2 = 4 subsets, so we expect 4 sums.
n = len(arr) = 2. Reaching idx == 2 in the recursion means every element has received an include/exclude decision.
Kick off the recursion at the root: dfs(0, 0) — no element decided yet, running sum 0.
Inside dfs(0, 0): is idx=0 == n=2? No — element arr[0]=2 still needs its decision, so we branch.
Decision 1 for arr[0]=2: INCLUDE it. Call dfs(1, 0 + 2) = dfs(1, 2).
Inside dfs(1, 2): idx=1 != 2, so element arr[1]=3 still needs a decision on top of the running sum 2.
Decision 1 for arr[1]=3: INCLUDE it too. Call dfs(2, 2 + 3) = dfs(2, 5) — this path chose {2, 3}.
Inside dfs(2, 5): idx=2 == n=2 — every element is decided. This leaf represents the subset {2, 3}.
Record the subset's total: append 5, so sums = [5]. That is the sum of the full subset {2, 3}.
Return from dfs(2, 5) back up to dfs(1, 2), which still owes its second (exclude) branch.
Back in dfs(1, 2), Decision 2 for arr[1]=3: EXCLUDE it. Call dfs(2, 2) — this path chose only {2}.
dfs(2, 2) hits the base case (idx=2 == n) and appends 2: sums = [5, 2]. Subset {2} is recorded.
Both branches of dfs(1, 2) are done, so it returns. Back at the root dfs(0, 0), Decision 2 for arr[0]=2: EXCLUDE it. Call dfs(1, 0).
Inside dfs(1, 0): INCLUDE arr[1]=3 first. Call dfs(2, 0 + 3) = dfs(2, 3) — this path chose only {3}.
dfs(2, 3) is a leaf and appends 3: sums = [5, 2, 3]. Subset {3} is recorded.
Back in dfs(1, 0), EXCLUDE arr[1]=3 as well: call dfs(2, 0) — the empty subset {} path.
dfs(2, 0) appends 0: sums = [5, 2, 3, 0]. All 4 leaves of the decision tree have now been visited.
The recursion has fully unwound. Sort the collected sums in place: [5, 2, 3, 0] becomes [0, 2, 3, 5].

Print All Permutations.desc: Initialize ans = [] — it will collect all 3! = 6 orderings of nums = [1, 2, 3] built by swapping in place.
Start the recursion: backtrack(0) must decide which value occupies position 0.
In backtrack(0): idx=0 != len(nums)=3 — the permutation is not complete, so we try candidates for slot 0.
The loop tries every i from idx=0 to 2 as the occupant of slot 0. First candidate: i=0 (keep 1 in front).
Choose: swap nums[0] with nums[0] — a self-swap, so nums stays [1, 2, 3] with 1 fixed at slot 0.
Explore: recurse backtrack(1) to fill slot 1 while the prefix [1] stays locked.
In backtrack(1): idx=1, first candidate i=1 (keep 2 at slot 1).
Choose: self-swap nums[1] with nums[1] — nums stays [1, 2, 3], prefix is now [1, 2].
Explore: recurse backtrack(2) to fill the last slot.
In backtrack(2): only i=2 is in range — self-swap nums[2] with nums[2], nums stays [1, 2, 3].
Explore: recurse backtrack(3) — every slot has been assigned.
In backtrack(3): idx=3 == len(nums)=3 — base case, a complete permutation sits in nums.
Append a COPY nums[:] = [1, 2, 3] (a copy, because nums keeps mutating). ans = [[1,2,3]].
backtrack(3) returned; backtrack(2) unchooses with the reverse self-swap — nums is untouched at [1, 2, 3]. Its loop ends and it returns to backtrack(1).
backtrack(1) advances its loop to i=2: try value nums[2]=3 in slot 1 instead of 2.
Choose: swap nums[1] and nums[2] — nums becomes [1, 3, 2]; prefix is now [1, 3].
Explore: recurse backtrack(2); it self-swaps slot 2 and calls backtrack(3), reaching the base case.
Base case appends nums[:] = [1, 3, 2]. ans = [[1,2,3], [1,3,2]] — both permutations starting with 1 are done.
Unchoose: after backtrack(2)'s no-op restore, backtrack(1) swaps nums[1] and nums[2] BACK — nums returns to [1, 2, 3]. This undo is what makes the next branch start clean.
backtrack(1) returned; backtrack(0) unchooses its i=0 self-swap — nums still [1, 2, 3], ready for a new slot-0 candidate.
backtrack(0) advances to i=1: put value nums[1]=2 into slot 0.
Choose: swap nums[0] and nums[1] — nums becomes [2, 1, 3]; every permutation in this branch starts with 2.
Explore: recurse backtrack(1) over the suffix [1, 3] exactly as before.
The first leaf of this branch appends [2, 1, 3] — ans now holds 3 permutations.
After unwinding, backtrack(1) swaps slots 1 and 2 giving nums = [2, 3, 1], recurses, and the base case appends it — ans holds 4 permutations.
Unchoose cascade: backtrack(1) restores nums to [2, 1, 3], returns; then backtrack(0) swaps nums[0] and nums[1] back — nums = [1, 2, 3] again.
backtrack(0) advances to its last candidate i=2: put value nums[2]=3 into slot 0.
Choose: swap nums[0] and nums[2] — nums becomes [3, 2, 1]; this final branch generates permutations starting with 3.
backtrack(1)'s first leaf appends [3, 2, 1] — ans holds 5 permutations.
backtrack(1) then swaps slots 1 and 2 (nums = [3, 1, 2]) and its leaf appends the 6th and final permutation.
Final unchoose cascade: backtrack(1) restores [3, 2, 1], then backtrack(0) swaps nums[0] and nums[2] back — nums ends as the original [1, 2, 3].
backtrack(0)'s loop is exhausted — return ans with all 6 permutations of [1, 2, 3].

N Queens.desc: Solve n=4. ans = [] will collect every complete board; for a 4x4 board there are exactly 2 valid arrangements to find.
Build a 4x4 board filled with '.', meaning every cell is currently empty.
cols = set() — a queen in column c makes the whole column unusable, and set membership checks are O(1).
diag1 (keys r-c) and diag2 (keys r+c) are also empty sets: every cell on the same ↘ diagonal shares r-c, every cell on the same ↗ diagonal shares r+c.
Start the search: backtrack(0) — place one queen per row, starting with row 0.
Row 0: try each column left to right. First candidate c=0.
Safety check for (0,0): col 0 not in cols, r-c=0 not in diag1, r+c=0 not in diag2 — all three sets are empty, so the cell is safe.
Choose: place a queen at (0,0) — board[0][0] becomes 'Q'.
Mark the threats: cols={0}, diag1 gets 0-0=0, diag2 gets 0+0=0. Column 0 and both diagonals through (0,0) are now blocked.
Explore: recurse backtrack(1) to place a queen somewhere in row 1.
Row 1: c=0 fails (0 in cols) and c=1 fails (r-c = 1-1 = 0 is in diag1 — same ↘ diagonal as the queen). Both cells are skipped by continue.
c=2 passes every check (2 not in cols, 1-2=-1 not in diag1, 1+2=3 not in diag2) — place a queen at (1,2).
Explore: recurse backtrack(2) with queens at (0,0) and (1,2).
Row 2 is a DEAD END: c=0 in cols, c=1 has r+c=3 in diag2, c=2 in cols, c=3 has r-c=-1 in diag1. The loop ends with nothing placed and backtrack(2) returns.
Unchoose in backtrack(1): remove the queen from (1,2) — board[1][2] back to '.', and 2, -1, 3 leave the three sets. Row 1 continues with c=3.
Row 1, c=3 is safe (3 not in cols, 1-3=-2 not in diag1, 1+3=4 not in diag2) — place a queen at (1,3).
Explore: recurse backtrack(2) again, now with queens at (0,0) and (1,3).
Row 2: c=0 is in cols, but c=1 is safe (1 not in cols, 2-1=1 not in diag1, 2+1=3 not in diag2) — place a queen at (2,1).
backtrack(3) finds row 3 completely blocked: c=0, c=1, c=3 are in cols and c=2 has r-c = 3-2 = 1 in diag1. Another dead end — backtrack(3) returns empty-handed.
Unchoose (2,1). backtrack(2) then tries c=2 (blocked: 2-2=0 in diag1) and c=3 (blocked: in cols) — row 2 is exhausted, so backtrack(2) returns too.
Unchoose (1,3) — row 1 has no columns left either, so backtrack(1) returns. The whole subtree under the (0,0) queen produced NO solution.
Unchoose (0,0) in backtrack(0): the board is empty again and all sets are cleared. Row 0 moves on to c=1.
Row 0, c=1 is trivially safe on the empty board — place a queen at (0,1). cols={1}, diag1={-1}, diag2={1}.
Explore: recurse backtrack(1) under the (0,1) queen.
Row 1: c=0 fails (r+c = 1+0 = 1 is in diag2), c=1 is in cols, c=2 fails (r-c = 1-2 = -1 in diag1). Three skips in a row.
Row 1, c=3 is safe — place a queen at (1,3). cols={1, 3}, diag1={-1, -2}, diag2={1, 4}.
backtrack(2), row 2: c=0 passes every check (0 not in cols, 2-0=2 not in diag1, 2+0=2 not in diag2) — place a queen at (2,0).
backtrack(3), row 3: c=0 and c=1 are in cols, but c=2 is safe (3-2=1 not in diag1, 3+2=5 not in diag2) — place the 4th queen at (3,2).
Explore: recurse backtrack(4) — we are past the last row.
Base case: r=4 == n=4 — all four rows hold a queen and no two attack each other.
Join each row into a string and record solution #1: ['.Q..', '...Q', 'Q...', '..Q.'].

The search keeps unchoosing and exploring: the (0,1) subtree yields nothing more, c=2 in row 0 leads (by the mirrored dead-end/backtrack dance) to queens at (0,2), (1,0), (2,3), (3,1) — solution #2 is appended: ['..Q.', 'Q...', '...Q', '.Q..'].
Row 0's last candidate c=3 mirrors the failed c=0 subtree, so nothing more is found. Every queen has been unchosen (board back to all dots) and we return ans with exactly 2 solutions.

Search in Rotated Sorted Array.desc: Initialize the search window over the whole array: low = 0 and high = len(nums) - 1 = 6. Input is nums = [4, 5, 6, 7, 0, 1, 2] (sorted then rotated at index 4) and target = 0.
Loop check: is low <= high? 0 <= 6 is True, so the search window [0..6] is non-empty and we enter the loop.
Compute the midpoint: mid = 0 + (6 - 0) // 2 = 3. This overflow-safe form is equivalent to (low + high) // 2 in Python.
Is nums[mid] the target? nums[3] = 7 and target = 0, so no match — we must decide which half to discard.
Which half is sorted? nums[low] = 4 <= nums[mid] = 7, so the LEFT half [4, 5, 6, 7] is the properly sorted one (the rotation point is to the right of mid).
Does target = 0 lie inside the sorted left half? We need 4 <= 0 < 7; but 0 < 4, so the target CANNOT be in [4, 5, 6, 7] — it must be in the right half.
Discard the left half: low = mid + 1 = 4. The search window shrinks to indices [4..6], i.e. values [0, 1, 2].
Second loop check: 4 <= 6 is True, so we keep searching inside the window [4..6].
New midpoint: mid = 4 + (6 - 4) // 2 = 5. nums[5] = 1 is the value we will inspect next.
Is nums[mid] the target? nums[5] = 1 and target = 0 — still no match, so we classify the halves again.
Which half is sorted now? nums[low] = nums[4] = 0 <= nums[mid] = 1, so the left half [0, 1] of the current window is sorted.
Range check on the sorted left half: is 0 <= target = 0 < 1 true? Yes! The target must live in indices [4..4], so we go left.
Discard the right part: high = mid - 1 = 4. The window collapses to the single index [4..4].
Third loop check: 4 <= 4 is True — one candidate index remains, so we examine it.
Midpoint of a one-element window: mid = 4 + (4 - 4) // 2 = 4, pointing at nums[4] = 0.
Match test: nums[4] = 0 equals target = 0 — we found the target after only 3 probes instead of scanning all 7 elements.
Return mid = 4: the index of target 0 in the rotated array. Total work: O(log n) — 3 iterations for 7 elements.

Balanced Parentheses.desc: Start with an empty stack. It will hold every opening bracket that is still waiting for its closing partner. Input string: s = "({})".
Build the lookup table mapping each CLOSING bracket to the opening bracket it must match: ')' needs '(', '}' needs '{', ']' needs '['.
Begin scanning the string left to right. First character: char = '(' (index 0 of "({})").
Is '(' a key in mapping? The keys are only the closers ')', '}', ']' — so no: '(' is an OPENING bracket and takes the else branch.
Push the opener '(' onto the stack — it now waits for a future ')'. Stack becomes ['('].
Next character from the loop: char = '{' (index 1). The stack still remembers the pending '('.
Is '{' in mapping? No — it is another opening bracket, so again we go to the else branch to push it.
Push '{' on top of '('. Stack is now ['(', '{'] — note the most recent opener sits on top, exactly the one that must close first.
Next character: char = '}' (index 2). This is a closing bracket, so a match test is coming.
Is '}' in mapping? Yes — '}' is a closer, so we must check it against the most recent unmatched opener (the stack top).
The stack is non-empty, so pop its top: top_element = '{'. Stack shrinks back to ['(']. (If the stack were empty we would use dummy '#' to force a failure.)
Match check: mapping['}'] = '{' and top_element = '{' — they are equal, so this pair is balanced and we do NOT return False; continue scanning.
Final character: char = ')' (index 3). One opener '(' is still waiting on the stack.
Is ')' in mapping? Yes — another closer, so we compare it with the current stack top.
Pop the top: top_element = '('. The stack is now empty [] — every opener has been claimed by a closer.
Match check: mapping[')'] = '(' equals top_element = '(' — the outermost pair also matches, so we survive the last iteration.
The for loop has consumed all 4 characters of "({})" — no more input, so execution falls through to the final return.
Final verdict: len(stack) == 0 is True (no unmatched openers remain), so isValid returns True — "({})" is balanced.

Inorder Traversal.desc: Initialize ans = [], the list that will collect node values in sorted left-root-right order. Input tree (level order): [2, 1, 3] — root 2 with left child 1 and right child 3.
Define the recursive helper dfs(node). It closes over ans, so every recursive call appends into the same shared list.
Kick off the recursion from the top: call dfs(root), where root is the node with value 2. Call stack: [dfs(2)].
Inside dfs(2): node is the real node 2, so 'not node' is False — we do not return early and proceed to the left subtree.
Go LEFT first: dfs(2) calls dfs(node.left) = dfs(1). Node 2 is paused; it will only be visited after its whole left subtree is done. Call stack: [dfs(2), dfs(1)].
Inside dfs(1): node 1 exists, so we skip the early return and dive further left.
Go LEFT from node 1: dfs(1) calls dfs(node.left) = dfs(None) — node 1 is a leaf, its left child is None. Call stack: [dfs(2), dfs(1), dfs(None)].
Base case hit: node is None, so 'not node' is True and dfs(None) returns immediately — an empty subtree contributes nothing.
Back in dfs(1): its left subtree is finished, so we VISIT the root of this call — append 1. ans becomes [1].
Go RIGHT from node 1: dfs(1) calls dfs(node.right) = dfs(None) — the leaf has no right child either.
Base case again: node is None, return immediately. dfs(1) has now fully finished (left, visit, right) and returns control to dfs(2).
Back in dfs(2): the entire left subtree {1} is done, so we VISIT root 2 — append 2. ans becomes [1, 2]. Notice 1 came before 2, exactly the inorder promise.
Go RIGHT from the root: dfs(2) calls dfs(node.right) = dfs(3). Call stack: [dfs(2), dfs(3)].
Inside dfs(3): node 3 exists, so no early return — first its (empty) left subtree must be explored.
Go LEFT from node 3: dfs(3) calls dfs(None) since the leaf 3 has no left child.
Base case: node is None, return at once — nothing to the left of 3.
Back in dfs(3): left side done, VISIT node 3 — append 3. ans becomes [1, 2, 3].
Go RIGHT from node 3: dfs(3) calls dfs(None) — no right child. This is the last recursive call.
Final base case: node is None, return. dfs(3) finishes, then dfs(2) finishes — the whole call stack unwinds back to inorderTraversal.
All recursion complete: return ans = [1, 2, 3] — left subtree (1), root (2), right subtree (3), the sorted inorder sequence.

Validate BST.desc: Kick off the recursion: check(node=5, low=-inf, high=inf). The root may hold any value at all. Tree is [5,1,4,null,null,3,6].
node 5 is not None, so we skip the empty-subtree base case and actually test it.
Window test for the root: -inf < 5 < inf holds, so 5 fits its (unrestricted) window.
Recurse into the LEFT child: check(node=1, low=-inf, high=5). Going left, the parent value 5 becomes the new upper bound.
node 1 is not None — test it against its inherited window (-inf, 5).
Window test: -inf < 1 < 5 holds — 1 is a legal left child of 5.
Recurse into 1's left child: check(None, -inf, 1) — node 1 has no left child.
node is None: an empty subtree cannot violate anything, so return True.
Left side of 1 was fine; now the right child: check(None, 1, 5) — node 1 has no right child either.
None again: return True. Both of node 1's subtrees are (trivially) valid.
Back at node 1, the return computes True and True = True — 1's whole subtree is a valid BST, and this True flows up to the root's call.
Back at the root: the left half passed, so evaluate the RIGHT child: check(node=4, low=5, high=inf). Going right, 5 becomes the new LOWER bound.
node 4 is not None — it must now prove it fits the window (5, inf).
Window test: we need 5 < 4 < inf, but 5 < 4 is FALSE — node 4 sits in the root's right subtree yet is smaller than 5.
Violation found: return False from check(4, 5, inf). Note we never even looked at 4's children (3 and 6) — one bad node is enough.
Back at the root's return: True (left) and False (right) = False. The root's call returns False.
check(root, -inf, inf) came back False, so is_valid_bst returns False — the tree is NOT a valid BST.

Clone Linked List with Random Pointer.desc: head is node 1, so the list is not empty — we skip the early return and start cloning. Randoms in the input: 1's random is node 3, 2's random is node 1, 3's random is None.
Phase 1 begins: curr = head, standing on original node 1. We will weave a clone directly after every original node.
Loop check: curr is node 1 (not None), so we enter the weaving loop for the first iteration.
Create clone 1' = Node(1): a brand-new object copying only the value 1. Its next and random are still None.
clone.next = curr.next: 1' now points at original node 2, so the rest of the list is not lost when we rewire.
curr.next = clone: original 1 now points at its own clone. The chain reads 1 -> 1' -> 2 -> 3 — the clone is woven in.
curr = clone.next jumps OVER the clone 1' and lands on original node 2 — this is how we avoid ever cloning a clone.
Second iteration: create clone 2' = Node(2) for the original node 2.
After the two pointer assignments, 2' is woven in right after 2: the chain is now 1 -> 1' -> 2 -> 2' -> 3.
curr = clone.next skips over 2' and reaches the last original node, 3.
Third iteration weaves 3' after 3. Every original now has its clone right behind it: 1 -> 1' -> 2 -> 2' -> 3 -> 3'.
clone.next is None (3' is the tail), so curr becomes None — there are no more originals to clone.
Loop check fails: curr is None. Phase 1 is complete — this interleaved layout will now play the role of the hash map.
Phase 2: reset curr to head (original node 1) so we can wire the random pointer of every clone.
Original 1's random points at original node 3 — it is not None, so clone 1' needs its random set.
The magic line: curr.next is 1' and curr.random.next is node 3's immediate neighbour — its own clone 3'. So 1'.random = 3', found in O(1) with no map at all.
curr = curr.next.next skips our clone 1' and lands on the next ORIGINAL node, 2.
Original 2's random is original node 1 — again not None, so clone 2' gets its random next.
2'.random = curr.random.next = node 1's next = 1'. Clone randoms so far: {1'->3', 2'->1'}.
Skip clone 2'; curr moves to the last original node, 3.
Original 3's random is None — the condition is False, so we copy nothing and 3'.random correctly stays None.
curr = curr.next.next: 3' is the tail so its next is None — curr becomes None and the wiring pass ends.
Loop check fails (curr is None). Every clone's random is wired: {1'->3', 2'->1', 3'->None} — mirroring the original perfectly.
Phase 3: new_head = head.next = 1'. We grab the answer's head BEFORE unweaving, so it can never be lost.
curr = head (original node 1). Now we separate the two interleaved chains: originals restored, clones extracted.
clone = curr.next grabs 1', the clone woven right after original node 1.
curr.next = clone.next: original 1 points at original 2 again — 1' is cut out of the original chain.
clone.next (original node 2) is truthy, so 1'.next = 2.next = 2': the clones begin forming their own chain.
curr = curr.next moves to original node 2 so we can unweave the next original/clone pair.
Second iteration: clone = curr.next = 2', the clone sitting right after original node 2.
Original 2's next is restored to original node 3 — the original chain is now 1 -> 2 -> 3 up to here.
2'.next = 3.next = 3' — the clone chain grows to 1' -> 2' -> 3'.
curr = curr.next steps to original node 3, the final pair left to unweave.
Final iteration: clone = curr.next = 3', the last clone in the weave.
curr.next = clone.next = None: original node 3 becomes the tail again. The ORIGINAL list is now fully restored to 1 -> 2 -> 3.
clone.next is None here, so the conditional expression assigns None: 3' stays the tail of the clone chain.
curr = curr.next = None — the while condition will fail next, so the unweaving loop is finished.
Return new_head = 1'. The answer is 1' -> 2' -> 3' with randoms 1'->3', 2'->1', 3'->None — a fully independent deep copy, while the original 1 -> 2 -> 3 is untouched.

Preorder Traversal.desc: Initialize result = [], the list that will collect node values in Root -> Left -> Right order. Our tree: root 1, children 2 and 3, and 4, 5 under node 2.
root is node 1, so the tree is not empty — the early-return guard is skipped and we proceed to set up the stack.
Seed the stack with the root: stack = [1]. The stack always holds nodes whose subtrees still await processing.
Loop check: the stack holds [1], which is non-empty, so we enter the main loop.
Pop the top of the stack: node = 1, and the stack becomes empty for the moment.
Visit node 1 IMMEDIATELY by appending its value: result = [1]. Root before children — that is exactly what makes this preorder.
Node 1 has a right child (3), so we push it FIRST — it must wait underneath until the entire left subtree is finished. stack = [3].
Node 1 also has a left child (2); pushed LAST, it sits on top of the stack and will therefore pop FIRST. stack = [3, 2].
Loop check again: stack = [3, 2] is non-empty, so we continue with a second iteration.
Pop the top: node = 2 — the LEFT child surfaces before the right one, thanks to our push order. stack = [3].
Visit node 2: result = [1, 2]. We are now descending into the left subtree while 3 waits at the bottom of the stack.
Node 2's right child 5 is pushed first: stack = [3, 5]. It will wait until 2's left side is done.
Node 2's left child 4 goes on top: stack = [3, 5, 4]. Notice the stack now mirrors 'work owed': 4 first, then 5, then 3.
Third iteration: pop node = 4, the deepest-left node. stack = [3, 5].
Visit node 4: result = [1, 2, 4]. This matches preorder on paper: 1, 2, 4 so far.
Node 4 is a leaf: node.right is None, so the condition is False and nothing is pushed.
node.left is None as well — the stack stays [3, 5]. Node 4's subtree is completely finished.
Pop node = 5: with 2's left side done, its right child surfaces next. stack = [3].
Visit node 5: result = [1, 2, 4, 5]. The entire subtree rooted at 2 has now been printed.
Node 5 is also a leaf — no right child, so nothing to push here.
Pop node = 3 — the root's right child, deferred ever since step 7, finally gets its turn. stack = [].
Visit node 3: result = [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]. Every node has now been visited exactly once.
Loop check: the stack is empty — no subtree is owed a visit anymore, so the loop terminates.
Return result = [1, 2, 4, 5, 3]: root first, then the whole left subtree (2, 4, 5), then the right subtree (3). Preorder complete.

Search in BST.desc: Call searchBST(root=node 8, val=6). The BST is 8 with left child 3 and right child 10; node 3 has children 1 and 6.
Base case check: root is not None, and root.val = 8 which is not equal to val = 6, so the condition is False and we do not return here.
Compare val < root.val: 6 < 8 is True. Because it is a BST, every value smaller than 8 lives in the left subtree, so the right subtree (10, 14) can be thrown away entirely.
Return searchBST(root.left, 6) — we recurse into node 3. This is the whole trick: one comparison halves the search space.
New call frame begins with root = node 3, val = 6. The subtree under 3 is 1 on the left and 6 on the right.
Base case again: node 3 exists and 3 != 6, so we keep descending rather than returning.
Compare 6 < 3 — this is False, so the target cannot be in node 3's left subtree (which only holds the value 1).
The else branch is taken because 6 is greater than 3; larger keys always sit to the right in a BST.
Return searchBST(root.right, 6) — recurse into node 6, the right child of 3.
Third call frame starts with root = node 6, val = 6. This node has children 4 and 7.
Base case check: root.val = 6 equals val = 6, so the OR condition is True — we found the node we were looking for.
Return root, the node holding 6. Note we return the whole node, so the caller also gets its subtree [6, 4, 7], not just the value.
Frame 2 (root = 3) receives node 6 from its recursive call and immediately returns that same node upward — recursion only passes the answer along.
Frame 1 (root = 8) receives node 6 and returns it as the final answer. Total work: 3 comparisons for a tree of 7 nodes — O(height).

BFS Traversal.desc: Start bfsOfGraph with V = 5 and adj = [[1,2],[0,3],[0,4],[1],[2]]. So 0 is joined to 1 and 2; 1 is joined to 3; 2 is joined to 4.
bfs = [] — this list will collect vertices in the order we dequeue them, and it is what we finally return.
visited = [False, False, False, False, False]. Shown as 0/1 below. Without this flag a cycle would make us loop forever.
queue = deque([0]) — a FIFO queue seeded with the source vertex 0. FIFO is exactly what makes the traversal go level by level.
visited[0] = True. Critical: we mark on ENQUEUE, not on dequeue, so vertex 0 can never be pushed a second time.
while queue: the queue holds [0], which is truthy, so we enter the main loop.
node = queue.popleft() takes 0 off the FRONT of the queue. The queue is now empty.
bfs.append(0) records vertex 0 as fully visited. bfs = [0].
Loop over adj[0] = [1, 2]. First neighbor is 1.
visited[1] is False, so `not visited[1]` is True — vertex 1 is brand new and we take the body of the if.
visited[1] = True. Mark it right now so that when vertex 2 later also sees 1 as a neighbour, it will skip it.
queue.append(1) pushes 1 to the BACK. queue = [1].
Next neighbour of 0 is 2.
visited[2] is still False, so vertex 2 has not been seen — enter the if body.
visited[2] = True — vertex 2 is claimed.
queue.append(2). queue = [1, 2] — both level-1 vertices are queued, and adj[0] is exhausted.
Back at the while check: queue = [1, 2] is non-empty, so we go around again.
node = queue.popleft() = 1 (the oldest entry). queue = [2].
bfs.append(1) → bfs = [0, 1].
Scan adj[1] = [0, 3]. First neighbour is 0.
visited[0] is True, so `not visited[0]` is False — we skip 0. This is the guard that stops us bouncing back to the source forever.
Next neighbour of 1 is 3.
visited[3] was False, so we set visited[3] = True.
queue.append(3) → queue = [2, 3]. Notice 3 sits BEHIND 2, so the whole of level 1 finishes before level 2 starts.
queue = [2, 3] is non-empty; loop again.
node = queue.popleft() = 2. queue = [3].
bfs.append(2) → bfs = [0, 1, 2].
adj[2] = [0, 4]. Neighbour 0 has visited[0] = True, so it is skipped immediately.
Neighbour 4 is unvisited, so visited[4] = True.
queue.append(4) → queue = [3, 4]. Every one of the 5 vertices has now been discovered.
node = queue.popleft() = 3. queue = [4].
bfs.append(3) → bfs = [0, 1, 2, 3].
adj[3] = [1] and visited[1] is True, so nothing is enqueued from vertex 3.
node = queue.popleft() = 4. queue is now empty.
bfs.append(4) → bfs = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4].
adj[4] = [2], and visited[2] is True, so we enqueue nothing. The queue stays empty.
while queue: the deque is empty, which is falsy, so the loop ends. Every vertex was pushed and popped exactly once.
return bfs = [0, 1, 2, 3, 4] — the breadth-first order: source 0, then its neighbours 1 and 2, then their neighbours 3 and 4.

Implement Trie.desc: Client code runs trie = Trie(). Python enters Trie.__init__ to build an empty trie object.
self.root = TrieNode() creates the single sentinel root node. The root itself stores no character — it is just the starting point of every word.
Inside TrieNode.__init__ for that root node.
self.children = {} — an empty dict mapping a character to the child node reached by that character. A dict lookup is O(1), so each step down the trie is O(1).
self.is_word = False. The root is not the end of any word yet. This flag is what separates a stored word from a mere prefix.
Operation 1: trie.insert('cat').
curr = self.root — we always start walking from the root.
Loop over 'cat'; the first character is 'c'.
'c' not in root.children (which is {}) is True — this edge does not exist yet.
root.children['c'] = TrieNode() creates the child for 'c'. The trie is now root -> c.
curr = curr.children['c'] — step down onto the 'c' node. curr.children is {} and curr.is_word is False.
Next character of 'cat' is 'a'.
'a' is not a child of node('c'), so we create it: trie is now root -> c -> a.
curr moves down to node('a'). Path so far is 'ca'.
Final character of 'cat' is 't'.
't' is missing from node('a').children, so we create node('t'): trie is root -> c -> a -> t.
curr moves down to node('t'). The loop over 'cat' is now finished.
curr.is_word = True on node('t'). THIS is what records that 'cat' is a complete stored word and not just a path. Insert cost was 3 steps = O(len(word)).
Operation 2: trie.search('cat') — we expect True.
curr = self.root, back to the top of the trie.
First character of 'cat' is 'c'.
'c' IS in root.children, so the early-exit if is False and we do not return False.
curr = node('c'). Search never creates nodes — it only walks existing ones.
Character 'a' is found under node('c'), so curr moves to node('a'). Path so far is 'ca'.
Character 't' is found under node('a'), so curr moves to node('t'). The whole word has been walked.
return curr.is_word. node('t').is_word is True, so search('cat') returns True.
Operation 3: trie.search('ca') — this shows why the is_word flag matters.
Both 'c' and 'a' exist, so the loop walks root -> c -> a and finishes with curr = node('a').
return curr.is_word — node('a').is_word is False because we never inserted the word 'ca'. So search('ca') returns False even though the path exists.
Operation 4: trie.startsWith('ca') — the same walk, but a different verdict.
The loop walks 'c' then 'a' successfully; curr ends on node('a'). No character was ever missing.
return True — startsWith ignores is_word entirely; reaching the end of the prefix path is enough. So 'ca' is a prefix (of 'cat') even though it is not a word.
Operation 5: trie.search('dog') — a word that shares no prefix with anything stored.
First character of 'dog' is 'd'.
'd' not in root.children ({'c'}) is True — the very first edge is missing.
return False immediately, after inspecting just 1 character. That early exit is the trie's advantage over scanning a list of words.
